docs.text: The admin ¶ The optional hinoki.admin module gives staff a list, search, create, edit, bulk delete and a dashboard for your models, with the same access policies and CSRF protection as the rest of the app. It is included in the framework package; nothing is mounted unless you ask, and importing it never touches a database. The following excerpt follows the Blog admin module . The PostAdmin class configures the model; build_admin() creates the cookie-authenticated editors policy, registers the class and returns the Admin . The app factory mounts that API. The snippet shows the relevant imports and function context; consult the linked module for the complete cookie-auth implementation. from blog.adminsite import CookieAuth from blog.models import Post from blog.security import WRITE from hinoki import Access from hinoki.admin import Admin , ModelAdmin , Badge , Tab , Fieldset class PostAdmin ( ModelAdmin [ Post ]): label = "Posts" columns = ( "title" , "published" , "author_id" , "created_at" ) search = ( "title" ,) ordering = ( "-created_at" , "-id" ) bulk_delete = True readonly = ( "created_at" ,) assign = { "author_id" : lambda principal : principal . user . id } # set by the server badges = { "published" : { True : Badge ( "Published" , "ok" ), False : Badge ( "Draft" , "warn" )}} tabs = ( Tab ( "Published" , { "published" : True }), Tab ( "Drafts" , { "published" : False })) fieldsets = ( Fieldset ( "Organization" , ( "author_id" , "published" )),) def build_admin ( secret : str , theme : str = "studio" ) -> Admin : editors = Access ( auth = CookieAuth (), permissions = [ WRITE ]) admin = Admin ( access = editors , secret = secret , prefix = "/admin" , theme = theme , site = "Blog Studio" , ) admin . register ( Post , PostAdmin , slug = "posts" ) return admin search names the columns the list's search box and the global search look in: a row matches when any of them contains the typed text, compared case-insensitively as text (so a number or date column matches on its printed form). Without search the box is inert. Row visibility, field assignment and which columns are shown are decided in the admin class; hooks ( queryset , can , display , stats , check , save , remove ) override what you need. queryset(principal) is the primary way to decide which rows a caller sees: counts and page numbers come from it. can(principal, "view", row) is also applied row by row to what a list page or the dashboard fetched, so a denied row is not shown; it can only trim the page already fetched, so a page may hold fewer rows than per_page and the totals still count the queryset. Mass assignment, excluded columns and out-of-scope rows are refused by the framework, and every form carries a signed CSRF token bound to the signed-in subject. Datetime fields in the admin use the including app's settings.timezone (UTC when the app has no built-in settings). Forms display stored instants in that timezone and interpret edited datetime-local values there before saving them as UTC-aware datetimes. Times that do not exist or occur twice during a daylight-saving clock change are rejected for correction. API datetimes with offsets remain absolute instants; utc_today() continues to use UTC. Bulk actions ¶ Add an async handler and declare it with BulkAction on the model admin. The list shows its action button after rows are selected: from typing import Any from hinoki import Caller from hinoki.admin import BulkAction , ModelAdmin async def publish ( posts : tuple [ Post , ... ], _principal : Caller [ Any ]) -> None : await Post . filter ( id__in = [ post . id for post in posts ]) . aupdate ( { "published" : True } ) class PostAdmin ( ModelAdmin [ Post ]): bulk_actions = ( BulkAction ( name = "publish" , label = "Publish selected" , confirm = "Publish the selected posts?" , handler = publish , ), ) The action name is also the permission checked by ModelAdmin.can(principal, name, row) . Hinoki checks model access before showing the button and checks every selected row against the scoped queryset and row permission both before confirmation and before execution. The confirmation includes the selected row count. If any selected row is unavailable or denied, the whole action is refused. The handler receives only the selected rows and the caller. During execution, Hinoki locks the selected model rows until the action transaction finishes, so another transaction cannot change their row-level authorization fields between the check and the handler's writes. Handlers should still apply their domain conditions to writes, especially when those conditions involve related records or external state. Each action requires confirmation and runs inside the admin write transaction. A failure rolls back the selected work; successful actions redirect to the list with a notice. Actions accept at most 200 distinct rows. bulk_delete = True adds the built-in delete action. Four styles, each with light and dark ¶ Each theme sets navigation, list presentation, typography and color. All four use the same components and provide light and dark modes; the system preference selects the initial mode, and the toggle overrides it. Style Navigation List Edit Look Studio (default) sidebar cards with a table drawer beside the list soft violet, rounded Console horizontal top bar dense monospaced grid drawer neon cyan / teal, square Paper quiet text index, centred column document rows its own page serif type, terracotta Bento dark icon rail (bottom tab bar on phones) a grid of cards its own page hard ink outlines and offset shadows, bold type, solid colour tiles, yellow accent Studio Console Paper Bento Pick one with Admin(theme="bento") , or build your own: a Theme is a set of --hn-* design tokens for the two schemes plus a layout ( sidebar , topbar , index , rail ) and a list_style ( table , rows , cards ). The text and surface colour pairs of every built-in theme are tested against WCAG AA contrast. Bento's pages were checked in Chromium and Firefox at 1440, 390, 360 and 320 px; WebKit was not run. Mounting under a prefix ¶ Admin(prefix="/admin") sets the admin's own path. The admin can also be included under a Mount ( Hinoki(include=[Mount("/ops", admin.api())]) ): its links, assets and the CSRF cookie path then use /ops/admin , so the pages work at the mounted address.

docs.text: Building a backend with an AI agent and Hinoki ¶ What exists today (2026-11-13), what it guarantees, and what it does not. 1. Start a project an agent can work in ¶ uv run hinoki new shop --dir ~/projects # lower-case letters and digits only cd ~/projects/shop && uv sync && uv run pytest The generated project contains a health route, rules that are already on ( HNK-ACC-001 actions name an access policy, HNK-TXN-001 writes use a transaction, HNK-SCH-001 fields such as password_hash never appear in a response schema), AGENTS.md (commands, conventions, and where the agent's authority ends), CLAUDE.md (a pointer to it), .mcp.json (starts the read-only development MCP) and hinoki-rules.toml (the owner's exceptions). The project's own tests pass and hinoki check exits 0; the test suite of this repository generates a project and runs both on every change. 2. What the agent gets ¶ AGENTS.md : the same conventions this repository uses: public unless protected on purpose, transaction=True for writes, Schema classes in responses, no model responses, explicit relation loading, create from a Schema with server values winning, migrations as reviewed SQL. The development MCP ( hinoki mcp , read only): inspect_project (the real registry), list_rules , explain_action (signature, Schema types, access, diagnostics for one action), check_project (rule diagnostics with stable IDs and locations) explain_error (what a validation or HTTP error code means and how to fix it) and propose_model (source text for a model, its In/Patch/Out Schema classes and CRUD actions from a field list; returned, never written). The tools never write code, rules or waivers. Optional run_scenario , off by default: hinoki mcp --scenarios read lets the agent send GET/HEAD/OPTIONS/QUERY requests to the app in-process and see status and body; --scenarios write allows any method. It runs the real handlers and the app's lifespan even in read mode (a GET handler may write), so it is not annotated read-only and should only face a disposable database. A failed startup is reported without its message (which may hold a connection string); the details go to the server's stderr. Only the owner can switch it on; the agent cannot. Errors that say what to do : validation errors list every problem with its path and a stable code; explain_error maps a code to its meaning and fix; a registration error names the action and parameter. See the development MCP guide for tool arguments, result shapes and the effectful scenario option. 3. The loop ¶ The agent asks the MCP for the project ( inspect_project ) to read the registered routes and models. It makes a small change (a model, a Schema , an action). It runs pytest , ruff , mypy and hinoki check . A rule violation is a stable ID, a location and an explanation. The fix is to change the code. Waivers are the owner's decision : hinoki-rules.toml is read by the tools, never written, and a waiver needs a reason, an owner and a bounded target. An agent that edits it to pass a check is violating AGENTS.md ; the framework cannot stop someone with write access, it makes the change visible in review (put the file under CODEOWNERS). 4. Limits (what this does not do) ¶ The development MCP describes and checks a project; to let an agent use a running app, publish selected actions with hinoki.mcpapp.expose_as_mcp (allowlist, caller's own credentials, reads by default; see Application MCP ). The development MCP was exercised with the official mcp Python client ( tests/mcpclient/verify.py : initialize, tools/list , tools/call ); other clients are untested. propose_model is a starting point: it can scope rows to an owner ( owner= ), paginates the list and takes unique_together , but business rules, state transitions and relations beyond the owner are yours to write. Rules decide declarations, not what a function body does; static import rules read the project's own files and report dynamic imports as unverifiable. The guide was verified twice: by generating a project and running its tests and check , and by having a fresh agent add an owner-scoped Bookmark resource from the generated AGENTS.md alone. That run found the problems now fixed (the framework path in the generated pyproject.toml , the missing test client, the database variable for check , the missing recipe, explain_error gaps, propose_model without ownership). It is one run by one agent, not a benchmark.

docs.text: Expose an application over MCP ¶ expose_as_mcp turns selected HTTP actions into tools for an MCP client. It is opt-in and uses an explicit allowlist. A call is dispatched through the app's ASGI adapter, so the action's authentication, access policy, validation and transaction still apply. from hinoki.mcpapp import expose_as_mcp mcp_routes = expose_as_mcp ( app , tools = [ "tracker.api.list_tasks" ], access = agent_access , ) app . include ( * mcp_routes ) By default, only GET , HEAD and QUERY actions are exposed; a QUERY action is declared as a read and its tool takes the request body. Set allow_writes=True only when write tools are intended and the configured access policy permits them. The allowlist must match included actions; a bad or empty selection fails during setup. The tool name, description, path/query parameters and JSON body shape come from the action's OpenAPI operation. Path values are encoded as path segments, unknown arguments are rejected, and output is bounded. The MCP route cannot expose itself as a tool. Use bearer credentials for a remote MCP client when possible. Cookie-based authentication with write tools needs particular care. The endpoint accepts JSON POST requests. Set allowed_origins to the exact browser origins when browser clients are expected; other cross-site browser requests are rejected. access is required. For an intentionally public endpoint, pass access=None, public=True explicitly. This application endpoint is distinct from hinoki mcp TARGET , the development MCP over stdio. That CLI is read-only by default; explicitly enabling --scenarios write registers effectful scenario calls that can run mutating handlers. It does not provide MCP resources, prompts, sessions or OAuth discovery.
docs.title: Application MCP

docs.text: Authentication and access policies ¶ Hinoki keeps credential parsing in an authentication provider and permission checks in an Access policy. Endpoints are public unless a policy is attached; protect each private action deliberately. Define a provider ¶ Subclass BearerAuth[User] , APIKeyAuth[User] or HeaderAuth[User] . The provider returns a Caller with a stable id, your user object and its permissions. authenticate / resolve_token may be async or synchronous; synchronous hooks run on the bounded sync executor. This example reuses the complete Blog example's user model. from blog.models import User from hinoki import BearerAuth , Caller class TokenAuth ( BearerAuth [ User ]): async def resolve_token ( self , token : str ) -> Caller [ User ] | None : user = await User . aget_or_none ( token = token ) if user is None : return None permissions = frozenset ({ "posts:write" }) if user . is_editor else frozenset () return Caller ( id = str ( user . id ), user = user , permissions = permissions , ) The Blog security module contains the same provider and its reusable policies. Absent credentials let the provider decline; invalid supplied credentials produce 401 . A valid caller without a required permission receives 403 . Attach a policy ¶ from blog.models import User from blog.security import editor from blog.schemas import PostOut from hinoki import Caller , http @http . get ( "/posts/mine" , access = editor ) async def list_my_posts ( caller : Caller [ User ]) -> list [ PostOut ]: # Replace with the application's scoped query. return [] Caller[T] is injected when annotated. Use caller.user for the application user and caller.permissions for the resolved permission set. Do not accept an owner id from untrusted input when it should come from the caller. RouteGroup can provide a default policy for a function group. An action may override it intentionally. The Actions.require_access rule can flag routes with no policy. Passwords and JWT ¶ hinoki.crypto.PasswordHasher provides Argon2id hashing and verification; JWTKey and JWTAuth issue and verify configured token algorithms. Read keys from settings.Secret fields and reveal them only when constructing the provider. Validate audience, issuer, expiry and key rotation settings for your deployment. See the crypto API reference . For JWTAuth , Rust verifies the signature and registered claims using the current key snapshot. now() and the configured issuer, audience, leeway and expiry policy are read for each verification. A request already verifying with a captured key snapshot finishes with that snapshot; a later verification observes key rotation. Rust does not turn token claims into a Caller : the application's resolve_claims hook still runs for every valid token, and remains responsible for loading or rejecting the identity and deciding its permissions. Sync, async and sync functions returning awaitables follow the normal hook execution path. Hinoki does not create users, sessions or permission rules for your application. Those remain application data and policy.

docs.title: Method and limits

docs.text: Command line ¶ The hinoki command accepts a module:attribute target for an application, factory, settings class or model module as documented by each subcommand. Targets are imported from the current project directory. Targets such as notes.main:app , tracker.app:create_app and blog.main:create_app refer to the checked-in project in examples/ . Run those commands from examples/ ; when using the repository checkout, prefix them with uv run --project .. to use the locked environment at the parent. Commands and options ¶ Command Purpose hinoki new NAME Create a starter project with settings, rules, tests and agent instructions. hinoki app list List registered apps, their model and migration modules, and dependencies without importing app code or opening a database. --format json is machine readable. hinoki app create NAME Add a registered modular app with its own models and migration package. hinoki doctor [TARGET] Summarize environment, manifest and app construction diagnostics without serving or connecting to a database. hinoki dev TARGET Run an app with reload during development. hinoki serve TARGET Run without reload, using the server settings group. hinoki check TARGET Run the application's configured rules; --rules and --package select rule and source targets. hinoki routes TARGET List every method, path, handler and access policy in path order. --path and --method filter; --format json is machine readable. Nothing is served. hinoki openapi TARGET Print or write the generated OpenAPI document, or check a JSON file for drift. Nothing is served and no database is opened. hinoki version Show the Hinoki version; --verbose includes Python, platform, native core and optional Granian details. --format json is machine readable. hinoki settings TARGET Show effective settings and their source, with secrets redacted. --dotenv and --toml select optional files. hinoki migrations ... Plan, inspect and apply project app migrations in dependency order. Legacy explicit targets remain available without a manifest. hinoki manage [TARGET] [COMMAND] Run an app-defined command with its declared module resources; a project manifest supplies the default target. hinoki shell [TARGET] Open an interactive Python shell with the app's modules and registered models. hinoki mcp TARGET Serve project context to an MCP client over stdio. Scenario tools are off by default. doctor ¶ uv run hinoki doctor uv run hinoki doctor notes.main:app --format json With no target, doctor uses project.application from hinoki.toml . If there is no manifest or default target, it reports environment checks and marks app checks as skipped. An explicit TARGET can be an app or factory. Loading it imports your Python code, so module-level code and the factory may have their own side effects. Hinoki does not start app or module lifespans, run hooks, start a server, run architecture rules, connect to a database, or write files. The report covers manifest validity, Python/native extension and optional Granian availability, route registration, configured typed settings, and in-memory OpenAPI generation. An app with no settings object reports that check as skipped; a custom non- Settings object is a warning. JSON output has schema_version: 1 and stable check IDs. Settings values and exception messages are not included. Exit status is 0 when no diagnostic failed, 1 for invalid manifest or app diagnostics, and 2 when a requested target cannot be loaded. Warnings and skipped checks remain visible. Database connectivity and applied migration state are intentionally separate: use hinoki migrations status for the live ledger and hinoki migrations plan --check for model-to-file drift. new ¶ hinoki new notes --dir . NAME is a lowercase package name containing letters and digits; it cannot be hinoki or a Python standard-library module name, because those names would shadow imports used by the generated project. --dir chooses the parent directory and defaults to the current directory. The target PATH/NAME must not exist or must be empty; nothing is overwritten, and nothing is installed or run. This repository's pre-alpha Hinoki framework is not published on PyPI; the hinoki name belongs to an unrelated legacy package. The generated pyproject.toml therefore names this repository as the source under [tool.uv.sources] : Given Source written --hinoki /path/to/checkout that checkout, editable --hinoki https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki@REV (or git+https://... ) that repository, pinned to REV when given nothing, running from a source checkout the checkout you ran it from nothing, any other installation the public repository, default branch The result is cd PATH/NAME && uv sync && uv run pytest : the project has a health route, typed settings, rules, one test that needs no database, a README.md , AGENTS.md and .mcp.json . Checkout paths and Git source values are escaped as TOML strings in the generated pyproject.toml . app ¶ The generated hinoki.toml registers the default app and its models and migrations. Add modules without moving files by creating another app: uv run hinoki app create billing This creates NAME/apps/billing/{models.py,migrations/} and registers both dotted module paths. Cross-app foreign keys require the referencing app to list the referenced app in requires in hinoki.toml ; migrations are then planned/applied in dependency order. The project registry is explicit: Hinoki does not scan arbitrary installed packages or run imports at install time. List the registered apps from the project root or any subdirectory: uv run hinoki app list uv run hinoki app list --format json The text output shows each app in dependency order with its model module, migration package and prerequisites. JSON contains the same fields under an apps key. The command only reads and validates hinoki.toml : it does not import app modules, connect to a database or start the app. Without a manifest, it prints an error and exits 2. dev and serve ¶ hinoki dev notes.main:app --host 127 .0.0.1 --port 8000 hinoki serve notes.main:app --workers 4 hinoki serve notes.main:app --server rust --workers 2 Both commands accept --host and --port ; they override settings.server.host and .port . serve also accepts --workers , overriding .workers . Both accept --server granian|rust , overriding .server (default granian ). Otherwise values come from the app's settings.AppSettings.server group. dev enables reload and runs one worker. Granian is provided by the optional server extra. --server rust runs the application on the Rust HTTP server (see Running an application for what it does and does not do). A setting that the chosen server cannot honour ( access_log with rust ; max_connections , header_read_timeout or body_read_timeout with granian ) makes the command print error: server.<name> is not supported by the <server> server and exit with status 2. A build whose native extension has no Rust server exits 2 with a message instead of falling back to Granian. With several workers the command runs a supervisor that starts one process per worker; SIGTERM or Ctrl-C stops them gracefully, and a worker that dies stops the rest and makes the command exit non-zero. check ¶ hinoki check tracker.app:create_app \ --package tracker --phase startup --format text Options: --rules MODULE:ATTRIBUTE selects a RuleSet ; the app's rules are used by default. --package PACKAGE selects a package for static import checks. Repeat it for multiple packages. Without it, the package containing the target is scanned. --phase startup|static selects a phase; the default runs both. --waivers PATH selects a waiver file; the default is hinoki-rules.toml in the current directory. --format text|json selects human-readable or versioned JSON output. --allow-effects also runs checks declared as effectful, which may access files, network or databases. Exit status is 0 when no rules fail, 1 for violations, and 2 when the target or checks cannot run. openapi ¶ hinoki openapi notes.main:app hinoki openapi notes.main:app --output openapi.json hinoki openapi notes.main:app --check openapi.json The command builds the app without serving it or opening a database; it works even when openapi_url is disabled. With no file option it prints deterministic JSON (sorted keys, two-space indentation and a trailing newline). --output FILE writes those bytes. --check FILE compares parsed JSON, so formatting differences do not count as drift. Exit status is 0 when the file matches or is written, 1 when its JSON differs, and 2 when the target cannot load or the check file is missing or invalid JSON. --output and --check cannot be used together. version ¶ hinoki version hinoki version --verbose hinoki version --verbose --format json The default prints hinoki X.Y.Z . --verbose adds the Python version, platform, native extension path and Granian version; Granian is reported as not installed when its optional package is absent. Use --format json for machine-readable output. Details the binding does not expose, including its bundled SQLite library version, are omitted rather than inferred. settings ¶ hinoki settings blog.settings:BlogSettings \ --prefix BLOG_ --dotenv .env --toml settings.toml --format json hinoki settings blog.settings:BlogSettings --example > .env.example TARGET can be a settings class or an app with typed settings. --prefix , --dotenv and --toml override sources declared by the settings class. --format text|json selects output; --example prints a .env.example with defaults and types, leaving secrets and required fields blank. Values of settings.Secret are redacted. manage ¶ hinoki manage --help hinoki manage greet Peppe Commands are declared on the app with Hinoki(commands=[...]) . Each command subclasses hinoki.management.Command , gives itself a lower-case name, and adds arguments through add_arguments(parser) . In a scaffolded project, hinoki manage lists commands and hinoki manage greet Peppe runs one; the manifest's project.application supplies the app target. Outside a registered project, use hinoki manage TARGET COMMAND . --help after a command shows its arguments. from argparse import ArgumentParser , Namespace from hinoki import Hinoki from hinoki.management import Command , CommandContext class Greet ( Command ): name = "greet" help = "print a greeting" def add_arguments ( self , parser : ArgumentParser ) -> None : parser . add_argument ( "name" , nargs = "?" , default = "world" ) def handle ( self , _context : CommandContext , args : Namespace ) -> None : print ( f "Hello, { args . name } !" ) app = Hinoki ( commands = [ Greet ]) The same example is in examples/project/app.py ; the examples manifest supplies its target when you run the command from the examples/ project directory. handle(context, args) may be synchronous or asynchronous. A sync handler runs on Hinoki's bounded executor. It can read context.settings and retrieve resources with context.get(Type) or context.find(Type) . Declare module classes in the command's requires tuple; Hinoki starts those modules and their dependencies for the command, then closes them before it exits. Other app modules are not started. A command with no requirements starts no app modules. Commands run inside the project process and can modify data. Use disposable databases when developing or testing a command that writes. A handler returns None for success or an exit code from 0 through 255. Unknown commands and invalid arguments exit 2; a command failure exits nonzero. App settings load when Hinoki constructs the app, but module resources open only for the selected command. shell ¶ uv run hinoki shell uv run hinoki shell blog.main:app --models blog.models In a project with hinoki.toml , the target defaults to project.application and the shell loads every registered app's model module. Repeat --models to select model modules explicitly. Outside a project, pass a target; --models is optional. The interactive namespace contains app , its validated settings , and concrete model classes. Conflicting model class names fail before the prompt. The shell keeps one event loop and supports top-level await : >>> await Note . all () [Note(id=1, title='Hello')] >>> app . title 'Hinoki Blog' Use async ORM queries with await ; synchronous ORM methods cannot block the shell's event loop. Unmanaged tasks are cancelled on exit and cleanup is bounded by app.runtime.shutdown_timeout . Installed module resources are started and closed for the session, so ORM queries use the app's configured database. App on_startup and on_shutdown hooks do not run, and migrations are never applied. The shell requires a TTY; Ctrl-D exits, Ctrl-C at the prompt exits, and Ctrl-C during a cell interrupts that cell. It executes Python with the current user's process privileges and may write to the configured database, so use a development database when experimenting. migrations ¶ In a project created by hinoki new , migration modules are read from the manifest; users do not supply model or migration paths: uv run hinoki migrations plan --name add-index --dry-run uv run hinoki migrations plan --check uv run hinoki migrations plan --app billing --name add-invoice-index uv run hinoki migrations status uv run hinoki migrations apply uv run hinoki migrations sql --app billing 0001 -initial status and apply cover all registered apps in dependency order. Writing a plan in a multi-app project requires --app ; read-only plan --check and plan --dry-run without --app cover every app in dependency order. sql likewise requires an app in a multi-app project. --name is optional for a focused plan: Hinoki derives a stable slug from the first planned schema change (for example, create-table-notes ); pass --name initial-notes to override it. All-app previews cannot use --name . Numbering is automatic. apply initializes the configured local SQLite database when no database URL is set. In a manifest project the implicit .hinoki/local.sqlite3 file is rooted beside hinoki.toml , even if you run the command from a subdirectory; explicit relative SQLite URLs remain relative to the current working directory. Added apps have separate migration ledger namespaces, so identical numbered filenames do not collide; the scaffolded root app retains its existing unprefixed migration keys. --app billing includes its declared prerequisite apps for migration application. Use plan --check in CI to fail when model changes are missing from committed migration files. It exits 1 when operations are pending and 0 when the files match the models. It is read-only: it imports registered model modules and the selected migration package but does not write migration files or connect to a database. Project planning loads every registered app's models to validate cross-app foreign keys, even when --app selects one migration package. Without --app , it checks every app in dependency order; --app NAME limits the check to that app and its prerequisites. Destructive operations are reported as pending too. This checks model-to-file drift only; migrations status checks which migration files have been applied to a live database. plan --dry-run without --app previews every app and exits successfully when it prints planned operations. The all-app preview is hypothetical and writes no files; a dependent plan shown there may need its prerequisite migration generated and reviewed first. Ordinary app-local destructive changes are previewed without requiring --allow-destructive . Before writing a focused plan, Hinoki verifies that cross-app foreign-key targets exist in the prerequisite app's recorded migration state and have a compatible primary-key column. It also refuses parent teardowns while any recorded state of another app still refers to the target, including for --dry-run and --check and even with --allow-destructive . An all-app preview fails without partial diffs in this case. Remove and apply the child foreign key in a separate deployment phase before preparing the parent teardown. See migrations for the limits of this file-based check. Without a hinoki.toml , the explicit legacy form remains: hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations plan \ --models myapp.models --name add-index --dry-run hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations plan \ --models myapp.models --name add-index --allow-destructive export HINOKI_DATABASE_URL = " $APP_DATABASE__URL " hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations status hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations apply hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations sql 0001 -initial plan requires --models MODULE ; --name is an optional slug override and is derived from the first planned schema change when omitted. --dry-run prints operations without writing files. Destructive operations require --allow-destructive . Without HINOKI_DATABASE_URL , plan/status/apply target the local SQLite file at .hinoki/local.sqlite3 ; --database URL selects another supported backend. A URL given as an argument is visible in the process list and shell history, so keep a URL containing a password in the environment. When the connection fails, the command prints error: database: … with a fix: line and exits 1; the URL is not printed. sql NAME prints a migration's SQL. Use a disposable database while reviewing migrations. mcp ¶ hinoki mcp tracker.app:create_app \ --rules tracker.rules:tracker_rules \ --package tracker --models tracker.models The development server uses MCP over stdio. It accepts --rules , repeatable --package , repeatable --models , and --waivers with the same target meanings as check . --scenarios off|read|write controls whether run_scenario is registered: read allows GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and QUERY; write allows every supported method. Scenarios start the real app, run handlers and lifespan hooks, and may write data even for a GET. Keep the tool server owner-controlled and point the app at a disposable database. The development MCP is separate from application MCP, which is mounted with expose_as_mcp and an explicit action allowlist. See the development MCP guide for tool inputs and results. Import target examples ¶ hinoki dev notes.main:app hinoki check tracker.app:create_app hinoki settings blog.settings:BlogSettings hinoki migrations plan --app blog --name add-index --dry-run When a target import fails, check that the command runs from the project directory, the package has __init__.py files where needed, and the attribute name is correct.

The report covers manifest validity, Python/native extension and optional Granian availability, route registration, configured typed settings, and in-memory OpenAPI generation. An app with no settings object reports that check as skipped; a custom non- Settings object is a warning. JSON output has schema_version: 1 and stable check IDs. Settings values and exception messages are not included. Exit status is 0 when no diagnostic failed, 1 for invalid manifest or app diagnostics, and 2 when a requested target cannot be loaded. Warnings and skipped checks remain visible. Database connectivity and applied migration state are intentionally separate: use hinoki migrations status for the live ledger and hinoki migrations plan --check for model-to-file drift.
docs.title: doctor

docs.text: hinoki new notes --dir . NAME is a lowercase package name containing letters and digits; it cannot be hinoki or a Python standard-library module name, because those names would shadow imports used by the generated project. --dir chooses the parent directory and defaults to the current directory. The target PATH/NAME must not exist or must be empty; nothing is overwritten, and nothing is installed or run. This repository's pre-alpha Hinoki framework is not published on PyPI; the hinoki name belongs to an unrelated legacy package. The generated pyproject.toml therefore names this repository as the source under [tool.uv.sources] : Given Source written --hinoki /path/to/checkout that checkout, editable --hinoki https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki@REV (or git+https://... ) that repository, pinned to REV when given nothing, running from a source checkout the checkout you ran it from nothing, any other installation the public repository, default branch The result is cd PATH/NAME && uv sync && uv run pytest : the project has a health route, typed settings, rules, one test that needs no database, a README.md , AGENTS.md and .mcp.json . Checkout paths and Git source values are escaped as TOML strings in the generated pyproject.toml .
docs.title: new

docs.text: The generated hinoki.toml registers the default app and its models and migrations. Add modules without moving files by creating another app: uv run hinoki app create billing This creates NAME/apps/billing/{models.py,migrations/} and registers both dotted module paths. Cross-app foreign keys require the referencing app to list the referenced app in requires in hinoki.toml ; migrations are then planned/applied in dependency order. The project registry is explicit: Hinoki does not scan arbitrary installed packages or run imports at install time. List the registered apps from the project root or any subdirectory: uv run hinoki app list uv run hinoki app list --format json The text output shows each app in dependency order with its model module, migration package and prerequisites. JSON contains the same fields under an apps key. The command only reads and validates hinoki.toml : it does not import app modules, connect to a database or start the app. Without a manifest, it prints an error and exits 2.
docs.title: app

docs.text: hinoki dev notes.main:app --host 127 .0.0.1 --port 8000 hinoki serve notes.main:app --workers 4 hinoki serve notes.main:app --server rust --workers 2 Both commands accept --host and --port ; they override settings.server.host and .port . serve also accepts --workers , overriding .workers . Both accept --server granian|rust , overriding .server (default granian ). Otherwise values come from the app's settings.AppSettings.server group. dev enables reload and runs one worker. Granian is provided by the optional server extra. --server rust runs the application on the Rust HTTP server (see Running an application for what it does and does not do). A setting that the chosen server cannot honour ( access_log with rust ; max_connections , header_read_timeout or body_read_timeout with granian ) makes the command print error: server.<name> is not supported by the <server> server and exit with status 2. A build whose native extension has no Rust server exits 2 with a message instead of falling back to Granian. With several workers the command runs a supervisor that starts one process per worker; SIGTERM or Ctrl-C stops them gracefully, and a worker that dies stops the rest and makes the command exit non-zero.
docs.title: dev and serve

docs.text: hinoki check tracker.app:create_app \ --package tracker --phase startup --format text Options: --rules MODULE:ATTRIBUTE selects a RuleSet ; the app's rules are used by default. --package PACKAGE selects a package for static import checks. Repeat it for multiple packages. Without it, the package containing the target is scanned. --phase startup|static selects a phase; the default runs both. --waivers PATH selects a waiver file; the default is hinoki-rules.toml in the current directory. --format text|json selects human-readable or versioned JSON output. --allow-effects also runs checks declared as effectful, which may access files, network or databases. Exit status is 0 when no rules fail, 1 for violations, and 2 when the target or checks cannot run.
docs.title: check

docs.text: hinoki openapi notes.main:app hinoki openapi notes.main:app --output openapi.json hinoki openapi notes.main:app --check openapi.json The command builds the app without serving it or opening a database; it works even when openapi_url is disabled. With no file option it prints deterministic JSON (sorted keys, two-space indentation and a trailing newline). --output FILE writes those bytes. --check FILE compares parsed JSON, so formatting differences do not count as drift. Exit status is 0 when the file matches or is written, 1 when its JSON differs, and 2 when the target cannot load or the check file is missing or invalid JSON. --output and --check cannot be used together.
docs.title: openapi

docs.text: hinoki version hinoki version --verbose hinoki version --verbose --format json The default prints hinoki X.Y.Z . --verbose adds the Python version, platform, native extension path and Granian version; Granian is reported as not installed when its optional package is absent. Use --format json for machine-readable output. Details the binding does not expose, including its bundled SQLite library version, are omitted rather than inferred.
docs.title: version

docs.text: hinoki settings blog.settings:BlogSettings \ --prefix BLOG_ --dotenv .env --toml settings.toml --format json hinoki settings blog.settings:BlogSettings --example > .env.example TARGET can be a settings class or an app with typed settings. --prefix , --dotenv and --toml override sources declared by the settings class. --format text|json selects output; --example prints a .env.example with defaults and types, leaving secrets and required fields blank. Values of settings.Secret are redacted.
docs.title: settings

docs.text: hinoki manage --help hinoki manage greet Peppe Commands are declared on the app with Hinoki(commands=[...]) . Each command subclasses hinoki.management.Command , gives itself a lower-case name, and adds arguments through add_arguments(parser) . In a scaffolded project, hinoki manage lists commands and hinoki manage greet Peppe runs one; the manifest's project.application supplies the app target. Outside a registered project, use hinoki manage TARGET COMMAND . --help after a command shows its arguments. from argparse import ArgumentParser , Namespace from hinoki import Hinoki from hinoki.management import Command , CommandContext class Greet ( Command ): name = "greet" help = "print a greeting" def add_arguments ( self , parser : ArgumentParser ) -> None : parser . add_argument ( "name" , nargs = "?" , default = "world" ) def handle ( self , _context : CommandContext , args : Namespace ) -> None : print ( f "Hello, { args . name } !" ) app = Hinoki ( commands = [ Greet ]) The same example is in examples/project/app.py ; the examples manifest supplies its target when you run the command from the examples/ project directory. handle(context, args) may be synchronous or asynchronous. A sync handler runs on Hinoki's bounded executor. It can read context.settings and retrieve resources with context.get(Type) or context.find(Type) . Declare module classes in the command's requires tuple; Hinoki starts those modules and their dependencies for the command, then closes them before it exits. Other app modules are not started. A command with no requirements starts no app modules. Commands run inside the project process and can modify data. Use disposable databases when developing or testing a command that writes. A handler returns None for success or an exit code from 0 through 255. Unknown commands and invalid arguments exit 2; a command failure exits nonzero. App settings load when Hinoki constructs the app, but module resources open only for the selected command.
docs.title: manage

docs.text: uv run hinoki shell uv run hinoki shell blog.main:app --models blog.models In a project with hinoki.toml , the target defaults to project.application and the shell loads every registered app's model module. Repeat --models to select model modules explicitly. Outside a project, pass a target; --models is optional. The interactive namespace contains app , its validated settings , and concrete model classes. Conflicting model class names fail before the prompt. The shell keeps one event loop and supports top-level await : >>> await Note . all () [Note(id=1, title='Hello')] >>> app . title 'Hinoki Blog' Use async ORM queries with await ; synchronous ORM methods cannot block the shell's event loop. Unmanaged tasks are cancelled on exit and cleanup is bounded by app.runtime.shutdown_timeout . Installed module resources are started and closed for the session, so ORM queries use the app's configured database. App on_startup and on_shutdown hooks do not run, and migrations are never applied. The shell requires a TTY; Ctrl-D exits, Ctrl-C at the prompt exits, and Ctrl-C during a cell interrupts that cell. It executes Python with the current user's process privileges and may write to the configured database, so use a development database when experimenting.
docs.title: shell

docs.text: In a project created by hinoki new , migration modules are read from the manifest; users do not supply model or migration paths: uv run hinoki migrations plan --name add-index --dry-run uv run hinoki migrations plan --check uv run hinoki migrations plan --app billing --name add-invoice-index uv run hinoki migrations status uv run hinoki migrations apply uv run hinoki migrations sql --app billing 0001 -initial status and apply cover all registered apps in dependency order. Writing a plan in a multi-app project requires --app ; read-only plan --check and plan --dry-run without --app cover every app in dependency order. sql likewise requires an app in a multi-app project. --name is optional for a focused plan: Hinoki derives a stable slug from the first planned schema change (for example, create-table-notes ); pass --name initial-notes to override it. All-app previews cannot use --name . Numbering is automatic. apply initializes the configured local SQLite database when no database URL is set. In a manifest project the implicit .hinoki/local.sqlite3 file is rooted beside hinoki.toml , even if you run the command from a subdirectory; explicit relative SQLite URLs remain relative to the current working directory. Added apps have separate migration ledger namespaces, so identical numbered filenames do not collide; the scaffolded root app retains its existing unprefixed migration keys. --app billing includes its declared prerequisite apps for migration application. Use plan --check in CI to fail when model changes are missing from committed migration files. It exits 1 when operations are pending and 0 when the files match the models. It is read-only: it imports registered model modules and the selected migration package but does not write migration files or connect to a database. Project planning loads every registered app's models to validate cross-app foreign keys, even when --app selects one migration package. Without --app , it checks every app in dependency order; --app NAME limits the check to that app and its prerequisites. Destructive operations are reported as pending too. This checks model-to-file drift only; migrations status checks which migration files have been applied to a live database. plan --dry-run without --app previews every app and exits successfully when it prints planned operations. The all-app preview is hypothetical and writes no files; a dependent plan shown there may need its prerequisite migration generated and reviewed first. Ordinary app-local destructive changes are previewed without requiring --allow-destructive . Before writing a focused plan, Hinoki verifies that cross-app foreign-key targets exist in the prerequisite app's recorded migration state and have a compatible primary-key column. It also refuses parent teardowns while any recorded state of another app still refers to the target, including for --dry-run and --check and even with --allow-destructive . An all-app preview fails without partial diffs in this case. Remove and apply the child foreign key in a separate deployment phase before preparing the parent teardown. See migrations for the limits of this file-based check. Without a hinoki.toml , the explicit legacy form remains: hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations plan \ --models myapp.models --name add-index --dry-run hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations plan \ --models myapp.models --name add-index --allow-destructive export HINOKI_DATABASE_URL = " $APP_DATABASE__URL " hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations status hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations apply hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations sql 0001 -initial plan requires --models MODULE ; --name is an optional slug override and is derived from the first planned schema change when omitted. --dry-run prints operations without writing files. Destructive operations require --allow-destructive . Without HINOKI_DATABASE_URL , plan/status/apply target the local SQLite file at .hinoki/local.sqlite3 ; --database URL selects another supported backend. A URL given as an argument is visible in the process list and shell history, so keep a URL containing a password in the environment. When the connection fails, the command prints error: database: … with a fix: line and exits 1; the URL is not printed. sql NAME prints a migration's SQL. Use a disposable database while reviewing migrations.
docs.title: migrations

docs.text: hinoki mcp tracker.app:create_app \ --rules tracker.rules:tracker_rules \ --package tracker --models tracker.models The development server uses MCP over stdio. It accepts --rules , repeatable --package , repeatable --models , and --waivers with the same target meanings as check . --scenarios off|read|write controls whether run_scenario is registered: read allows GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and QUERY; write allows every supported method. Scenarios start the real app, run handlers and lifespan hooks, and may write data even for a GET. Keep the tool server owner-controlled and point the app at a disposable database. The development MCP is separate from application MCP, which is mounted with expose_as_mcp and an explicit action allowlist. See the development MCP guide for tool inputs and results.
docs.title: mcp

docs.text: hinoki dev notes.main:app hinoki check tracker.app:create_app hinoki settings blog.settings:BlogSettings hinoki migrations plan --app blog --name add-index --dry-run When a target import fails, check that the command runs from the project directory, the package has __init__.py files where needed, and the attribute name is correct.

docs.text: Parsers and renderers ¶ A parser turns a request body into Python data; a renderer turns a handler's result into response bytes. Built-ins use Rust for selected parsing and JSON encoding work; Python still selects codecs, calls customization hooks and assembles framework objects. Built in Rust work Python work and options JSONParser Strict JSON decoding (no NaN, no lone surrogates, depth limit) prepare(data) hook and media_type FormParser application/x-www-form-urlencoded parsing with a field cap Builds the Python mappings; max_fields MultiPartParser multipart/form-data parsing and byte/part limits Builds UploadedFile and form objects; max_parts , max_part_bytes (each part, including text fields) TextParser — Decodes UTF-8 in Python; media_type JSONRenderer Encodes dict , list , Schema , UUID, datetime and dump() objects prepare(value, request) and default callbacks run in Python; indent , sort_keys , media_type HTMLRenderer , TextRenderer — Type-check and UTF-8 encode strings in Python; media_type Content negotiation ( Accept , quality values, wildcards) also runs in Rust; with nothing acceptable the answer is 406 before the handler runs. Upload files ¶ An action that binds an UploadedFile and has no parsers of its own gets MultiPartParser() with its default limits (100 parts, 1 MiB per part), unless the application's parsers= already include a MultiPartParser , which is then used. Other actions accept multipart only when it is listed. The parser handles bounded multipart bytes in Rust, then Python creates UploadedFile objects. For typed handler binding, annotate a parameter as UploadedFile , UploadedFile | None = None , or list[UploadedFile] ; the parameter name selects the multipart field. A single value rejects duplicates, while a list preserves repeated values. The same objects are visible through request.FILES ; text fields are available in request.POST . See endpoint upload declarations for a complete example and status-code behavior. The complete request body and every part are buffered in memory. The default body cap is 1 MiB; increasing it also increases potential memory use across concurrent requests. This parser does not stream or spool files. Keep both the runtime body cap and max_part_bytes bounded, and treat filenames and media types as untrusted client input. Choose them ¶ Per action, or for the whole application (an action's own choice wins): app = Hinoki ( renderers = [ JSONRenderer ( sort_keys = True ), TextRenderer ()]) @http . get ( "/report" , renderers = [ JSONRenderer ( indent = 2 )]) async def report () -> dict [ str , int ]: ... @http . post ( "/hook" , parsers = [ JSONParser (), TextParser ()]) async def hook ( request : Request ) -> None : ... # request.data is a dict or a str Configure the Rust JSON encoder ¶ JSONRenderer ( indent = 2 , sort_keys = True ) # pretty, stable output JSONRenderer ( default = str ) # Decimal, Path, ... become text default is a Python callback for a value the encoder does not know and must return something that is JSON (returning the same object is an error). It does not override what the encoder already handles (UUID, datetime, Schema , anything with dump() ). With sort_keys=True object keys are ordered by their encoded text (quotes and escapes included), which is deterministic but not always json.dumps order for unusual keys, and integer keys sort as text. The public renderer accepts indent from 0 to 16, or None for compact output. Inherit and override ¶ from hinoki import JSONParser , JSONRenderer class Envelope ( JSONRenderer ): media_type = "application/vnd.myapp+json" def prepare ( self , value , request ): # reshape, then Rust encodes return { "data" : value , "request_id" : request . request_id } class SnakeCase ( JSONParser ): def prepare ( self , data ): # Rust decodes, then reshape return rename_keys ( data ) if isinstance ( data , dict ) else data For a different format write a Renderer ( media_type , render(value, request) -> bytes ) or a Parser ( media_type , parse(raw, content_type) -> Parsed ); set consumes_objects = True on a renderer that can take Schema instances directly. Media types must be distinct within one list; a failing parse raises InvalidBody(code, message) (a 400 with that stable code).

docs.text: Concepts ¶ This page connects the main parts of Hinoki. The guides explain each API in detail. A model is stored data; a Schema is API data ¶ Model describes a database row and its queries (SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB). Schema validates the values an endpoint accepts or returns. A response schema should expose only the fields clients are meant to see. Model-derived Schema classes are a convenience, not a replacement for deciding that boundary. A declaration is reused ¶ An action's Python signature and decorator options describe routing, binding, access, transaction behavior, expected errors, OpenAPI and MCP metadata. A route can be included as a standalone function, grouped in an API resource class, or collected in an includable RouteGroup of functions with shared defaults. One request ¶ The server passes an ASGI request through the Python adapter, the compiled router and binding layer. Hinoki validates inputs, resolves authentication and access, runs the handler, then encodes and renders its response. Runtime response values are not validated against their return annotations. For a transactional action, commit happens after successful response encoding and rendering; failures roll back before HTTP error translation. The ASGI boundary still crosses Python objects; the runtime is not an all-Rust server. Worker resources ¶ Each server worker owns its module lifespan and database pool. Startup creates resources; shutdown closes them. A pool is not opened at import or shared across workers. Scripts outside the server manage their own short-lived connections. Optional rules ¶ Rules inspect declared routes, schemas, imports or other known project structure. They report a violation or say they could not verify the promise. They do not prove arbitrary function behavior. Enable the checks that suit the application and run them both at startup and in development. Where to continue ¶ Request lifecycle Transactions Sync and async Architecture patterns
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: Generate CRUD routes ¶ CrudAPI generates model-backed routes on an ordinary API class. Declare the model in the class header, set schemas and options as class attributes, and include the class once in the app. Handwritten @http.* methods and mixins can live beside the generated actions. from typing import Any from hinoki import Caller , CrudAPI , Hinoki , Schema , http from hinoki.orm import QuerySet from app.models import Post from app.security import editor class PostOut ( Schema , model = Post ): ... class PostCreate ( Schema ): title : str slug : str body : str class Posts ( CrudAPI , model = Post , path = "/posts" ): read_schema = PostOut create_schema = PostCreate access = editor owner = "author_id" def get_queryset ( self , principal : Caller [ Any ] | None ) -> QuerySet [ Post ]: return Post . filter ( published = True ) . order_by ( "-id" ) @http . get ( "/health" ) async def health ( self ) -> dict [ str , str ]: return { "status" : "ok" } app = Hinoki ( include = [ Posts ]) The generated actions are ordinary API routes, visible to OpenAPI, the hinoki routes command and the route registry. The class is mounted once; no import-time or global auto-registration occurs. A model's read schema and write schemas must match its fields. See Schemas for model-derived schemas. Generated actions ¶ List and retrieve are generated by default. Writes are opt-in: Class declaration Action Method and path Success Always list GET /posts Paginated Page[PostOut] Always retrieve GET /posts/{item_id} PostOut create_schema = PostCreate create POST /posts 201 , PostOut update_schema = PostPatch update PATCH /posts/{item_id} 200 , PostOut deletable = True delete DELETE /posts/{item_id} 204 , no body Generated writes require access = ... , unless public_writes = True is set deliberately. Reads are public by default; read_access = ... protects them. Writes run in a transaction. pagination selects the page-number policy for the generated list route. Reuse and customization ¶ CRUD configuration and Python methods compose through normal inheritance. Subclasses inherit the model and options, override options/hooks, and can set a new path= . A model-derived schema from another model is rejected during class creation. Mixins can provide reusable decorated routes or hooks. Class-level access and read_access apply to generated actions only; handwritten and inherited decorated methods keep the policy on their own @http.* decorator, so protect those routes explicitly. Use get_queryset(principal) to build the list/detail query. It may be def or async def ; it builds a query and should not perform database I/O. When reads are public, principal is None ; when read_access is set, it is the authenticated Caller . Apply tenant or visibility filters here. owner is an independent write safeguard, not read authorization. Writes are also constrained by this query, primary key and owner column, including in the mutation statement. Override to_schema(item) with def or async def for a response shape that needs loaded relations; relations are never loaded implicitly. Override written_queryset(principal) with either form to load response relations after a successful write, independently of filters that might hide the changed row from subsequent list requests. Generated write routes call these overridable hooks inside their transaction. Each hook may be a normal def or async def . Sync hooks run on Hinoki's bounded worker executor, where synchronous ORM methods are available; async hooks run on the event loop and should use the async ORM methods. This applies to get_queryset , written_queryset , to_schema , and each perform_* hook. For a synchronous hook, use synchronous ORM methods and return the model: def slug_for ( title : str ) -> str : return title . casefold () . replace ( " " , "-" ) class Posts ( CrudAPI , model = Post , path = "/posts" ): read_schema = PostOut create_schema = PostCreate access = editor owner = "author_id" def perform_create ( self , values : dict [ str , Any ], principal : Caller [ Any ] ) -> Post : values [ "slug" ] = slug_for ( str ( values [ "title" ])) return Post . create ( ** values ) An async hook uses the async ORM method: async def perform_create ( self , values : dict [ str , Any ], principal : Caller [ Any ] ) -> Post : values [ "slug" ] = slug_for ( str ( values [ "title" ])) return await Post . acreate ( ** values ) A sync override uses Post.create(**values) ; it should not call async ORM methods or return an un-awaited coroutine. perform_update(item, scoped_queryset, values, principal) and perform_delete(item, scoped_queryset, principal) receive the target and the query already limited by visibility, key and ownership. Call super() to keep the default scoped database mutation. Hooks may use transactional database operations; they do not run after commit, so do not send mail or publish external events directly from them. Hooks are trusted application code: do not bypass the supplied scoped queryset with an unscoped model write or raw SQL. Hinoki checks the persisted item after create/update for model identity and server-assigned field invariants, but cannot sandbox arbitrary hook side effects. Replace a generated action with a same-name decorated method, or use replaces=Crud.CREATE (or another Crud member) on a differently named route. An undecorated method named list , retrieve , create , update or delete intentionally shadows and removes that generated route. A differently named method without replaces= is a separate route and may collide by path/method; route registration reports duplicates. Security and validation ¶ Set owner = "author_id" to assign that column from the authenticated caller on create and constrain update/delete. identity_key extracts the owner value from Caller.user ; its default reads .id . assign maps additional server-owned columns to functions of the caller's user object. Client schemas cannot accept server-assigned fields. Generated writes require an access policy even when owner is configured. At class declaration Hinoki rejects abstract models, unknown schema fields, unsafe nullable fields, missing required create values, update schemas that can overwrite omitted fields, primary-key updates, unknown assigned columns, and incompatible derived schemas. only= and exclude= schemas remain subject to these same checks. Their queryset= callback is not caller-aware; perform_* hooks are available on those API subclasses too. For response relations after a write that becomes hidden by the old queryset, its fallback read cannot preserve eager-loads. Migrate to the class declaration and override written_queryset(principal) when the response needs relations. Existing output= schemas may contain computed fields; class-based schemas may do the same through to_schema . See the CRUD API reference . Generated CRUD suits ordinary model-backed operations. docs.text: CrudAPI generates model-backed routes on an ordinary API class. Declare the model in the class header, set schemas and options as class attributes, and include the class once in the app. Handwritten @http.* methods and mixins can live beside the generated actions. from typing import Any from hinoki import Caller , CrudAPI , Hinoki , Schema , http from hinoki.orm import QuerySet from app.models import Post from app.security import editor class PostOut ( Schema , model = Post ): ... class PostCreate ( Schema ): title : str slug : str body : str class Posts ( CrudAPI , model = Post , path = "/posts" ): read_schema = PostOut create_schema = PostCreate access = editor owner = "author_id" def get_queryset ( self , principal : Caller [ Any ] | None ) -> QuerySet [ Post ]: return Post . filter ( published = True ) . order_by ( "-id" ) @http . get ( "/health" ) async def health ( self ) -> dict [ str , str ]: return { "status" : "ok" } app = Hinoki ( include = [ Posts ]) The generated actions are ordinary API routes, visible to OpenAPI, the hinoki routes command and the route registry. The class is mounted once; no import-time or global auto-registration occurs. A model's read schema and write schemas must match its fields. See Schemas for model-derived schemas.
docs.title: Generate CRUD routes

docs.text: List and retrieve are generated by default. Writes are opt-in: Class declaration Action Method and path Success Always list GET /posts Paginated Page[PostOut] Always retrieve GET /posts/{item_id} PostOut create_schema = PostCreate create POST /posts 201 , PostOut update_schema = PostPatch update PATCH /posts/{item_id} 200 , PostOut deletable = True delete DELETE /posts/{item_id} 204 , no body Generated writes require access = ... , unless public_writes = True is set deliberately. Reads are public by default; read_access = ... protects them. Writes run in a transaction. pagination selects the page-number policy for the generated list route.
docs.title: Generated actions

docs.text: CRUD configuration and Python methods compose through normal inheritance. Subclasses inherit the model and options, override options/hooks, and can set a new path= . A model-derived schema from another model is rejected during class creation. Mixins can provide reusable decorated routes or hooks. Class-level access and read_access apply to generated actions only; handwritten and inherited decorated methods keep the policy on their own @http.* decorator, so protect those routes explicitly. Use get_queryset(principal) to build the list/detail query. It may be def or async def ; it builds a query and should not perform database I/O. When reads are public, principal is None ; when read_access is set, it is the authenticated Caller . Apply tenant or visibility filters here. owner is an independent write safeguard, not read authorization. Writes are also constrained by this query, primary key and owner column, including in the mutation statement. Override to_schema(item) with def or async def for a response shape that needs loaded relations; relations are never loaded implicitly. Override written_queryset(principal) with either form to load response relations after a successful write, independently of filters that might hide the changed row from subsequent list requests. Generated write routes call these overridable hooks inside their transaction. Each hook may be a normal def or async def . Sync hooks run on Hinoki's bounded worker executor, where synchronous ORM methods are available; async hooks run on the event loop and should use the async ORM methods. This applies to get_queryset , written_queryset , to_schema , and each perform_* hook. For a synchronous hook, use synchronous ORM methods and return the model: def slug_for ( title : str ) -> str : return title . casefold () . replace ( " " , "-" ) class Posts ( CrudAPI , model = Post , path = "/posts" ): read_schema = PostOut create_schema = PostCreate access = editor owner = "author_id" def perform_create ( self , values : dict [ str , Any ], principal : Caller [ Any ] ) -> Post : values [ "slug" ] = slug_for ( str ( values [ "title" ])) return Post . create ( ** values ) An async hook uses the async ORM method: async def perform_create ( self , values : dict [ str , Any ], principal : Caller [ Any ] ) -> Post : values [ "slug" ] = slug_for ( str ( values [ "title" ])) return await Post . acreate ( ** values ) A sync override uses Post.create(**values) ; it should not call async ORM methods or return an un-awaited coroutine. perform_update(item, scoped_queryset, values, principal) and perform_delete(item, scoped_queryset, principal) receive the target and the query already limited by visibility, key and ownership. Call super() to keep the default scoped database mutation. Hooks may use transactional database operations; they do not run after commit, so do not send mail or publish external events directly from them. Hooks are trusted application code: do not bypass the supplied scoped queryset with an unscoped model write or raw SQL. Hinoki checks the persisted item after create/update for model identity and server-assigned field invariants, but cannot sandbox arbitrary hook side effects. Replace a generated action with a same-name decorated method, or use replaces=Crud.CREATE (or another Crud member) on a differently named route. An undecorated method named list , retrieve , create , update or delete intentionally shadows and removes that generated route. A differently named method without replaces= is a separate route and may collide by path/method; route registration reports duplicates.

docs.text: Configure a database ¶ Hinoki's ORM supports PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB. SQLite is the default for local development. The backend is selected by the database URL; an application uses the same Model and query APIs across these backends where their SQL features overlap. Configure the application ¶ Declare a database: DatabaseSettings field on your app settings. Hinoki then opens one bounded pool per worker during startup and closes it during shutdown; importing models or routes does not open a connection, and no modules= entry is needed. from hinoki import Hinoki , settings class BlogSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "BLOG_" , dotenv = ".env" , toml = "hinoki.toml" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = BlogSettings ) With nothing configured, the database is local SQLite at .hinoki/local.sqlite3 . Configure a server database either with separate connection fields or with one URL; setting both is an error when settings load. Connection fields ¶ engine selects the backend with the settings.DatabaseEngine values sqlite , postgresql , mysql and mariadb . name is the database name, or the file path for SQLite. options are key=value URL query pairs such as PostgreSQL's sslmode . host defaults to localhost ; the password is a secret setting. # hinoki.toml, or the file named by the settings class's toml= [database] engine = "postgresql" name = "blog" user = "blog" host = "db.example.test" port = 5432 options = [ "sslmode=verify-full" , "sslrootcert=/run/secrets/db-ca.pem" ] max_size = 10 # per worker; the default is 10 export BLOG_DATABASE__PASSWORD = '…' # or BLOG_DATABASE__PASSWORD_FILE Hinoki builds the connection URL from these fields, percent-encoding the user, password and name, and keeps it in DatabaseSettings.url . SQLite takes only name . For PostgreSQL, host may be a Unix-socket directory such as /var/run/postgresql ; it is encoded in the generated URL. Other engines require a host name or address. Environment values for options use the settings sequence syntax, with commas separating key=value pairs. If an option value itself contains a comma, put it in the TOML array or percent-encode it in a URL. Options cannot specify credentials or override user , host , port or database name; use their dedicated fields instead. The password always belongs in the secret password setting or in a credential-bearing URL supplied as a secret. One URL ¶ export BLOG_DATABASE__URL = 'postgresql://blog:password@db.example.test/blog' export BLOG_DATABASE__URL = 'postgresql://blog:password@db.example.test/blog?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=%2Frun%2Fsecrets%2Fdb-ca.pem' export BLOG_DATABASE__URL = 'mysql://blog:password@db.example.test/blog' export BLOG_DATABASE__URL = 'sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3' A DatabaseModule listed in modules= , or installed with app.install(...) , replaces the one Hinoki would create from the settings, for example to pass a URL chosen at runtime: DatabaseModule(url, max_size=4) . Use a secret manager or a BLOG_DATABASE__URL_FILE / BLOG_DATABASE__PASSWORD_FILE variable for deployment credentials. Hinoki redacts the URL in settings output and connection errors. Avoid placing a credential-bearing URL in shell history or a process argument. Database authentication uses the username and password; in a hand-written URL, percent-encode reserved characters in either component. SQLite files are protected by the operating-system account and filesystem permissions, not by database credentials. For non-secret pool settings, TOML works as well. Keep url in an environment variable or secret file; settings.Secret values are not read from TOML. [database] max_size = 12 See settings for source precedence and validation, and application modules for resource ownership and access to the provided Database instance. Backend URLs and behavior ¶ Backend URL example Use and constraints SQLite sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 Supported; recommended local default. No network authentication or TLS. SQLite allows one writer at a time; Hinoki uses bounded connections and a five-second busy timeout. Relative paths are resolved from the application working directory. PostgreSQL postgresql://user:password@host/database Supported. Uses PostgreSQL username/password authentication and native UUID, timestamp, JSON and byte types. sslmode defaults to prefer ; use sslmode=verify-full for remote databases. sslrootcert adds a PEM CA certificate to the system roots. Hinoki accepts disable , prefer , require , verify-ca and verify-full ; the last three all require TLS and certificate verification in Hinoki. MySQL mysql://user:password@host/database Supported. Uses username/password authentication and requires TLS by default, with certificate and host verification. The system trust store must trust the server certificate. require_ssl=false disables encryption and is only for an isolated disposable local server. MySQL uses InnoDB and MySQL-native JSON; RETURNING is unavailable. MariaDB mariadb://user:password@host/database Supported and tested separately on MariaDB 11.4. Uses the MySQL wire driver and SQL dialect. MariaDB's JSON alias is text; typed ORM dict / list fields are decoded by their model declaration. Low-level Database.fetch() returns MariaDB JSON values as bytes because server metadata cannot safely distinguish JSON from arbitrary text. TLS is required by default. SQL Server and Oracle are not supported by this release. MySQL and MariaDB are separate URL/backend identities and each has its own real-server conformance job; MySQL's URL scheme does not imply MariaDB compatibility. Any other URL scheme, such as oracle:// or mssql:// , fails when the pool is created with DatabaseError: unsupported database URL scheme ; the error does not repeat the URL, so credentials in it are not logged. Create and apply migrations ¶ Migrations use the same selected URL. With no explicit URL, the CLI uses the local SQLite database. For another backend, export the URL without passing it as a process argument: cd examples export HINOKI_DATABASE_URL = " $BLOG_DATABASE__URL " uv run --project .. hinoki migrations plan --app blog uv run --project .. hinoki migrations status uv run --project .. hinoki migrations sql --app blog 0001 -initial uv run --project .. hinoki migrations apply --app blog Review generated SQL and state before applying them. Use a disposable database first. Hinoki does not run migrations automatically at app startup. On a fresh local checkout, hinoki migrations ... apply uses the default SQLite URL when HINOKI_DATABASE_URL is unset. Opening that URL creates .hinoki/local.sqlite3 if it does not exist; applying creates the migration ledger and runs the pending SQL files. As with Django's separate makemigrations and migrate steps, first run plan to generate migration files from model changes, then run apply to create the tables. status also opens the selected database and creates its ledger table if needed. Migration behavior differs by backend: SQLite rebuilds a table when a safe direct alteration is unavailable and checks foreign keys before committing the migration. Keep the database file and its backups on storage with permissions limited to the application user. PostgreSQL applies migrations in a transaction. MySQL implicitly commits DDL. If a migration fails, earlier statements may already have changed the schema; Hinoki reports that partial application is possible. Inspect schema and migration status before retrying, and retain a recoverable backup. MariaDB uses the MySQL wire protocol, but is a separate backend and is tested against its own service. Its JSON type is a text alias: Model fields annotated dict or list are decoded by the typed ORM, while the low-level Database.fetch() API returns JSON column values as bytes. Hinoki creates MySQL and MariaDB foreign keys as table-level constraints for consistent behavior across the two dialects. MySQL ignores inline REFERENCES clauses; MariaDB behavior differs by server version. For schemas created by an older Hinoki version, inspect SHOW CREATE TABLE before relying on referential integrity or on_delete . A migration ledger entry alone does not establish that MySQL created the constraint. Write a reviewed repair migration where a constraint is missing; Hinoki does not silently rewrite applied migrations. See the migration guide for destructive-change review and planning details, and the database API reference for types, raw SQL placeholders and backend limits.

docs.text: Development MCP ¶ hinoki mcp TARGET starts a newline-delimited JSON-RPC MCP server on stdio. It reads the registered application, enabled rules and optional model modules. It writes protocol messages to stdout and diagnostics to stderr. It does not write source code, rule configuration or waivers. cd examples uv run --project .. hinoki mcp tracker.app:create_app \ --rules tracker.rules:tracker_rules \ --package tracker \ --models tracker.models TARGET is an app or a no-argument factory. --rules selects a RuleSet ; --package and --models can be repeated; --waivers selects the waiver file (default hinoki-rules.toml ). Rule checks with side effects are not run by this server. Tools ¶ The server returns each result as JSON in structuredContent and in a text content block. Results include tool_version . Tool errors set isError and include an error message. Tool Input Result inspect_project {} App title/version, registered actions, selected model metadata, and enabled rule count. Models are included only when supplied with --models . list_rules {} Enabled rules and read-only waiver entries, including their file path, target, reason, owner and expiry. explain_action {"action": "module.function"} Action signature and docstring, access and transaction declarations, generated OpenAPI operation, and diagnostics for the action. The action may also be named by class method or bare handler name when unique. explain_error {"code": "validation_error"} Meaning and fix for a framework error code, HTTP error code or rule ID. propose_model {"name": "Article", "fields": [...]} Suggested model, input/patch/output schemas and CRUD action source text. The returned text is not written to a file. Fields support str , int , float , bool , uuid and datetime , with optional nullable , unique and max_length . check_project {} or {"phase": "static"} Enabled rule diagnostics with waivers applied, plus ok and failing . phase accepts startup or static . Effectful checks are excluded. run_scenario is omitted unless explicitly enabled with --scenarios read or --scenarios write . Its input requires path , a plain URL path beginning with / ; optional fields are method (default GET ), query (query string without ? ), string-valued headers , and json . The result contains HTTP status , response headers , bounded body text, truncated , and parsed JSON when available. Scenarios run the real app lifespan and handlers in-process. read accepts GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and QUERY; a GET handler may still change data. write also accepts POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. Scenario requests have a 15-second limit and response bodies are capped at 20,000 bytes. The tool is marked as effectful. Enable it only under owner control and use a disposable database. See CLI options for startup configuration and application MCP for exposing selected routes as remote tools.
