docs.text: Documentation versions ¶ Hinoki keeps unreleased documentation separate from release documentation. Development ¶ The dev documentation follows main and may change at any time. Before the first release, the site root redirects here. Treat it as documentation for the current pre-release code. Releases ¶ Each release is built from its matching vX.Y.Z tag. Release pages remain available at their versioned path; stable and latest point to the most recent release. Changes merged to main update only dev and do not replace a released version. Use the version menu in the header to move between available docs. When a page does not exist in an older version, the menu opens that version's home page.

docs.text: Endpoints ¶ Hinoki endpoints are ordinary Python functions decorated with an HTTP method. The decorator records metadata; Hinoki.include(...) registers the function or an API class. The registered declarations also supply the generated OpenAPI document . Declare an action ¶ from hinoki import Hinoki , Schema , http class Greeting ( Schema ): name : str @http . post ( "/greetings" , status = 201 ) async def greet ( data : Greeting ) -> Greeting : return data app = Hinoki ( include = [ greet ]) Use @http.get , @http.post , @http.put , @http.patch , @http.delete or @http.query ( from hinoki import http ). Hinoki also answers HEAD through each GET route: it runs the GET response path and returns the same status and representation headers without a body. The GET handler therefore runs for HEAD requests too. A 405 response's Allow header includes HEAD whenever GET is available. Supported decorator arguments include status , access , transaction , pagination , parsers , renderers , errors and replaces . Each is checked when the route is declared or registered. Read with a body: @http.query ¶ QUERY is the HTTP method for a read whose input does not fit a query string: it is safe and idempotent like GET , and carries a body like POST . Declare it the same way as the other methods: from hinoki import Schema , http class TaskSearch ( Schema ): text : str limit : int = 20 @http . query ( "/tasks/search" ) async def search_tasks ( data : TaskSearch ) -> list [ TaskOutput ]: rows = await Task . filter ( title__contains = data . text ) . limit ( data . limit ) return TaskOutput . from_models ( rows ) curl -X QUERY http://127.0.0.1:8000/tasks/search \ -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"text": "docs"}' The body is bound, parsed and validated exactly as for POST : the same parsers, size limit and 400 / 413 / 415 / 422 answers. A QUERY action must not change state. Hinoki does not wrap it in a transaction: RouteGroup(atomic=True) applies to POST , PUT , PATCH and DELETE only. Pass transaction=True on the action if the read needs one. RouteGroup.query(...) and @http.query inside an API class work like the other methods. A 405 answer lists QUERY in Allow where it is available. HEAD is answered through GET routes only. Hinoki sends no Accept-Query or cache headers by itself; add them to the response where they matter. The method is recent. Granian passes it through to Hinoki over ASGI and WSGI (both are tested), but a proxy, gateway, firewall or HTTP client in front of your service may reject a method it does not know, and browsers send a CORS preflight for it. Check the path your traffic takes, and keep a GET or POST route beside it when clients cannot send QUERY . In the OpenAPI document a QUERY operation appears under the path's x-query field; see OpenAPI . Bind request values ¶ Typed path parameters are taken from the path, query parameters from the query string, and a body parameter from the request body. A handler may declare request: Request as its first parameter when it needs headers, cookies or raw request data. The request is injected only when that parameter is explicitly annotated. from uuid import UUID from hinoki import Request , Schema from hinoki import http class TaskView ( Schema ): id : UUID locale : str @http . get ( "/tasks/ {task_id} " ) async def get_task ( request : Request , task_id : UUID ) -> TaskView : locale = request . headers . get ( "accept-language" , "en" ) return TaskView ( id = task_id , locale = locale ) Request path, query and body values are validated before the handler runs; a Schema body uses Schema.validate() and reports nested field errors with its parameter prefix. Discriminated request variants belong in a wrapper Schema field ( Annotated[Cat | Dog, Field(discriminator="kind")] ); bare union body parameters are not supported. Hinoki does not coerce input values into different types. Return annotations describe OpenAPI and output serialization; response values are not validated at runtime. Use a wrapper Schema for a discriminated response union too; bare union return annotations are rejected by OpenAPI generation. Upload files ¶ Bind a file by the multipart field name. An action that declares a file parameter and no parsers= gets MultiPartParser() automatically, with its default limits, unless the application's parsers= include one; pass parsers=[MultiPartParser(...)] to change them. UploadedFile contains the client filename, claimed content type and in-memory bytes ; it does not save files or validate their content. from hinoki import Hinoki , MultiPartParser , Request , UploadedFile , http @http . post ( "/documents" , status = 201 , parsers = [ MultiPartParser ( max_parts = 4 , max_part_bytes = 512_000 )], ) async def create_document ( request : Request , document : UploadedFile ) -> dict [ str , object ]: title = request . POST . get ( "title" , "" ) # Validate content and choose a generated storage name before saving. return { "title" : title , "filename" : document . filename , "size" : document . size } @http . post ( "/batch" ) # MultiPartParser() selected automatically def create_batch ( documents : list [ UploadedFile ]) -> dict [ str , int ]: return { "count" : len ( documents )} app = Hinoki ( include = [ create_document , create_batch ]) UploadedFile requires exactly one part with that name. list[UploadedFile] requires at least one and keeps repeated parts in order. To make a single file optional, write file: UploadedFile | None = None . These declarations cannot be combined with a Schema body parameter. Use request.POST for adjacent text fields or request.FILES when names/repetitions are dynamic. Parser precedence for a file action: its own parsers= (which must then include MultiPartParser , or registration fails), then an application-wide Hinoki(parsers=[...]) that includes a MultiPartParser , then the automatic MultiPartParser() . An application parser list without multipart does not apply to file actions, and actions without file parameters keep their parsers. All declared files require multipart/form-data . A missing file is a 422 validation error; a wrong media type is 415 ; malformed multipart is 400 ; a part or complete body over its configured limit is 413 payload_too_large . A zero-byte body with no Content-Type is treated as absent input for optional files; an explicitly multipart empty body is malformed, while a valid closing-boundary-only body has no parts. The default complete-body limit is 1 MiB, and the parser buffers bytes in memory. This API is for bounded small uploads, not streaming. Concurrent requests can multiply memory use. Keep limits conservative, never use the supplied filename as a filesystem path, and verify content instead of trusting the declared media type. See parsers and renderers and testing uploads . Group related paths ¶ For plain functions that share a prefix or defaults, use RouteGroup . The group collects its handlers and can be included once as a unit: from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import Hinoki , RouteGroup , Schema class TaskInput ( Schema ): title : str class TaskOutput ( Schema ): id : UUID title : str tasks = RouteGroup ( "/tasks" , atomic = True ) @tasks . get ( "/" ) async def listing () -> list [ TaskOutput ]: return [] @tasks . post ( "/" , status = 201 ) async def create ( data : TaskInput ) -> TaskOutput : return TaskOutput ( id = uuid4 (), title = data . title ) app = Hinoki ( include = [ tasks ]) When composing a group action with another decorator, put the HTTP decorator outside it. The group records the callable when @tasks.get runs: @tasks . get ( "/audited" ) @audit async def audited () -> str : return "ok" For a standalone function passed directly to Hinoki.include , the final decorated function is dispatched, so either order works with wrappers that use functools.wraps . For class-based APIs, put a shared path on the class and keep actions together: from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import API , Schema from hinoki import http class TaskInput ( Schema ): title : str class TaskOutput ( Schema ): id : UUID title : str class Tasks ( API , path = "/tasks" ): @http . get ( "/" ) async def listing ( self ) -> list [ TaskOutput ]: return [] @http . post ( "/" , status = 201 ) async def create ( self , data : TaskInput ) -> TaskOutput : return TaskOutput ( id = uuid4 (), title = data . title ) Then the application can include Tasks as one item. The path prefix is visible on the class; the full paths remain beside their actions. Use RouteGroup when functions are a better fit, especially when several actions share access, transaction defaults, or declared errors. A group must contain at least one action and becomes immutable after successful inclusion. Organising a large application ¶ When the ordinary list/retrieve/create/update/delete routes fit a model, CrudAPI can generate them from a model and schemas declared on one API class. Mount that class once in Hinoki ; generated and handwritten decorated actions can share it. Start with Generate CRUD routes ; use handwritten actions for domain workflows or to replace an individual generated action. Give each feature one module that owns its routes and exports them as a list, with paths relative to the feature. Choose where each feature lives in the root declaration with Mount , so the paths stay visible in one place: # tasks/routes.py (paths are relative: "/" and "/{task_id}") routes = [ tasks_group , TaskReports , export_tasks ] # main.py from hinoki import Hinoki , Mount from billing.routes import routes as billing from tasks.routes import routes as tasks app = Hinoki ( include = [ health , Mount ( "/tasks" , tasks ), Mount ( "/billing" , billing ), ] ) For a versioned API, let each feature module export its routes and compose them under one version mount. Each CRUD class keeps its resource path; the version prefix is declared once in api/v1.py : # api/people.py from hinoki import CrudAPI from app.models import Person from app.schemas import PersonOut class People ( CrudAPI , model = Person , path = "/people" ): read_schema = PersonOut # Each feature exports a list of routes relative to that feature. routes = [ People ] # api/teams.py from hinoki import CrudAPI from app.models import Team from app.schemas import TeamOut class Teams ( CrudAPI , model = Team , path = "/teams" ): read_schema = TeamOut routes = [ Teams ] # api/v1.py from hinoki import Mount from app.api import people , teams routes = Mount ( "/api/v1" , people . routes , teams . routes ) # app.py from hinoki import Hinoki from app.api import v1 app = Hinoki ( include = [ v1 . routes ]) The resulting paths include /api/v1/people , /api/v1/people/{item_id} , /api/v1/teams , and /api/v1/teams/{item_id} . Add api/v2.py with its own Mount("/api/v2", ...) when a new version is needed. Feature route lists and mixins can be shared where their behavior is genuinely the same. Route collisions are still checked after prefixes are composed. include spreads nested lists and tuples in place, so order is the order you wrote. Mount(prefix, *items) prepends its prefix to every route it holds; mounts nest and prefixes join from the outside in. The prefix starts with / and does not end with one. Items you do not mount keep their own paths, so small apps can stay a flat list. Mounting changes only the path: access, errors and transactions are unchanged, and a route that ends up at the same method and path as another still fails at declaration time. A RouteGroup reached twice, an item that is not an action, class or group, or a module passed instead of its list is refused and named; a module gets a hint to export a list. If a feature declares its own prefix (a RouteGroup("/tasks") or API, path="/tasks" ), mounting adds to it. Pick one place for each prefix: feature-relative paths with Mount at the root is the layout that keeps the whole map readable in main.py . To see the resulting map without starting the server, run hinoki routes blog.main:create_app --path /posts (the blog example): GET /posts public blog.api.Posts.listing POST /posts TokenAuth[posts:write] hinoki.crud.create DELETE /posts/{item_id} TokenAuth[posts:write] hinoki.crud.delete GET /posts/{item_id} public blog.api.Posts.one POST /posts/{item_id}/publish TokenAuth[posts:write] blog.api.Posts.publish Use --path or --method to narrow it, and --format json for scripts. The list is sorted by path. Responses, errors and pagination ¶ Return a value matching the declared response type, or return Reply when the handler needs to set an explicit status, headers or body. Declare expected APIError subclasses in errors=(...) ; their status, stable code and message feed the OpenAPI document and strict test client. Paginated actions declare a pagination policy. See pagination for the query parameters and response envelope. See authentication , parsers and renderers , and error handling . Migrating from the top-level decorators ¶ Earlier revisions exported get , post , put , patch and delete from hinoki . They now live in the hinoki.http namespace: # before from hinoki import get @get ( "/tasks" ) async def listing () -> list [ TaskOut ]: ... # now from hinoki import http @http . get ( "/tasks" ) async def listing () -> list [ TaskOut ]: ... from hinoki import get raises ImportError . If a module also needs the standard library's http (for HTTPStatus ), import it explicitly: from http import HTTPStatus .

docs.text: Errors ¶ Hinoki separates malformed requests, authentication failures and application errors. Handlers may declare the application errors they can raise so clients and generated tools can inspect the contract. Built-in HTTP errors ¶ Every public error type lives in one namespace: from hinoki import errors . It holds errors.BadRequest , errors.Unauthorized , errors.Forbidden , errors.NotFound and errors.Conflict , each derived from errors.APIError , plus the framework's own failures ( errors.RegistrationError , errors.ValidationError , errors.ObjectNotFound , errors.ErrorRegistry and the others listed in the reference ). They carry an HTTP status and a stable code . Raise them when the response is an expected part of the API: from hinoki import errors , http class TaskAlreadyDone ( errors . Conflict ): code = "task_already_done" message = "The task is already done." @http . post ( "/tasks/ {task_id} /complete" , errors = ( errors . NotFound , TaskAlreadyDone )) async def complete ( task_id : UUID ) -> TaskOutput : ... An action may declare several errors. The runtime maps a declared APIError to its status and response body. Unexpected exceptions remain server errors; do not expose exception text to clients. Validation and binding errors ¶ Input that does not match a path, query, header or body annotation fails before the handler runs. Schema validation is strict and reports field paths with 422 . Unsupported content types receive 415 ; malformed supported content receives a parser error. A body larger than execution.max_body_bytes , or a multipart part larger than its parser's max_part_bytes , receives 413 payload_too_large . Query strings over execution.max_query_bytes receive 414 uri_too_long ; combined headers over execution.max_header_bytes receive 431 headers_too_large . A Host outside the allowed_hosts setting receives 400 disallowed_host , and a CORS preflight from an origin outside cors.origins receives 403 cors_origin_denied ( settings ). These are framework-level failures and do not need to be listed in the action's errors= . When security.redirect_https is enabled, a plain HTTP request receives 308 with an HTTPS Location before routing or body parsing. The redirect requires an explicit allowed_hosts list and preserves the request method and target. See browser security settings . ModelValidationError is raised before an ORM insert or update when a Model field constraint or custom validator refuses a value. In an HTTP request it uses the same 422 validation_error response shape as Schema validation, including field paths, codes and messages. The admin displays the field messages in its form. Keep Schema validation at the request boundary; Model checks also cover non-HTTP writes. See Model field constraints and validators . Every HTTP request receives a request ID in the configured server.request_id_header header ( x-request-id by default). Hinoki generates the ID unless server.trust_request_id=True and the request comes from a configured trusted proxy with a valid inbound ID. Built-in error bodies also include request_id . Use the ID to connect a client report with the server log entry. Unhandled exceptions are logged with the ID and returned as 500 internal_error without exposing exception text. The debug setting adds the exception type, message and traceback to that answer for development. Check the contract ¶ Use ASGIClient(..., strict_errors=True) in tests to fail if a handler returns an error that it did not declare. hinoki check can also enforce rules about access and transaction declarations; see rules . Earlier revisions exported these names from hinoki itself and kept the HTTP errors in hinoki.httperrors ; both are gone. Use errors.<Name> ; from hinoki import NotFound raises ImportError .

ModelValidationError is raised before an ORM insert or update when a Model field constraint or custom validator refuses a value. In an HTTP request it uses the same 422 validation_error response shape as Schema validation, including field paths, codes and messages. The admin displays the field messages in its form. Keep Schema validation at the request boundary; Model checks also cover non-HTTP writes. See Model field constraints and validators . Every HTTP request receives a request ID in the configured server.request_id_header header ( x-request-id by default). Hinoki generates the ID unless server.trust_request_id=True and the request comes from a configured trusted proxy with a valid inbound ID. Built-in error bodies also include request_id . Use the ID to connect a client report with the server log entry. Unhandled exceptions are logged with the ID and returned as 500 internal_error without exposing exception text. The debug setting adds the exception type, message and traceback to that answer for development.

docs.text: Use ASGIClient(..., strict_errors=True) in tests to fail if a handler returns an error that it did not declare. hinoki check can also enforce rules about access and transaction declarations; see rules . Earlier revisions exported these names from hinoki itself and kept the HTTP errors in hinoki.httperrors ; both are gone. Use errors.<Name> ; from hinoki import NotFound raises ImportError .

docs.text: Installation ¶ Hinoki is pre-alpha and this repository is not published on PyPI. The hinoki project name currently resolves to an unrelated legacy package. Install this repository from source with uv and a stable Rust toolchain: git clone https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki cd hinoki uv sync --locked uv sync builds the native extension and installs the development tools. Create a project ¶ The CLI creates a small app with typed settings, default rules, tests and agent instructions: uv run hinoki new bookmarks --dir .. cd ../bookmarks uv sync uv run pytest The generated project includes a health route, a test that needs no database, a README.md with its commands and a development MCP configuration. Review AGENTS.md for its project commands and conventions. pyproject.toml names this repository as the source for uv , so it does not install the unrelated package by name; see hinoki new to choose a checkout or a git revision with --hinoki . Continue with the Quick start to run the Notes API, create its table with a reviewed migration and make a request.

docs.text: Glossary: one word, one meaning ¶ "Schema" means four different things in this field, so the docs use it for one of them only. Write Means Schema (code font) The Hinoki class for typed, validated request and response data: class NoteIn(Schema) . Always capitalised and in code font. table state, migration state What the migration planner records about the database tables ( migrations/NNNN-name.state.json ). Never "the database schema". OpenAPI document The generated /openapi.json description of the API. Its components.schemas entries are "OpenAPI schema objects". JSON Schema The standard of that name, which the OpenAPI document uses to describe bodies. Always with its proper name. Model A class that maps to a table ( class Note(Model) maps to notes ). docs.text: Guides ¶ One page for each part of an application. Start with the data and endpoint guides, then add access, rules and runtime concerns as you need them. New to Hinoki? Take the tutorial first, or follow the quick start . Data ¶ Models and queries : Models map Python classes to derived or explicitly named database tables, with typed queries and opt-in write-time field validation. Configure a database : Set the backend URL, install the database module and apply migrations safely. Schemas and validation : A Schema describes API data, with typed validation, normalization, rejection checks and class-level unknown-field policies. Model-derived schemas : A Schema can take its fields and constraints from a Model. Model options : Options that describe a model beyond its columns are decorators, read like the action decorators. Utilities : Hinoki includes a small set of helpers where the framework can define clear behavior. Relations : Foreign keys, explicit many-to-many association models, and how to load related rows. Migrations : Hinoki uses model declarations and recorded migration state to write SQL migration files. Endpoints ¶ Endpoint declarations : Hinoki endpoints are ordinary Python functions decorated with an HTTP method. Generate CRUD routes : Generate model-backed list, retrieve and selected write actions, with access and ownership rules. OpenAPI : The OpenAPI 3.1 document is generated from registered routes, signatures and schema declarations. Errors : Hinoki separates malformed requests, authentication failures and application errors. Pagination : An action opts into page-number pagination with PageNumberPagination() . Parsers and renderers : A parser turns a request body into Python data; a renderer turns a handler's result into response bytes. Security and checks ¶ Authentication and access : Hinoki keeps credential parsing in an authentication provider and permission checks in an Access policy. Rules : Rules are optional, typed promises about your application that a tool checks and that fail with a stable ID, a location and an explanation. Runtime ¶ Application modules : Modules own resources whose lifetime belongs to a worker, such as a database pool. Transactions : An action opts into a database transaction with transaction=True. Settings : Typed, immutable settings classes with environment, dotenv and TOML sources, and redacted secrets. Serving : Run an application with hinoki dev while you work and hinoki serve in production-style runs, on Granian or the opt-in Rust server. Testing : Hinoki has two useful levels of application tests: call the operation functions directly, then exercise the app through its ASGI interface. Command line : Run framework tools and app-defined management commands from the project directory. Interactive shell : Explore app settings and models with a persistent, async-capable Python prompt. Typing : Hinoki's public APIs use Python annotations so a type checker can catch mistakes in handlers, decorators and schema construction. Integrations ¶ Admin : An optional module that gives staff a list, search, create, edit, bulk delete and a dashboard for your models; it is included in the framework package and mounted explicitly. Application MCP : expose_as_mcp turns selected HTTP actions into tools for an MCP client. Development MCP : CLI-hosted tools describe an app and its rules to an agent. Development tools : Scaffold a project and give a coding agent rules, error explanations and an MCP server. Operating ¶ Sync and async : Hinoki runs on one event loop per worker; synchronous handlers run on a bounded worker pool. Benchmarks : retained measurements with their environment, method and limits. Where to go next ¶ Concepts : the request lifecycle, architecture patterns and the vocabulary. Reference : public symbols, signatures and docstrings. Status : what works today and what does not yet.
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: Migrations ¶ Hinoki compares each registered app's models with that app's migration state recorded in files. It can write a migration plan, but never applies schema changes when an application starts. hinoki new creates an explicit hinoki.toml ; hinoki app create NAME adds another app and its migration package. Create a migration ¶ uv run hinoki migrations plan --name add-published uv run hinoki migrations plan --app billing --name add-invoice-index The manifest must register the selected app. A single-app project defaults to that app; in a multi-app project, writing a plan requires --app . Read-only --dry-run and --check without --app cover every registered app in dependency order. The planner targets the local SQLite default unless a URL is provided through HINOKI_DATABASE_URL or --database . It writes a numbered .sql file and a matching .state.json file into the registered migration package. Numbering and a stable slug derived from the first schema change are automatic; an optional --name replaces only that slug for a focused plan. Review both files before applying the change. Cross-app model references require an explicit requires dependency in hinoki.toml ; this lets Hinoki validate references and order migrations without assigning another app's tables to the current app's migration state. --dry-run previews ordinary destructive changes without --allow-destructive and writes no files. An all-app preview is hypothetical: it can show a child app change against a prerequisite's current candidate models before that prerequisite has a recorded migration. Do not treat displayed plans as ready to apply in that order. An all-app preview cannot use --name ; select one app to preview a named migration. Cross-app migration safety ¶ Before writing a focused app plan, Hinoki checks cross-app foreign keys against the prerequisite app's recorded migration state. The referenced table and column must already be recorded, the column must be a primary key, and its logical type must be compatible. If the prerequisite has not been planned yet, plan and review it first. The prerequisite migration does not need to have been applied to the database before the dependent app can be planned. Hinoki also refuses to plan a parent table or referenced-column teardown while any recorded state snapshot of another app still refers to it. This guard applies to focused/all-app plans, --dry-run , and --check , and cannot be overridden with --allow-destructive . An all-app command fails without printing partial diffs. This prevents a generated parent drop from preceding a child foreign-key removal. Perform cross-app teardowns as reviewed, separately deployed phases: remove and apply the child reference first, then prepare and apply the parent teardown. The planner does not infer live database safety from migration files. The state file stores logical column types that are stable across backends; the generated SQL uses the selected backend's types. Existing state files that recorded SQLite or MySQL-specific type names are normalized when planning, so switching the planner's backend does not appear as a destructive type change. New Model classes may omit table= ; Hinoki derives a plural snake-case table name from the Python class. Keep table= explicit for models with existing migration history so later Python class renames do not change physical table identity. A changed implicit name appears as a drop/create plan and the destructive guard still applies. Hinoki refuses generated names reserved for its migration ledger or SQLite internals. See Models and queries for display-name overrides and the fallback naming rules. Check migration drift ¶ To check that model changes have a migration file in CI, run: uv run hinoki migrations plan --check It exits 1 when operations are pending, including destructive operations, and 0 when every selected app matches its latest migration state file. It does not write migration files or connect to a database. It imports registered model and migration modules (cross-app foreign keys require every model module), so those imports must be safe in CI. In a multi-app project, no --app checks every app in dependency order; --app NAME checks one app and its prerequisites. This check concerns file state only. Use migrations status to compare files with a live database's applied migration ledger. --dry-run without --app previews every registered app and exits successfully when changes are pending. For example, billing can depend on accounts : [[apps]] name = "billing" models = "sample.apps.billing.models" migrations = "sample.apps.billing.migrations" requires = [ "accounts" ] Apply and inspect ¶ export HINOKI_DATABASE_URL = " $BLOG_DATABASE__URL " uv run hinoki migrations status uv run hinoki migrations sql --app accounts 0001 -initial uv run hinoki migrations apply With no URL, status and apply use sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 and create the migration ledger/database as needed. In a manifest project this implicit path is anchored at the directory containing hinoki.toml , even when the command runs from a subdirectory. Without a manifest it stays relative to the current working directory. An explicit relative SQLite URL from HINOKI_DATABASE_URL or --database remains relative to the current working directory. Both commands operate on every registered app in dependency order. --app NAME limits them to that app and its prerequisites. sql requires --app in a multi-app project. The scaffolded root app keeps the traditional unprefixed migration ledger keys, so a project can add a manifest without replaying its existing migration history; added apps use namespaced keys, so accounts/0001-initial.sql and billing/0001-initial.sql are distinct records. Set HINOKI_DATABASE_URL or use --database URL to target another supported backend. A URL argument is visible in the process list and shell history, so do not pass a URL containing a password that way. A failed connection is reported as error: database: … with exit code 1, without the URL. Existing projects without a hinoki.toml can continue using explicit --models MODULE and --dir PATH options. These options cannot be combined with a project manifest; use the manifest as the single source for registered apps. Use a disposable database to review a migration before running it against important data. SQLite uses table rebuilds when a schema change cannot be expressed safely with ALTER TABLE . Review the generated SQL carefully. Dropping columns, changing types or constraints, and adding non-null columns can be destructive and require --allow-destructive . Hinoki holds the SQLite pool during a migration, suspends foreign-key enforcement on reserved connections, runs PRAGMA foreign_key_check before commit, and rolls the migration back if references are invalid. MySQL and MariaDB migrations declare foreign keys at table level. For databases migrated with an older Hinoki version, inspect SHOW CREATE TABLE : MySQL ignores inline REFERENCES clauses, while MariaDB behavior varies by server version. Add any missing constraint through a reviewed manual migration; applied migrations are never rewritten automatically. Automatic removal of a foreign key column is refused for these backends because the planner cannot know whether an older migration actually created its constraint. Destructive changes ¶ Operations that can remove data are reported as destructive and are not written unless --allow-destructive is passed to plan . Read the generated migration before opting in. Changing a constraint on an existing column may require a hand-written migration. Migrations are files committed with the application. Do not run them from every server worker's startup hook. For the connection lifecycle, see settings .

docs.text: Model options ¶ Options that describe a model beyond its columns are decorators , read like the action decorators. Hinoki has no nested class Meta . Only what is needed when the class is created stays a class keyword. from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import ( Model , OnDelete , field , foreign_key , indexed , ordered_by , timestamps , unique , ) from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Member ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) @unique ( "owner_id" , "url" ) @indexed ( "owner_id" , "created_at" ) @ordered_by ( "-created_at" , "-id" ) @timestamps () class Bookmark ( Model , table = "saved_links" , label = "Saved link" , plural = "Saved links" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) owner_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Member , on_delete = OnDelete . RESTRICT , related_name = "bookmarks" ) url : str = field ( max_length = 500 ) created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) updated_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) Option Form Effect table table="saved_links" (optional class keyword) overrides the default plural snake-case table name derived from the class labels label= , plural= (optional class keywords) override the humanized singular and plural display names derived from the class composite uniqueness @unique("a", "b") a UNIQUE (a, b) constraint; a single column uses field(unique=True) index @indexed("a", "b") a CREATE INDEX planned by the migration tool; adding or removing one is a non-destructive migration default order @ordered_by("-created_at", "id") every query without order_by (lists, pages) is ordered this way; "-" is descending; an explicit order_by replaces it, counts and bulk updates ignore it update timestamp @timestamps() refresh a declared updated_at: datetime field for every ORM update statement; use @timestamps("modified_at", clock=...) to customize Column names are checked when the decorator is applied; a typo fails at import with the model and the unknown names. Stacked decorators are stored in reading order (top to bottom). A model inherits the options of its abstract bases . A decorator on the subclass replaces everything inherited for that kind of option ( @indexed replaces the inherited indexes, and so on) and leaves the other kinds inherited. A model that subclasses a table model does not inherit that parent's options. Apply options before the model is used: the migration planner, the query layer and the admin read them from the class. The fallback table/display names use a small deterministic English suffix rule, not an inflector. Use explicit values for irregular, already-plural or localized names. Pin table= when a class has an existing migration history; changing an implicit name is a guarded drop/create, not a table rename. Index names are ix_<table>_<columns> , shortened deterministically (with a hash) past PostgreSQL's 63 bytes. Not yet: partial or expression indexes, per-column index options, and soft delete. For timestamps, see utilities ; fields are declared explicitly and migrations remain visible.

docs.text: Schemas derived from models ¶ from blog.models import Post from hinoki import Schema , derive The validation example below is independent and includes its own imports. A Schema can take its fields and constraints from a Model . Put the source model on the class; use one @derive(...) decorator when you need to select or make fields optional. Without the decorator, every model column is derived. from hinoki import Schema , derive @derive ( only = ( "title" , "slug" , "body" )) class PostCreate ( Schema , model = Post ): ... @derive ( exclude = ( "author_id" , "internal_note" )) class PostOut ( Schema , model = Post ): author_name : str @derive ( only = ( "title" , "body" ), partial = True ) class PostPatch ( Schema , model = Post ): ... class PostAll ( Schema , model = Post ): ... Option Effect model=Post source model; with no decorator, derives every column only=("a", "b") take exactly these columns exclude=("a",) take every column except these partial=True make every selected derived field optional ( UNSET when absent) partial=("a",) make only the named selected fields optional only and exclude cannot be combined. An empty only=() is invalid; exclude=() is equivalent to selecting all columns. Model field types, maximum lengths, defaults and nullability are used. Annotations in the class body add fields or override a derived field, and methods and checks in the body are kept. Methods can use zero-argument super() as usual. Unknown columns, a non-model, an empty only , or optional names outside the selection fail when the class is declared. Selection options require model= on the class. Relations are not derived as nested values; declare the API shape explicitly. Model derivation is explicit but includes all columns by default, so use only or exclude when the API must omit private fields. Add validation checks ¶ Use @field_check("name") for a rule on one or more structurally valid fields, and @object_check for a rule over the whole object. Raise Invalid(code, message, path=...) to report a problem. Checks are synchronous and must not perform I/O; database-dependent rules belong in an operation. from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Invalid , Schema , field_check , object_check class SignUp ( Schema ): username : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 3 , max_length = 32 )] password : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 12 )] confirmation : str @field_check ( "username" ) def username_characters ( self , value : str ) -> None : if not value . replace ( "_" , "" ) . isalnum (): raise Invalid ( "username_characters" , "use letters, numbers and _ only" ) @field_check ( "password" ) def reject_common_password ( self , value : str ) -> None : if value . lower () in { "password12345" , "qwerty123456" }: raise Invalid ( "common_password" , "choose a less common password" ) @object_check def passwords_match ( self ) -> None : if self . password != self . confirmation : raise Invalid ( "mismatch" , "passwords do not match" , path = "confirmation" ) Structural errors are reported before custom checks. All applicable check failures are returned together. See schemas for the validation contract and conversion methods.

docs.text: Models and queries ¶ Model maps a Python class to one database table. SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB are supported. Its annotated fields define the columns; queries are explicit and do not load relations implicitly. See configure a database for setup and backend-specific limits. Define a model ¶ from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , OnDelete , field , foreign_key , indexed , ordered_by , unique from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Member ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) email : str = field ( unique = True , max_length = 254 ) @indexed ( "owner_id" , "created_at" ) @ordered_by ( "-created_at" , "-id" ) class Task ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) owner_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Member , on_delete = OnDelete . RESTRICT , related_name = "tasks" ) title : str = field ( max_length = 120 ) done : bool = False created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) For a fresh model, Hinoki derives a plural snake-case table name and human display names from the class: Member becomes members , Member and Members ; UserProfile becomes user_profiles , User profile and User profiles . table= , label= and plural= are optional overrides. Keep an explicit table= when it pins an existing migration history or when the physical table needs another name. This matters when renaming a Python class: changing an implicit table name is planned as a table drop/create and is protected by the destructive-migration guard, not treated as a data-safe rename. Irregular or localized plurals such as Person / People should set table= and plural= explicitly. The fallback inflection is deterministic, small and English-oriented; it does not guess irregular nouns. It splits underscores and CamelCase into words, lowercases them for the table, and applies these suffixes to the final word: consonant plus y becomes ies ; s , x , z , ch and sh take es ; other words take s . Display labels retain uppercase acronyms ( APIKey becomes API key / API keys ). Thus Person defaults to persons , and Analysis to analysises ; provide explicit values when those mechanical defaults are not right. Generated identifiers must be portable ASCII SQL names of at most 63 characters. Names beginning with SQLite's reserved sqlite_ prefix and Hinoki's hinoki_migrations ledger name are rejected with an override hint. Physical-table conflicts are reported when models are aggregated for migrations, projects or one Admin instance. A model has exactly one primary key. Fields are keyword-only when constructing a model. Single-column uniqueness is field(unique=True) ; use @unique("a", "b") for a composite constraint. There is no nested class Meta . Supported field metadata includes primary key, uniqueness, maximum string length, defaults and foreign-key behavior. Optional built-in constraints and custom synchronous validators can also check values before ORM writes. Database types are inferred from annotations; unsupported types fail during model or migration validation. Model field constraints and validators ¶ field() metadata describes the database column and its migration: max_length becomes a bounded string column and a derived Schema constraint, unique becomes a database constraint, and default / default_factory provide values when constructing an instance. A foreign_key(...) declares the referenced table and its OnDelete behavior. The Python annotation supplies the column type and nullability. Use constraints=Field(...) for built-in value checks and validators=(...) for synchronous, application-specific checks. Existing max_length= remains a shorthand: from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import Field from hinoki.orm import Model , field def normalized ( value : str ) -> None : if value != value . strip (): raise ValueError ( "surrounding whitespace is not allowed" ) class Product ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) sku : str = field ( max_length = 32 , constraints = Field ( min_length = 3 , pattern = r "[A-Z0-9-]+" ), ) price : float = field ( constraints = Field ( gt = 0 )) name : str = field ( max_length = 120 , validators = ( normalized ,)) Built-in checks support string/list lengths, string patterns and membership, and numeric bounds and membership. Before applying checks, runtime type validation follows annotations for fields that declare constraints or validators, including nested list and dict values. Invalid declarations fail when the model class is created. Validators run immediately before inserts and ORM updates, including filtered bulk updates; they do not run on construction, assignment or reads. A refusal raises ModelValidationError with details containing each field's path , stable code and message , before SQL is sent. In an HTTP request it produces the standard 422 validation response; the admin displays the field messages. Custom validators are synchronous; raise ValueError to refuse a value. Do not perform database I/O or mutate values inside a validator. Rules involving other rows, permissions or current state belong in an operation. These checks complement, rather than replace, a Schema at the HTTP boundary. Schema validation can report request errors before calling an operation; Model validation also protects CLI, admin and direct ORM writes. Database constraints remain authoritative, and their enforcement varies by backend; see Schema validation . Hinoki stores PostgreSQL UUID, timestamp, JSON and byte values in their native column types. SQLite stores UUIDs and timestamps as text, JSON as JSON text and bytes as blobs. SQLite has one writer at a time; its transactions use a bounded connection pool and a busy timeout. SQLite string contains matching follows SQLite's case-folding behavior (ASCII case-insensitive). Query rows ¶ Class methods and querysets offer sync and async variants for common operations. Async variants are preferred in async handlers: task = await Task . aget ( id = task_id ) tasks = await Task . all () . filter ( owner_id = member_id , done = False ) . order_by ( "title" ) page = await Task . all () . filter ( done = False ) . apaginate ( PageParams ( page = 1 , page_size = 20 )) Filters accept validated field names and supported comparison/membership operators. Values are bound parameters; SQL identifiers are compiled from model metadata. Query methods do not issue SQL until an evaluation method such as awaiting the query, aget , acount , aupdate or adelete is called. @ordered_by supplies ordering only when a query does not specify order_by . An explicit order replaces it. Counts and bulk updates do not inherit default ordering. Reusable queries ¶ A reusable query is a typed class method that returns a QuerySet . Hinoki has no hidden default manager: Model.all() always means every row. from datetime import datetime from typing import Self from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , QuerySet , field class Task ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) title : str = field ( max_length = 200 ) done : bool = False deleted_at : datetime | None = None @classmethod def active ( cls ) -> QuerySet [ Self ]: return cls . filter ( deleted_at = None ) open_tasks = await Task . active () . filter ( done = False ) . order_by ( "title" ) everything = await Task . all () # the explicit way around the policy Pass the method where the framework asks for a base query, so every operation built on it sees the same rows: from hinoki import CrudAPI class Tasks ( CrudAPI , model = Task , path = "/tasks" ): read_schema = TaskOut def get_queryset ( self , principal ): return Task . active () class TaskAdmin ( ModelAdmin [ Task ]): def queryset ( self , principal ): return Task . active () Choose the place by what the rule is: Rule Where Why Row order @ordered_by(...) ( model options ) declared once, replaced by any explicit order_by A policy the whole app shares, such as hiding soft-deleted rows a named class method such as Task.active() , used in CrudAPI.get_queryset() or the admin's queryset() visible at each call site and in review; nothing is hidden implicitly Rows that depend on the caller CrudAPI.get_queryset(principal) or ModelAdmin.queryset(principal) the caller is available there; model-level code never sees it Authorization must not depend on a default that a call to all() or a raw query can skip: keep ownership and permission checks in access= , owner= and ModelAdmin.can() , and treat a reusable query as convenience, not as the security boundary. To generate write routes as well, provide create_schema= or update_schema= and/or set deletable = True ; protect generated writes with access = ... . See Generate CRUD routes for the full route and ownership contract. Create and update ¶ task = await Task . acreate ( TaskInput ( title = "Write docs" ), owner_id = member_id ) task . done = True await task . asave () # updates changed columns Server-supplied keywords take precedence over values from a Schema . A loaded model remembers its stored values; asave() updates changed columns and refuses primary-key changes. For a conditional write, use aupdate_where so ownership and state checks are part of the SQL condition. QuerySet.aupdate(...) and adelete() act on every row the filters match; they ignore ordering and refuse a queryset with limit or offset , so select the rows first and then filter on their keys ( filter(id__in=[...]) ). The model constructor is statically typed. Some keyword-based model methods still have broader type-checker signatures; see typing . Writes that do not read the row back ¶ By default every write returns the row as the database stored it: PostgreSQL and SQLite add RETURNING with every column, and MySQL/MariaDB select the row again in the same transaction. When the caller does not need that row, pass returning=False ; the statement then has no RETURNING (and no follow-up SELECT on MySQL/MariaDB): task = await Task . acreate ( title = "Draft" , owner_id = me , returning = False ) # as sent count = await Task . aupdate ( id = task . id , done = True , returning = False ) # rows written count = await Task . aupdate_where ({ "owner_id" : me }, { "done" : True }, returning = False ) count = await Task . filter ( owner_id = me ) . aupdate ({ "done" : False }, returning = False ) Method Default returning=False acreate , insert ( create ) the stored row the same instance, holding the values that were sent aupdate ( update ) the stored row, Model.NotFound if no row matches int row count; 0 when no row matches, no NotFound aupdate_where , QuerySet.aupdate ( update_where , update ) list of stored rows int row count What returning=False gives back is the client's side of the write. An insert sends every column, after defaults and factories ran in Python, so the returned instance holds exactly those values and remembers them, so a later asave() updates the row instead of inserting it again. An update returns no values at all; the @timestamps column is still set by the clock and validation still runs. Nothing is re-read from the database, so anything the database changes on the way in is not reflected: timestamp precision, numeric scale, JSON normalization, column types that store a different representation and triggers. Read the row with aget when you need the stored values. The count is the number the database reports. PostgreSQL and SQLite count the rows the statement matched; MySQL and MariaDB, with the driver's default connection settings, count the rows whose values actually changed, so a row that already held the new values counts 0. The cost of the default is the data sent back. In a raw-SQL measurement on PostgreSQL 17 with 16 statements in flight, a statement returning every column of a narrow row took 83.7 µs per operation against 75.8 µs returning only the key (+10%); with a ~10 KB jsonb column it took 143.4 µs against 75.9 µs (+89%). This is a single-machine measurement, not a guarantee for other workloads. returning is a keyword-only option of these methods, so a model cannot declare a field named returning : the class definition raises RegistrationError and asks for another name. Share fields: abstract models and mixins ¶ Fields, options and methods that several models need can live in a base class. An abstract model has no table of its own: it is not migrated, cannot be queried or saved, and exists to be subclassed. from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field , indexed , ordered_by , timestamps from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Keyed ( Model , abstract = True ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) @timestamps () @indexed ( "updated_at" ) @ordered_by ( "-updated_at" ) class Tracked ( Model , abstract = True ): created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) updated_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) class Article ( Keyed , Tracked ): title : str = field ( max_length = 120 ) Article has the columns created_at , updated_at , id and title , is ordered by -updated_at , has the index and refreshes updated_at on every update. Tracked.all() raises ModelError : query Article . abstract=True is not inherited. A subclass is a table model unless it says abstract=True again; its table name is derived unless table= overrides it. An abstract model needs no primary key; a table model needs exactly one, its own or an inherited one. Options declared on abstract bases are inherited: every base's @unique constraints and @indexed indexes, and the order and timestamp column of the first base (in the order the bases resolve) that sets one. Applying a decorator on the subclass replaces what was inherited for that kind of option; it does not add to it. To keep an inherited index while adding one, declare both on the subclass. Options you do not touch stay inherited. A replacement made in an abstract base holds for everything below it: a model reads its options from the abstract bases it lists, and each of those already carries what it inherited and replaced. Plain mixins work too: a class that is not a model contributes the fields it annotates, field(...) and foreign_key(...) included, and its methods. An annotation marked ClassVar is not a field. A type checker does not see a plain mixin's fields as constructor arguments, so prefer an abstract model when you construct instances with those fields. One name, two types. If two bases give the same field name different types and the class does not declare that field itself, the class is refused with an error naming both bases. The same type from two bases is accepted, and a class (or an abstract subclass) that redeclares a field decides its type. A type checker still reports a redeclaration with an incompatible type, as it does for any class. Subclassing a table model is allowed: the subclass gets a copy of the parent's columns in a separate table, derived from the subclass name unless table= overrides it. hinoki migrations plan shows the new table. The two tables are unrelated: there is no join between them and a query on the parent does not return the subclass's rows. A table model does not pass its options on; only abstract bases do. Column order follows Python's dataclass rules: the fields of model bases come first, starting from the last base listed, then the fields of plain mixins, then the class's own. Hinoki does not depend on the order; a new table is created with it. A foreign key in an abstract model or a mixin needs a reverse name that differs per subclass; see relations . Relations ¶ Declare a foreign-key column with foreign_key(OtherModel, ...) . It creates the other_id column and a named relation ( row.other ), but reading the relation does not fetch data. Load it explicitly with select_related or prefetch_related . For many-to-many data, declare an association model with two foreign keys and a composite @unique constraint; see relations and loading . Schema options ¶ Use model option decorators for indexes, ordering and composite uniqueness. Use schemas to define request and response data; a model does not decide which columns cross the HTTP boundary. Migrations ¶ Model changes do not alter a database. Generate and review migration files, then apply them deliberately with the migration commands .

docs.text: By default every write returns the row as the database stored it: PostgreSQL and SQLite add RETURNING with every column, and MySQL/MariaDB select the row again in the same transaction. When the caller does not need that row, pass returning=False ; the statement then has no RETURNING (and no follow-up SELECT on MySQL/MariaDB): task = await Task . acreate ( title = "Draft" , owner_id = me , returning = False ) # as sent count = await Task . aupdate ( id = task . id , done = True , returning = False ) # rows written count = await Task . aupdate_where ({ "owner_id" : me }, { "done" : True }, returning = False ) count = await Task . filter ( owner_id = me ) . aupdate ({ "done" : False }, returning = False ) Method Default returning=False acreate , insert ( create ) the stored row the same instance, holding the values that were sent aupdate ( update ) the stored row, Model.NotFound if no row matches int row count; 0 when no row matches, no NotFound aupdate_where , QuerySet.aupdate ( update_where , update ) list of stored rows int row count What returning=False gives back is the client's side of the write. An insert sends every column, after defaults and factories ran in Python, so the returned instance holds exactly those values and remembers them, so a later asave() updates the row instead of inserting it again. An update returns no values at all; the @timestamps column is still set by the clock and validation still runs. Nothing is re-read from the database, so anything the database changes on the way in is not reflected: timestamp precision, numeric scale, JSON normalization, column types that store a different representation and triggers. Read the row with aget when you need the stored values. The count is the number the database reports. PostgreSQL and SQLite count the rows the statement matched; MySQL and MariaDB, with the driver's default connection settings, count the rows whose values actually changed, so a row that already held the new values counts 0. The cost of the default is the data sent back. In a raw-SQL measurement on PostgreSQL 17 with 16 statements in flight, a statement returning every column of a narrow row took 83.7 µs per operation against 75.8 µs returning only the key (+10%); with a ~10 KB jsonb column it took 143.4 µs against 75.9 µs (+89%). This is a single-machine measurement, not a guarantee for other workloads. returning is a keyword-only option of these methods, so a model cannot declare a field named returning : the class definition raises RegistrationError and asks for another name.
docs.title: Writes that do not read the row back

docs.text: Fields, options and methods that several models need can live in a base class. An abstract model has no table of its own: it is not migrated, cannot be queried or saved, and exists to be subclassed. from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field , indexed , ordered_by , timestamps from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Keyed ( Model , abstract = True ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) @timestamps () @indexed ( "updated_at" ) @ordered_by ( "-updated_at" ) class Tracked ( Model , abstract = True ): created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) updated_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) class Article ( Keyed , Tracked ): title : str = field ( max_length = 120 ) Article has the columns created_at , updated_at , id and title , is ordered by -updated_at , has the index and refreshes updated_at on every update. Tracked.all() raises ModelError : query Article . abstract=True is not inherited. A subclass is a table model unless it says abstract=True again; its table name is derived unless table= overrides it. An abstract model needs no primary key; a table model needs exactly one, its own or an inherited one. Options declared on abstract bases are inherited: every base's @unique constraints and @indexed indexes, and the order and timestamp column of the first base (in the order the bases resolve) that sets one. Applying a decorator on the subclass replaces what was inherited for that kind of option; it does not add to it. To keep an inherited index while adding one, declare both on the subclass. Options you do not touch stay inherited. A replacement made in an abstract base holds for everything below it: a model reads its options from the abstract bases it lists, and each of those already carries what it inherited and replaced. Plain mixins work too: a class that is not a model contributes the fields it annotates, field(...) and foreign_key(...) included, and its methods. An annotation marked ClassVar is not a field. A type checker does not see a plain mixin's fields as constructor arguments, so prefer an abstract model when you construct instances with those fields. One name, two types. If two bases give the same field name different types and the class does not declare that field itself, the class is refused with an error naming both bases. The same type from two bases is accepted, and a class (or an abstract subclass) that redeclares a field decides its type. A type checker still reports a redeclaration with an incompatible type, as it does for any class. Subclassing a table model is allowed: the subclass gets a copy of the parent's columns in a separate table, derived from the subclass name unless table= overrides it. hinoki migrations plan shows the new table. The two tables are unrelated: there is no join between them and a query on the parent does not return the subclass's rows. A table model does not pass its options on; only abstract bases do. Column order follows Python's dataclass rules: the fields of model bases come first, starting from the last base listed, then the fields of plain mixins, then the class's own. Hinoki does not depend on the order; a new table is created with it. A foreign key in an abstract model or a mixin needs a reverse name that differs per subclass; see relations .
docs.title: Share fields: abstract models and mixins

docs.text: Declare a foreign-key column with foreign_key(OtherModel, ...) . It creates the other_id column and a named relation ( row.other ), but reading the relation does not fetch data. Load it explicitly with select_related or prefetch_related . For many-to-many data, declare an association model with two foreign keys and a composite @unique constraint; see relations and loading .

docs.text: Use model option decorators for indexes, ordering and composite uniqueness. Use schemas to define request and response data; a model does not decide which columns cross the HTTP boundary.

docs.text: Model changes do not alter a database. Generate and review migration files, then apply them deliberately with the migration commands .

docs.text: Application modules and resources ¶ Modules own resources whose lifetime belongs to a worker or a management command, such as a database pool. They are created during startup, made available through ModuleContext , and closed when that run ends. Declare modules ¶ This excerpt uses the health route and Tasks API from your application; the imports and application-specific declarations are omitted here. class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "APP_" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , include = [ health , Tasks ]) The settings' database: DatabaseSettings field makes Hinoki install DatabaseModule before any declared module, so a module that requires = (DatabaseModule,) finds it. Declaring DatabaseModule in modules= , or installing an instance, replaces that automatic module. When a module class is passed, Hinoki constructs it from the settings class. A module instance is useful when setup needs explicit runtime arguments. The database pool is opened after the worker starts and closed during shutdown; importing the model module does not open a connection. Provide and retrieve dependencies ¶ A module calls ctx.provide(Type, value) during lifespan startup. Other modules can declare dependencies and retrieve the provided value with ctx.get(Type) . Dependencies determine startup and shutdown order. Missing, duplicate or circular providers fail application startup. A module instance whose class extends a required module class satisfies that dependency. For example, a custom DatabaseModule subclass can replace the settings-provided database while modules requiring DatabaseModule continue to start after it. Module lifespan hooks are async. Keep startup bounded, fail fast when a required service is unavailable, and close each owned resource in finally . Startup and shutdown hooks ¶ For an action at the edge of a worker's life that owns no resource, such as warming a cache, logging the build or flushing a counter, list functions on the application instead of writing a module ( ProjectSettings , health and Tasks are those of the previous example): import logging from hinoki import Hinoki , ModuleContext from hinoki.db import Database log = logging . getLogger ( "app" ) async def warm_cache ( ctx : ModuleContext ) -> None : await ctx . get ( Database ) . fetch ( "SELECT 1" ) def say_goodbye ( ctx : ModuleContext ) -> None : log . info ( "worker stopping" ) app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , include = [ health , Tasks ], on_startup = [ warm_cache ], on_shutdown = [ say_goodbye ], ) A hook takes the worker's ModuleContext ( ctx.settings , ctx.get(Type) , ctx.tasks ). It is async def , or a plain def that runs on the bounded sync executor like a sync handler. Model methods reach the worker's database inside a hook as they do inside a request. Pass hooks as a list or tuple when constructing Hinoki ; the app's on_startup and on_shutdown tuples are read-only. Hooks must be callables, not async generators, and must return None . A plain def may instead return an awaitable, which Hinoki awaits; use async def when the hook needs to await work directly. Startup hooks Shutdown hooks Run Once per worker, after every module has started, in the listed order Once per worker, before background tasks, the sync executor and the modules are closed, in the listed order Time limit Share lifecycle.startup_timeout with the modules Each has its own lifecycle.shutdown_timeout Requests Answered 503 not_ready until the last hook returns Answered 503 not_ready from the moment shutdown begins A hook fails or times out Startup fails: later hooks do not run, no shutdown hook runs, the modules already started are closed, and the server is told that startup failed. The log has the traceback; the message names the hook ( startup hook 'warm_cache' failed to start: TimeoutError ) It is logged and reported as a shutdown error; the remaining hooks and the module cleanup still run Shutdown hooks run only after a startup that completed, and a shutdown hook is not the finally of a startup hook. Use this rule to choose: a resource you own is a module (its lifespan closes it even when a later step of startup fails); an action is a hook . A plain def hook that is still running when its time limit passes cannot be interrupted; it keeps its executor thread until it returns. Hooks run where the application serves requests: under hinoki dev / serve and any ASGI server, on the first request of each WSGI worker, and in the test clients . hinoki manage commands, check , routes and migrations do not run them. Standalone scripts ¶ For app maintenance tasks, declare a management command and list its required module classes in Command.requires . Hinoki starts only those modules and their dependencies for one command run, so a database module is opened and closed without starting the HTTP server or unrelated modules. Standalone scripts outside Hinoki's server or management-command runner have no module lifespan. Open their own Database and close it explicitly; do not import a module-global pool. The blog seed script demonstrates this pattern. See settings and database ownership , serving and sync and async .

docs.text: OpenAPI document ¶ Hinoki.openapi() builds an OpenAPI 3.1 document from the routes registered with the app. Paths, parameters, request bodies, response schemas, declared errors and supported authentication schemes come from the action declarations and type annotations. Generate the document from a project target without starting a server: cd examples uv run --project .. hinoki openapi notes.main:app --output openapi.json uv run --project .. hinoki openapi notes.main:app --check openapi.json The command does not open a database and works even when openapi_url is disabled. It writes stable, sorted JSON, and --check compares parsed JSON so whitespace-only changes do not report drift. See the command-line guide for output and exit-status details. Serve the document and viewers ¶ All three URLs are disabled by default. Set openapi_url to serve JSON; add docs_url for the bundled Swagger UI or redoc_url for ReDoc: from hinoki import Hinoki app = Hinoki ( openapi_url = "/openapi.json" , docs_url = "/docs" , redoc_url = "/redoc" , ) The corresponding docs.openapi_url , docs.docs_url and docs.redoc_url settings provide the same defaults. A viewer requires openapi_url . Hinoki(...) arguments override settings; passing None disables a page. The packaged viewers work without a CDN. The generated OpenAPI document, Swagger UI, ReDoc and their assets answer HEAD with the same status and representation headers as GET , without a response body. Each request still has its own request ID in the configured response header ( x-request-id by default). QUERY operations ¶ The document is OpenAPI 3.1, which has no field for the QUERY method (OpenAPI 3.2 adds query ). An action declared with @http.query is therefore written under the path item's x-query extension field, with the same operation object as any other method: operation ID, parameters, request body, responses and security. The document stays valid 3.1. Tools that only read the standard method fields do not see these operations: Swagger UI and ReDoc do not list them, and a client generator skips them unless it is told about x-query . The application MCP and explain_action read the field. What is generated ¶ A unique operationId is derived from the handler's qualified name. If names collide, Hinoki appends a numeric suffix. The first line of the handler docstring becomes summary ; the remaining lines become description . Path, query and pagination parameters come from the bound handler signature. Body fields and successful response fields come from Schema annotations. Parser and renderer media types supply the content types. Typed UploadedFile parameters generate a multipart/form-data request body with binary file properties. Repeated files use an array of binary items; optional single-file bindings are not required in the body or property list. Text keys read dynamically through request.POST are not inferred or listed. A declared errors=(...) adds response entries for those APIError classes. Request binding and schema validation errors are documented as 422 where the action has request inputs. access=... adds a security requirement when its authentication provider supplies an OpenAPI scheme. Authentication responses are included in the operation. Admin HTML routes marked hide_from_docs are omitted. Discriminated unions declared as Schema fields become OpenAPI oneOf schemas with a discriminator and explicit tag-to-component mapping. Variant tag fields appear as required string enums; the runtime uses the same tags to select exactly one branch. List items, nested fields and nullable unions retain that structure. For route input and response documentation, put the union inside a wrapper Schema ; bare union return annotations are rejected instead of producing an incomplete schema. As elsewhere, the response annotation does not cause runtime response validation. oneOf : - $ref : "#/components/schemas/Cat" - $ref : "#/components/schemas/Dog" discriminator : propertyName : type mapping : cat : "#/components/schemas/Cat" dog : "#/components/schemas/Dog" See Schemas: discriminated unions for the Python declarations and validation behavior. For file binding syntax, limits and the in-memory boundary, see upload files . Add a useful docstring to each handler because it is the source for operation text: @http . get ( "/tasks/ {task_id} " ) async def get_task ( task_id : UUID ) -> TaskOutput : """Read one task. Returns the task visible to the authenticated caller. """ ... Current limits ¶ Per-action tags , deprecated , a caller-supplied operation_id and include_in_schema controls are not implemented. Response bodies are generated from annotations; runtime response validation against those annotations is not implemented. See project status for other API boundaries.

docs.text: Pagination ¶ An action opts into page-number pagination with pagination=PageNumberPagination() . A size you leave out comes from the application's pagination settings group; without settings the defaults are page_size=20 and max_page_size=100 . The framework parses and validates page and page_size , injects a PageParams value, and documents both query parameters in OpenAPI. This is the Tracker's authenticated list pattern: it limits each page to the caller’s own tasks. Include the route in an app whose settings declare a database, as the Tracker app factory does. from tracker.models import Member , Task from tracker.schemas import TaskOut from tracker.security import member_only from hinoki import Caller , http from hinoki.pagination import Page , PageNumberPagination , PageParams @http . get ( "/tasks" , access = member_only , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_tasks ( page : PageParams , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> Page [ TaskOut ]: rows = await Task . filter ( owner_id = caller . user . id ) . apaginate ( page ) return rows . map ( TaskOut . from_model ) Pages are one-based. page_size defaults to the strategy's configured size and cannot exceed its maximum. Invalid values produce a validation response before the handler runs; page is limited to 1 000 000 000, and longer or larger values answer 422 with the code le . Page contains items , page , page_size , total and the computed pages . Empty result sets have zero pages; a page beyond the end has an empty items list. Page.map() converts each item while preserving the counts and requested page. Defaults for the whole application ¶ settings.AppSettings has a pagination group, set in code, in the environment ( BLOG_PAGINATION__PAGE_SIZE=25 , BLOG_PAGINATION__MAX_PAGE_SIZE=200 ) or in TOML: from hinoki import settings class BlogSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "BLOG_" ): pass # BLOG_PAGINATION__PAGE_SIZE=25 BLOG_PAGINATION__MAX_PAGE_SIZE=200 Pass BlogSettings to Hinoki(settings=BlogSettings, ...) in your app factory; keep that app's database module and access policy in the same assembly. Precedence, from strongest to weakest: a size set on the action's PageNumberPagination(...) , the application's pagination settings, then 20 and 100. Each size is resolved separately, so PageNumberPagination(page_size=10) keeps its 10 and takes its maximum from the settings. The result must satisfy 1 <= page_size <= max_page_size : invalid settings fail when they load, and an action whose own size does not fit the resolved other one (for example PageNumberPagination(max_page_size=10) under a settings page_size of 25) fails when it is included, naming the action. The generated OpenAPI parameters show the resolved values. Use the queryset's apaginate / paginate methods for database rows. Page.of(rows, params) slices an in-memory sequence and counts that sequence; it is not a substitute for database pagination on large tables.
docs.title: Pagination
