docs.text: Structuring a Hinoki application: pattern and best practices ¶ Opinionated, with reasons. It describes how the framework's features fit together; each rule is something the framework either enforces, can check with an optional rule, or leaves to review (marked enforced , rule or convention ). The reference blog ( examples/blog ) and the small notes example ( examples/notes ) show the parts; examples/tracker is the layered example: api → operations → models , row permission in the statements, the direction enforced by Imports.forbid , operations tested without HTTP. 1. Three layers, one direction ¶ HTTP layer API classes / functions shapes, status codes, access policy, transaction=True │ (hinoki.routing, Access, Schema) ▼ Operations plain async functions one business operation each; no Request, no HTTP types │ (commands/queries) ▼ Persistence Model / QuerySet tables, relations, explicit loading HTTP layer turns a request into typed values ( Schema , path/query parameters, Caller ) and an operation's result into a response schema. It contains no business rules and no SQL. Operations hold the rules ("an editor may publish only their own draft"). They take plain arguments ( principal , a Schema , ids) so they can be called from an action, a CLI, a test, an admin hook ( ModelAdmin.save ) or an MCP tool. Why: an action that reads cookies or headers cannot be reused; an operation can. Persistence never imports the HTTP layer. Rule: Imports.forbid(source="shop.models", target="shop.api") (and the same for operations → api). Small apps may skip the middle layer (the notes example does). Add it when an action contains a rule you would want to call from somewhere else. 2. Where each concern lives ¶ Concern Put it Why Authentication An auth provider ( BearerAuth , JWTAuth , …) returning a Caller One path, identical for HTTP, admin and MCP Coarse permission Access(auth=…, permissions=[…]) on the action (or once for a function group: tasks = RouteGroup("/tasks", access=member_only, atomic=True) , then @tasks.get("/") ). Public is the default : protect on purpose. Rule: Actions.require_access A forgotten policy is the most common hole Row permission (ownership, tenant) Prefer the statement : scope aupdate / adelete by owner so the check and write are one operation. Avoids a check-then-write race. Hidden rows usually look missing (404). If the API promises a distinct 403 for another owner's row, preserve that contract with a conditional write and explicit fallback classification; document the information it reveals. Input validation The Schema (types, constraints, patterns) Strict, no coercion, validated in Rust before your code runs Business rules Operations Testable without HTTP Transactions transaction=True on the action (writes) Commit after the response is encoded, rollback before the error becomes HTTP. Rule: Transactions.require_atomic Errors Raise APIError subclasses and declare them on the action : @http.post(..., errors=(PostAlreadyPublished, errors.Forbidden)) . Translate database errors once with app.errors.handle(...) Failures are exceptions. The declaration (status and code come from the class) feeds OpenAPI, the MCP tool description and, in tests, ASGIClient(app, strict_errors=True) , which fails on an error answer the action did not declare. A returned Reply commits the transaction Secrets Settings/environment, passed to JWTKey , Admin(secret=…) , never defaults Nothing to leak from the repository 3. Schema classes and models ¶ Models describe tables; Schema classes describe the API. Never return a model. Name them by role: PostIn / PostCreate (what a client may set), PostPatch (every field UNSET by default), PostOut (what a client may see). Rules: Actions.forbid_model_responses() refuses an action whose return type is a Model (also inside list / Page /unions); Schemas.forbid_exposure("password_hash", …) keeps columns out of responses even through nesting and subclasses. Create from a Schema and add what only the server knows: await Post.acreate(data, author_id=principal.user.id) (server values win over the client's). Update with await row.aupdate_from(patch) (writes only what was sent). Respond with PostOut.from_model(row, author_name=row.author.name) . A server-assigned field must not exist in the input schema at all; the keyword override is a second line of defence. Constraints and patterns belong on the Schema , using the Rust pattern syntax (whole-value, no look-around). 4. Relations and queries ¶ Relations are never lazy. Load what the response shows ( select_related for single values, prefetch_related for collections) in the same place that builds the response, so the cost is visible in one function. Paginate every list ( pagination=… + PageParams ). Never return an unbounded list; never await a whole table to count or aggregate (use acount() , filters, or SQL). Filter and order only by names you choose; never pass client-supplied column names to filter or order_by (the admin only sorts by its displayed columns for this reason). 5. Sync and async ¶ Prefer async handlers. A sync handler runs on a bounded thread pool and may use the sync model methods ( Model.get , create , …) through the worker's event loop; it must not block for long, and the queue is bounded ( overloaded → 503). CPU-heavy work (password hashing) goes through PasswordHasher , which has its own bounded pool and releases the GIL. Never call blocking code from an async handler. 6. Modules ¶ An application is a set of modules with explicit dependencies and a lifespan ( DatabaseModule , your own Module ). Importing a module registers nothing and opens nothing. Resources are created in the worker's lifespan, once per worker; migrations are applied by a deploy step, never at startup, never from every worker. A standalone maintenance script such as examples/blog/seed.py owns and closes its short-lived database connection directly because it runs outside a server lifecycle. 7. Migrations ¶ hinoki migrations plan writes reviewable SQL and a state file; destructive operations are flagged and need --allow-destructive ; adding a NOT NULL column without a default is flagged. Review the SQL like code, apply with migrations apply against a disposable database first. 8. Testing ¶ Run the database tests against disposable servers for the backends you support: PostgreSQL uses HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL , with separate migration conformance runs for MySQL ( HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL ) and MariaDB ( HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL ). Without a URL, tests that require that backend are skipped; read the skip summary and do not treat another backend's green run as conformance for it. Drive the application through the ASGI harness (no sockets) for HTTP behaviour; test operations directly. For security code, use independent test vectors and known expected outputs; inject the clock ( JWTAuth.now ) so tests do not depend on elapsed time. Look at rendered UI in real browsers ( tests/browser/verify.py ) before calling it done. 9. Security defaults to keep ¶ HTTPS terminates somewhere you control (set Admin(secure_cookies=True) behind a proxy); Access on everything that is not public on purpose; CSRF on every cookie-authenticated form (the admin does it); strict CSP; passwords with Argon2id only; JWT keys with a fixed algorithm and a kid ; no token, password or hash in logs or error bodies; uploads held within the 1 MiB body cap unless you add streaming; real personal data never in tests or fixtures. 10. Rules to turn on from day one ¶ hinoki new generates a project with HNK-ACC-001 , HNK-TXN-001 and HNK-SCH-001 enabled. Add Imports.forbid for the layer direction in section 1. Waivers live in hinoki-rules.toml , are decided by the owner, have a reason and a bounded target, and are never edited by tools or agents to make a check pass. 11. Anti-patterns ¶ Returning a Model or a dict built from one. For a distinct 403 response on a write that can race, make the conditional write and fallback explicit. A business rule inside an action that another entry point also needs. Reply(4xx) inside a transaction=True action (it commits). Client-supplied column names reaching filter / order_by . Applying migrations at startup; creating a pool at import time. A broad waiver ( * ) or editing waivers to silence a rule. Catching Exception in an action to "keep going": let the framework translate it and roll back. 12. More than one service ¶ Split a system only for a reason you can name (independent deploys, different scaling, a team boundary), because every split costs something the framework cannot hide: No joins, no shared transaction. A foreign key never crosses a service. Store the other service's id as a plain value, and treat what it returns as a snapshot. A write that must touch two services is a sequence of calls that can half-fail: make each step idempotent (a client-supplied key, or a natural unique constraint) and decide what a retry does before writing the code. Each service owns its tables. Other services call its API; they never read its database. Migrations belong to the owner and are applied by its deploy step ( section 7 ). The caller is a Caller too. Service-to-service calls authenticate like any client (a JWT with a service identity and narrow permissions , verified by JWTAuth ); do not forward the end user's token unless the callee must act as that user. Wrap every remote call in an operation ( section 1 ) with a timeout and a mapped failure (a 502/503 you chose), never letting a client library's exception become the response. Share contracts, not models. Publish the response Schema classes (or the OpenAPI document) that other services depend on; keep Model s private. Not covered yet: a runnable two-service example and a client helper.

docs.text: HTTP layer API classes / functions shapes, status codes, access policy, transaction=True │ (hinoki.routing, Access, Schema) ▼ Operations plain async functions one business operation each; no Request, no HTTP types │ (commands/queries) ▼ Persistence Model / QuerySet tables, relations, explicit loading HTTP layer turns a request into typed values ( Schema , path/query parameters, Caller ) and an operation's result into a response schema. It contains no business rules and no SQL. Operations hold the rules ("an editor may publish only their own draft"). They take plain arguments ( principal , a Schema , ids) so they can be called from an action, a CLI, a test, an admin hook ( ModelAdmin.save ) or an MCP tool. Why: an action that reads cookies or headers cannot be reused; an operation can. Persistence never imports the HTTP layer. Rule: Imports.forbid(source="shop.models", target="shop.api") (and the same for operations → api). Small apps may skip the middle layer (the notes example does). Add it when an action contains a rule you would want to call from somewhere else.

docs.text: Quick start ¶ This walkthrough uses the default local SQLite database, so no database server or URL setup is needed. It creates the table with an explicit migration; Hinoki does not create or migrate tables when the app starts. To use PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB instead, see Configure a database . Plan and apply the migration ¶ examples/hinoki.toml registers Notes, Tracker and Blog as independent apps. From the repository root, enter examples/ and use the locked environment in the parent directory. The migration planner reads the Notes model and its recorded state and writes numbered SQL and state files for review: cd examples uv run --project .. hinoki app list uv run --project .. hinoki migrations plan --app notes uv run --project .. hinoki migrations sql --app notes 0001 -create-table-notes Review the SQL, then apply it explicitly. With no URL set, the migration command and the Notes app both use sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 : uv run --project .. hinoki migrations apply --app notes The local database file and migration ledger are created when apply runs. Use a disposable database while evaluating the example. Start the app and send a request ¶ uv run --project .. hinoki dev notes.main:app The database field of the Notes settings opens a pool for the worker and closes it at shutdown. It does not create tables. In another terminal, create a note and list the collection: curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"title":"First note","body":"Hello"}' curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes The POST returns 201 Created and a JSON object with the generated id , title and body . The GET returns a JSON array. Invalid input is rejected before the handler runs; see error handling for the response format. Where to go next ¶ Tutorial : build the Tracker example in seven steps, then learn the project and app workflow. Models and queries : fields, querysets and relation loading. Migrations : migration files, destructive changes and deployment workflow. Configure a database : choose another backend, set its URL and understand backend-specific behavior. API reference : public symbols and signatures.

docs.text: Relations, many-to-many and loading ¶ Hinoki stores relations as ordinary foreign-key columns and loads related rows only when a query asks for them. Attribute access never performs hidden I/O. Declare a foreign key ¶ from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , OnDelete , field , foreign_key class Author ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) name : str class Post ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) author_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Author , on_delete = OnDelete . RESTRICT , related_name = "posts" , ) title : str The author_id field is stored on posts . The forward relation is post.author ; author.posts is the reverse relation. The foreign-key type must match the referenced primary-key type. on_delete is required, so what happens to a row when the row it references is deleted is always a decision. Its value is a member of the OnDelete enum ( from hinoki.orm import OnDelete ): on_delete When the referenced row is deleted OnDelete.RESTRICT The delete is refused while referencing rows exist OnDelete.CASCADE The referencing rows are deleted too OnDelete.SET_NULL The column is set to NULL ; the field must be annotated | None OnDelete.NO_ACTION Like RESTRICT , checked by the database at the end of the statement Only enum members are accepted. Text such as on_delete="cascade" , which earlier revisions took, is reported by a type checker and refused with a RegistrationError when the module is imported. OnDelete.SET_NULL on a field without | None is refused the same way, before any migration is planned: class Note ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) post_id : UUID | None = foreign_key ( Post , on_delete = OnDelete . SET_NULL , default = None ) The rule is written into the REFERENCES ... ON DELETE clause of the generated migration and enforced by the database. Foreign keys in abstract models and mixins ¶ A foreign key declared in an abstract model or a mixin is registered once for each table model that inherits it. The forward relation keeps its name on every model. The reverse name must differ, so write it with the {model} placeholder, which becomes the inheriting class's name in lower case: class Owned ( Model , abstract = True ): team_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Team , on_delete = OnDelete . CASCADE , related_name = " {model} _set" ) class Article ( Owned ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) class Page ( Owned ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) Team gets the reverse relations article_set and page_set . With a fixed related_name , the second model that inherits the field is refused with an error naming both models. A table model that subclasses another table model copies the column and the forward relation; it gets a reverse relation of its own only when the name uses the placeholder, because a fixed name already belongs to its parent. A foreign key cannot reference an abstract model, which has no table. {model} is the only placeholder. Without related_name there is no reverse relation and nothing can collide. Load related rows explicitly ¶ Use select_related for a forward foreign key when a query needs one related row (one LEFT JOIN in the same statement; acount() and apaginate() leave that join out of their COUNT , since loading a to-one relation cannot change the row count, but keep a join that a filter such as author__name=... needs). Use prefetch_related for a reverse or collection relation; it issues a separate bounded query and attaches the results. posts = await Post . all () . select_related ( "author" ) for post in posts : print ( post . author . name ) Accessing an unloaded relation raises a relation-loading error. Load the relation explicitly so the query is visible in the calling code. One-to-one relations ¶ A one-to-one relation uses the same foreign-key declaration with unique=True ; there is no separate field helper. The unique constraint enforces that each target is referenced by at most one row. Keep the reverse relation explicit with related_name : from __future__ import annotations from typing import ClassVar from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , OnDelete , field , foreign_key from hinoki.orm.relations import Related class User ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) profile : ClassVar [ Related [ Profile | None ]] class Profile ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) user_id : UUID = foreign_key ( User , on_delete = OnDelete . CASCADE , unique = True , related_name = "profile" , ) user : ClassVar [ Related [ User ]] The forward profile.user relation has one required target. The reverse user.profile relation is Profile | None : a user may not have a profile. Load it explicitly and in a bounded number of queries: profiles = await Profile . all () . select_related ( "user" ) users = await User . all () . prefetch_related ( "profile" ) select_related joins the forward target into the profile query; prefetch_related uses one batched query for profiles and returns one profile or None per user. Neither access pattern performs lazy queries. If a database has drifted and contains multiple rows despite the unique declaration, prefetch_related raises MultipleObjectsReturned rather than choosing one. Migrations create the FK and unique constraint together; applying a unique constraint to existing duplicate data fails and requires an explicit data cleanup before retrying. When changing an existing foreign key to unique=True , SQLite rebuilds the table and may reject duplicates; MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL require a hand-written migration for the uniqueness change. Resolve duplicates before applying the constraint. Many-to-many relationships are represented by an explicit join model with two foreign keys and a composite @unique constraint. There is no implicit many-to-many table or through= shortcut. Model a many-to-many relationship ¶ Define a model for the association table. Each row links one post to one tag; the composite uniqueness constraint prevents the same pair from being inserted twice. from typing import ClassVar from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , OnDelete , field , foreign_key , unique from hinoki.orm.relations import Related class Post ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) title : str tag_links : ClassVar [ "Related[list[PostTag]]" ] class Tag ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) name : str post_links : ClassVar [ "Related[list[PostTag]]" ] @unique ( "post_id" , "tag_id" ) class PostTag ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) post_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Post , on_delete = OnDelete . CASCADE , related_name = "tag_links" ) tag_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Tag , on_delete = OnDelete . CASCADE , related_name = "post_links" ) Create a link by inserting a PostTag row. To read a post's tags, query the join model and load its tag foreign key in the same query: post = await Post . acreate ( title = "Release notes" ) tag = await Tag . acreate ( name = "docs" ) await PostTag . acreate ( post_id = post . id , tag_id = tag . id ) links = await PostTag . filter ( post_id = post . id ) . select_related ( "tag" ) tag_names = [ link . tag . name for link in links ] The reverse post.tag_links relation contains PostTag rows; load it with prefetch_related("tag_links") before accessing it. It does not return Tag objects or fetch data on attribute access. A join model can also carry its own fields, such as the time a tag was added. Include all three models in the migration plan so the association table and its uniqueness constraint are created together. This explicit form supports association rows and their foreign-key relations. Hinoki does not currently generate the join model or expose a direct post.tags relation. See models and queries and migrations for schema changes to foreign keys.

docs.text: A foreign key declared in an abstract model or a mixin is registered once for each table model that inherits it. The forward relation keeps its name on every model. The reverse name must differ, so write it with the {model} placeholder, which becomes the inheriting class's name in lower case: class Owned ( Model , abstract = True ): team_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Team , on_delete = OnDelete . CASCADE , related_name = " {model} _set" ) class Article ( Owned ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) class Page ( Owned ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) Team gets the reverse relations article_set and page_set . With a fixed related_name , the second model that inherits the field is refused with an error naming both models. A table model that subclasses another table model copies the column and the forward relation; it gets a reverse relation of its own only when the name uses the placeholder, because a fixed name already belongs to its parent. A foreign key cannot reference an abstract model, which has no table. {model} is the only placeholder. Without related_name there is no reverse relation and nothing can collide.
docs.title: Foreign keys in abstract models and mixins

docs.text: Use select_related for a forward foreign key when a query needs one related row (one LEFT JOIN in the same statement; acount() and apaginate() leave that join out of their COUNT , since loading a to-one relation cannot change the row count, but keep a join that a filter such as author__name=... needs). Use prefetch_related for a reverse or collection relation; it issues a separate bounded query and attaches the results. posts = await Post . all () . select_related ( "author" ) for post in posts : print ( post . author . name ) Accessing an unloaded relation raises a relation-loading error. Load the relation explicitly so the query is visible in the calling code.
docs.title: Load related rows explicitly

docs.text: A one-to-one relation uses the same foreign-key declaration with unique=True ; there is no separate field helper. The unique constraint enforces that each target is referenced by at most one row. Keep the reverse relation explicit with related_name : from __future__ import annotations from typing import ClassVar from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , OnDelete , field , foreign_key from hinoki.orm.relations import Related class User ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) profile : ClassVar [ Related [ Profile | None ]] class Profile ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) user_id : UUID = foreign_key ( User , on_delete = OnDelete . CASCADE , unique = True , related_name = "profile" , ) user : ClassVar [ Related [ User ]] The forward profile.user relation has one required target. The reverse user.profile relation is Profile | None : a user may not have a profile. Load it explicitly and in a bounded number of queries: profiles = await Profile . all () . select_related ( "user" ) users = await User . all () . prefetch_related ( "profile" ) select_related joins the forward target into the profile query; prefetch_related uses one batched query for profiles and returns one profile or None per user. Neither access pattern performs lazy queries. If a database has drifted and contains multiple rows despite the unique declaration, prefetch_related raises MultipleObjectsReturned rather than choosing one. Migrations create the FK and unique constraint together; applying a unique constraint to existing duplicate data fails and requires an explicit data cleanup before retrying. When changing an existing foreign key to unique=True , SQLite rebuilds the table and may reject duplicates; MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL require a hand-written migration for the uniqueness change. Resolve duplicates before applying the constraint. Many-to-many relationships are represented by an explicit join model with two foreign keys and a composite @unique constraint. There is no implicit many-to-many table or through= shortcut.
docs.title: One-to-one relations

docs.text: Define a model for the association table. Each row links one post to one tag; the composite uniqueness constraint prevents the same pair from being inserted twice. from typing import ClassVar from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , OnDelete , field , foreign_key , unique from hinoki.orm.relations import Related class Post ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) title : str tag_links : ClassVar [ "Related[list[PostTag]]" ] class Tag ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) name : str post_links : ClassVar [ "Related[list[PostTag]]" ] @unique ( "post_id" , "tag_id" ) class PostTag ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) post_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Post , on_delete = OnDelete . CASCADE , related_name = "tag_links" ) tag_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Tag , on_delete = OnDelete . CASCADE , related_name = "post_links" ) Create a link by inserting a PostTag row. To read a post's tags, query the join model and load its tag foreign key in the same query: post = await Post . acreate ( title = "Release notes" ) tag = await Tag . acreate ( name = "docs" ) await PostTag . acreate ( post_id = post . id , tag_id = tag . id ) links = await PostTag . filter ( post_id = post . id ) . select_related ( "tag" ) tag_names = [ link . tag . name for link in links ] The reverse post.tag_links relation contains PostTag rows; load it with prefetch_related("tag_links") before accessing it. It does not return Tag objects or fetch data on attribute access. A join model can also carry its own fields, such as the time a tag was added. Include all three models in the migration plan so the association table and its uniqueness constraint are created together. This explicit form supports association rows and their foreign-key relations. Hinoki does not currently generate the join model or expose a direct post.tags relation. See models and queries and migrations for schema changes to foreign keys.
docs.title: Model a many-to-many relationship

docs.text: Request lifecycle ¶ The order matters because validation, access and transactions have different failure behavior. Granian accepts the HTTP request and calls the ASGI application. (With --server rust the native server accepts it, answers what needs no application code and hands the rest to the same request pipeline; see serving .) Hinoki matches the method and path. For an action with an access policy, its authentication provider resolves a caller and the policy checks permissions. The request body has not been read yet, so an unauthenticated client cannot make the server buffer it. Hinoki negotiates the response type from Accept ( 406 when nothing fits), reads the body of POST / PUT / PATCH / QUERY requests, then binds and validates path, query, header and body values before the handler runs. For transaction=True , Hinoki opens a transaction before calling the handler. The handler returns. Hinoki prepares the response: a configured renderer turns the value into bytes. The declared response type is not checked at runtime. The transaction commits after successful response preparation. An exception or cancellation rolls back before an HTTP error is produced. An unhandled exception does not become a successful response. A failed commit is an error. A response renderer should not perform hidden database I/O. The default execution.request_timeout is 30 seconds and covers request processing through response preparation. Expiry returns 504 timeout ; an open transaction is rolled back. A synchronous handler already running in a worker thread cannot be forcibly stopped, so it continues occupying its executor slot until it returns, and its result is not sent. The default execution.max_body_bytes is 1 MiB; an oversized body returns 413 payload_too_large . MultiPartParser (selected automatically for actions that bind UploadedFile ) also bounds part count and per-part bytes; an oversized multipart part returns the same 413 code. Raw query strings default to an 8 KiB limit ( execution.max_query_bytes , 414 uri_too_long ), and combined header names/values default to 32 KiB ( execution.max_header_bytes , 431 headers_too_large ). These checks run before routing and header parsing. The ASGI server or reverse proxy should also enforce its own request-line and header limits. Each request gets a request ID in the configured server.request_id_header response header ( x-request-id by default). Hinoki generates it by default; with server.trust_request_id=True , it accepts a validated inbound ID only from a configured trusted proxy. Built-in error JSON includes the same value as request_id . Startup and shutdown have separate defaults of 30 and 10 seconds in lifecycle.startup_timeout and lifecycle.shutdown_timeout ; startup failure is reported through the ASGI lifespan protocol, and shutdown runs resource cleanup under its deadline. Application startup and shutdown hooks run inside those limits. The router, parsing, validation and selected serialization work use Rust, but the server hand-off (Granian and the ASGI adapter, or the Rust server's queue) crosses Python objects. See sync and async for what runs on which executor.
docs.title: Request lifecycle

docs.text: Rules: architecture you can check ¶ Rules are optional, typed promises about your application that a tool checks and that fail with a stable ID, a location and an explanation. They are not a linter for style and not an AI prompt: each rule is a Python object with deterministic behaviour. Nothing runs unless you enable rules. The built-in set is intentionally small: access declarations, atomic writes, model responses, schema exposure and import direction. Add a custom Rule only when a project has a concrete invariant that these checks cannot express. Enable them (the blog does) ¶ # examples/blog/rules.py blog_rules = RuleSet ( Actions . require_access ( match = "blog.api.*" , except_ = PUBLIC ), # HNK-ACC-001 Transactions . require_atomic (), # HNK-TXN-001 Schemas . forbid_exposure ( "token" , "password_hash" ), # HNK-SCH-001 Imports . forbid ( source = "blog.models" , target = "blog.api" ), # HNK-IMP-001 ) # examples/blog/main.py app = Hinoki ( ... , rules = blog_rules ) # startup rules fail the app if a promise is broken ID Rule Phase Checks HNK-ACC-001 Actions.require_access(match, except_) startup every matching action names an Access policy (public by default is the common hole) HNK-TXN-001 Transactions.require_atomic(methods) startup state-changing actions use transaction=True HNK-API-001 Actions.forbid_model_responses(match, except_) startup no action returns a Model (or a list/page of them): responses are Schema classes HNK-SCH-001 Schemas.forbid_exposure(*fields) startup named fields never appear in a response Schema , nested or in a subclass HNK-IMP-001 Imports.forbid(source, target) static modules under source never import target (read from the source files; dynamic imports are reported, not ignored) match and except_ patterns use fnmatch on the action's full qualified name ( pkg.api.Posts.create , named after the class it is mounted on). A bare name such as health matches nothing: write *.health . Run them ¶ The Blog target is part of the checked-in project in examples/ . Run this from that directory, using the locked environment in the parent directory: cd examples uv run --project .. hinoki check blog.main:create_app \ --rules blog.rules:blog_rules --package blog # 4 rule(s): 0 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived (exit 0) A broken promise (a deliberately bad app from the tests): tests/projects/rulesapp.py:7: HNK-ACC-001 [violated] GET /health (health) declares no access policy tests/projects/rulesapp.py:12: HNK-ACC-001 [violated] POST /items (create) declares no access policy tests/projects/rulesapp.py:12: HNK-TXN-001 [violated] POST /items (create) does not declare transaction=True 2 rule(s): 3 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived (exit 1) The other rules report the same way. This output comes from a small project whose api.py returns a Model , exposes token in a response Schema , and whose models.py imports api : shop/api.py:13: HNK-API-001 [violated] GET /members/{member_id} (one) returns the model Member; return a Schema fix: return a Schema (for example PostOut.from_model(row)) shop/api.py:7: HNK-SCH-001 [violated] MemberOut.token is exposed by GET /members fix: remove the field from the response Schema, or return a Schema that does not carry it shop/models.py:11: HNK-IMP-001 [violated] shop.models imports shop.api, which is forbidden for shop.models fix: move the code to an allowed layer, or depend on it through the layer in between 3 rule(s): 3 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived (exit 1) --format json prints the same diagnostics as versioned data ( schema_version , summary , and per diagnostic rule , severity , phase , status , message , location , explanation , subject , waiver ) for CI, editors and agents. --phase static|startup selects a phase; exit codes are 0 clean, 1 violations, 2 the check could not run. Statuses: violated (demonstrated), unverifiable (the check could not decide, for example a dynamic import, a rule that matched nothing, or a rule that crashed: this fails the build too, it is never a pass), waived . Exceptions (waivers) ¶ hinoki-rules.toml next to the project: [[waiver]] rule = "HNK-ACC-001" target = "tests.projects.rulesapp.health" # fnmatch on the diagnostic's subject, bounded (not "*") reason = "liveness probe is public by design" owner = "platform-team" expires = 2027-01-31 # optional tests/projects/rulesapp.py:7: HNK-ACC-001 [waived] GET /health (health) declares no access policy waived: liveness probe is public by design (platform-team, until 2027-01-31) A waiver needs a reason, an owner and a bounded target; an expired one stops applying and says so; a waiver that matches nothing is reported. A diagnostic that means "the rule could not do its job" cannot be waived. Waivers are the owner's decision : the tools read the file and never write it (put it under CODEOWNERS); AGENTS.md in a generated project tells agents the same. Your own rules ¶ Subclass hinoki.rules.Rule with a stable id , a phase , an explanation and check(project) yielding Diagnostic s (use self.diagnostic(message, location, subject=...) ). A rule that needs side effects (runs code, files, network, a database) declares them in effects and only runs with check --allow-effects . Seeing them from an agent ¶ The development MCP ( hinoki mcp ) exposes project inspection and rule diagnostics as read-only tools. See development tools . Rules inspect declarations and source structure; they do not prove what every function body does.
docs.title: Rules

docs.text: Schemas ¶ A Schema describes data that crosses the API boundary and validates it strictly. Models describe tables; a column reaches a client only when a Schema names it. from typing import Annotated from uuid import UUID from hinoki import Field , Schema class NoteIn ( Schema ): title : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 80 )] body : str = "" class NoteOut ( Schema ): id : UUID title : str body : str Strict, no coercion. "1" is not 1 ; unknown keys are refused by default; every problem is reported with its path (capped at 50). Validation, instance construction and JSON serialisation run in Rust. Partial updates. Declare title: str | Unset = UNSET : a field the client did not send stays UNSET and is left out of dump() and to_dict() , so row.aupdate_from(patch) writes only what was sent. Get data out. schema.to_dict() gives Python values (UUID and datetime stay objects), schema.dump() the JSON-compatible form; both skip UNSET . From rows. NoteOut.from_model(row, author_name=row.author.name) converts one row; NoteOut.from_models(rows) eagerly converts a synchronous iterable to a list. Relations must already be loaded (nothing fetches lazily). A derived schema keeps its selected fields. Conversion reads the expected attributes rather than checking the concrete model class; missing attributes raise AttributeError . Values passed as **extra are shared across rows. Into a row. await Note.acreate(data, author_id=me) and await row.aupdate_from(patch) : keyword values set by the server win over the client's, and a schema can never carry the primary key. Schema.validate(data) reports structural problems together. Values are not coerced. Declare field constraints with Field(...) ; use @field_normalize for narrow, typed string canonicalization and @field_check / @object_check for synchronous rejection checks. Wire aliases ¶ Use Field(alias=...) when the public JSON name should differ from the Python attribute. The alias is the only accepted input key; sending both names is an error. dump() writes aliases, including in nested schemas and lists, while to_dict() keeps Python attribute names. Validation errors and OpenAPI properties use the wire names. A custom check's default field path is translated to its alias; an explicit Invalid(path=...) is already a wire path. from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema class PersonOut ( Schema ): first_name : Annotated [ str , Field ( alias = "firstName" )] person = PersonOut . validate ({ "firstName" : "Aki" }) assert person . first_name == "Aki" assert person . dump () == { "firstName" : "Aki" } assert person . to_dict () == { "first_name" : "Aki" } An assigned declaration such as display_name: str = Field(alias="displayName") is also supported, including alongside default_factory . Aliases must be unique within a schema and cannot contain . , [ or ] , which are reserved by error paths. Model columns do not accept wire aliases; put API naming on the Schema . Class configuration ¶ SchemaConfig is an immutable typed configuration passed in the class declaration. By default, unknown string keys in decoded input are rejected. SchemaExtra.IGNORE discards them while keeping declared fields strict: from hinoki import Schema , SchemaConfig , SchemaExtra class VendorEvent ( Schema , config = SchemaConfig ( extra = SchemaExtra . IGNORE )): event_id : str revision : int event = VendorEvent . validate ( { "event_id" : "evt-1" , "revision" : 2 , "vendor_context" : { "trace" : "abc" }} ) assert event . dump () == { "event_id" : "evt-1" , "revision" : 2 } Ignored values are not stored as attributes or emitted by dump() . A wrong type, failed constraint or missing required field among the declared fields still raises ValidationError before either a sync or async handler runs. This option applies to decoded Schema.validate(...) input and request bodies. Generated constructor keywords and explicit from_model(..., **extra) overrides keep their normal strict signatures. Each nested Schema uses its own configuration. An alias remains the only accepted wire name. If given_name has alias givenName , sending only given_name is ignored as an extra and the required givenName field remains missing; sending both names is still a duplicate-field error. OpenAPI marks an IGNORE schema with additionalProperties: true , while its response serialization still includes only declared fields. Schema(...) validates the final Python values immediately and raises ValidationError for invalid values. Pass Python objects such as UUID , timezone-aware datetime and nested Schema instances. Schema.validate(decoded_data) is the wire-input path: it accepts JSON-compatible values, resolves aliases and returns field errors using wire names. Request body binding uses that path before calling the handler. from_model() also validates the constructed Schema; naive datetimes returned by database drivers remain unchanged and are allowed on that model-conversion path. Return annotations describe OpenAPI and serialization; Hinoki does not validate handler return values at runtime. Discriminated unions ¶ Use a discriminated union when one field can contain one of several known Schema shapes. Declare the union on a Schema field with Annotated[Cat | Dog, Field(discriminator="kind")] . Every variant needs the same required string field, the same wire alias for that field, and exactly one Field(one_of=(...)) tag. Hinoki selects the variant by that tag in Rust; it does not try each schema in order. from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema , http class Cat ( Schema ): kind : Annotated [ str , Field ( alias = "type" , one_of = ( "cat" ,))] name : str class Dog ( Schema ): kind : Annotated [ str , Field ( alias = "type" , one_of = ( "dog" ,))] walks : int Pet = Annotated [ Cat | Dog , Field ( discriminator = "kind" )] class PetRequest ( Schema ): pet : Pet @http . post ( "/pets" ) async def create_pet ( data : PetRequest ) -> PetRequest : return data PetRequest.validate({"pet": {"type": "cat", "name": "Mugi"}}) returns a PetRequest whose pet is a Cat ; manual construction takes an already validated variant instance, such as PetRequest(pet=Dog(kind="dog", walks=2)) . A dict is not coerced into a variant. list[Pet] , nested Schema fields, nullable unions and Unset use the same discriminator rules. Unknown tags produce a field error at the tag's wire path without echoing the submitted value. The handler is not called for an invalid body, whether it is synchronous or asynchronous. Each variant's tag field is required and cannot have a default. Tags must be unique strings, variants must be distinct Schema classes, and variant classes cannot override dump() because the override could remove or change the tag on the wire. Plain unions without Field(discriminator=...) , Literal , non-Schema variants, and unions directly in handler body or return annotations are not supported; wrap the union in a Schema for route input and output. This does not add runtime response validation. Projection options on dump() ¶ Use dump() when application code needs a JSON-compatible projection of a Schema. include and exclude accept Python field names and apply to the top-level fields only; exclusion wins if a field appears in both. There are no dotted paths or nested selection maps. Nested Schemas and supported lists are converted recursively, with by_alias applied at every Schema level. from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema class PersonOut ( Schema ): first_name : Annotated [ str , Field ( alias = "firstName" )] bio : str = "" person = PersonOut . validate ({ "firstName" : "Aki" }) assert person . dump () == { "firstName" : "Aki" , "bio" : "" } assert person . dump ( exclude_unset = True ) == { "firstName" : "Aki" } assert person . dump ( include = { "first_name" }, by_alias = False ) == { "first_name" : "Aki" } assert person . dump ( include = set ()) == {} exclude_unset=True omits values supplied by dataclass defaults or default factories when the caller did not provide that field. It does not compare values with defaults: explicitly passing bio="" , None , 0 , False or an empty collection keeps that value. UNSET is omitted regardless of this option. from_model() tracks attributes it actually reads and values passed via **extra ; missing optional attributes that use Schema defaults remain unset. A custom __post_init__ changing a field does not make it supplied. A custom __init__ has no reliable input-presence information, so exclude_unset=True raises TypeError for its instances. With no options, dump() preserves its current output and honors custom dump() overrides, including nested ones. Root-only include and exclude can select a custom-dumped nested value; recursive controls ( exclude_unset=True or by_alias=False ) refuse that value because Hinoki cannot safely inspect the override. A zero-argument override continues to work at runtime for automatic HTTP output, but widening the base signature means mypy flags that override; typed overrides that use the new options must accept the same keyword-only signature. Filtering a manually returned dictionary does not change the OpenAPI contract and is not an authorization mechanism; declare a response Schema containing only fields the caller may see. to_dict() remains the Python-value conversion and its existing exclude= behavior is unchanged. dump is reserved as a Schema method name. Declaring a field with that Python attribute name raises RegistrationError instead of treating the inherited method as a default value; rename the Python field to avoid the collision. A wire alias alone cannot resolve a Python attribute-name conflict. Built-in and custom validation ¶ Field(...) provides built-in structural constraints. format= accepts email , url , slug or hex_color and is shorthand for a regular-expression pattern. Numeric bounds apply to numbers; length limits apply to strings and collections; one_of restricts a value to the listed choices. from typing import Annotated from hinoki import ( Field , Invalid , Schema , field_check , field_normalize , object_check , ) class Registration ( Schema ): username : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 3 , max_length = 32 , pattern = r "[a-z0-9_]+" )] email : Annotated [ str , Field ( format = "email" )] password : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 12 )] confirmation : str @field_normalize ( "email" ) def lowercase_email ( self , value : str ) -> str : return value . lower () @field_check ( "password" ) def reject_common_password ( self , value : str ) -> None : if value . lower () in { "password12345" , "qwerty123456" }: raise Invalid ( "common_password" , "choose a less common password" ) @object_check def passwords_match ( self ) -> None : if self . password != self . confirmation : raise Invalid ( "password_mismatch" , "passwords do not match" , path = "confirmation" , ) Structural validation runs first and rejects wrong types, missing required values, unknown keys and failed constraints. @field_normalize("email") then receives a valid string and returns its canonical form; the result is checked against the same Field(...) constraints before it is applied. The same hook runs for Schema.validate(...) , direct Schema(...) construction and from_model(...) . It cannot rescue an input that failed the initial validation. Normalizers must be typed synchronous methods returning str ; they cannot perform I/O or reject input. After normalization, field checks receive final values and object checks can compare final fields. Raise Invalid(code, message) to reject a value; these checks return None and do not transform it. Non- None returns and async check methods are programming errors. Applicable custom-check failures are returned together in errors.ValidationError.details . Checks must be side-effect free; do not query the database or call external services. Put checks that depend on current data in an operation. These decorators validate a Schema instance passed through Schema.validate ; they are not run on a Model . Model fields have separate checks that run before ORM writes, described in Model field constraints and validators . See also the glossary for what "schema" does and does not mean in these docs.
docs.title: Schemas

docs.text: A Schema describes data that crosses the API boundary and validates it strictly. Models describe tables; a column reaches a client only when a Schema names it. from typing import Annotated from uuid import UUID from hinoki import Field , Schema class NoteIn ( Schema ): title : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 80 )] body : str = "" class NoteOut ( Schema ): id : UUID title : str body : str Strict, no coercion. "1" is not 1 ; unknown keys are refused by default; every problem is reported with its path (capped at 50). Validation, instance construction and JSON serialisation run in Rust. Partial updates. Declare title: str | Unset = UNSET : a field the client did not send stays UNSET and is left out of dump() and to_dict() , so row.aupdate_from(patch) writes only what was sent. Get data out. schema.to_dict() gives Python values (UUID and datetime stay objects), schema.dump() the JSON-compatible form; both skip UNSET . From rows. NoteOut.from_model(row, author_name=row.author.name) converts one row; NoteOut.from_models(rows) eagerly converts a synchronous iterable to a list. Relations must already be loaded (nothing fetches lazily). A derived schema keeps its selected fields. Conversion reads the expected attributes rather than checking the concrete model class; missing attributes raise AttributeError . Values passed as **extra are shared across rows. Into a row. await Note.acreate(data, author_id=me) and await row.aupdate_from(patch) : keyword values set by the server win over the client's, and a schema can never carry the primary key. Schema.validate(data) reports structural problems together. Values are not coerced. Declare field constraints with Field(...) ; use @field_normalize for narrow, typed string canonicalization and @field_check / @object_check for synchronous rejection checks.
docs.title: Schemas

docs.text: Use Field(alias=...) when the public JSON name should differ from the Python attribute. The alias is the only accepted input key; sending both names is an error. dump() writes aliases, including in nested schemas and lists, while to_dict() keeps Python attribute names. Validation errors and OpenAPI properties use the wire names. A custom check's default field path is translated to its alias; an explicit Invalid(path=...) is already a wire path. from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema class PersonOut ( Schema ): first_name : Annotated [ str , Field ( alias = "firstName" )] person = PersonOut . validate ({ "firstName" : "Aki" }) assert person . first_name == "Aki" assert person . dump () == { "firstName" : "Aki" } assert person . to_dict () == { "first_name" : "Aki" } An assigned declaration such as display_name: str = Field(alias="displayName") is also supported, including alongside default_factory . Aliases must be unique within a schema and cannot contain . , [ or ] , which are reserved by error paths. Model columns do not accept wire aliases; put API naming on the Schema .
docs.title: Wire aliases

docs.text: SchemaConfig is an immutable typed configuration passed in the class declaration. By default, unknown string keys in decoded input are rejected. SchemaExtra.IGNORE discards them while keeping declared fields strict: from hinoki import Schema , SchemaConfig , SchemaExtra class VendorEvent ( Schema , config = SchemaConfig ( extra = SchemaExtra . IGNORE )): event_id : str revision : int event = VendorEvent . validate ( { "event_id" : "evt-1" , "revision" : 2 , "vendor_context" : { "trace" : "abc" }} ) assert event . dump () == { "event_id" : "evt-1" , "revision" : 2 } Ignored values are not stored as attributes or emitted by dump() . A wrong type, failed constraint or missing required field among the declared fields still raises ValidationError before either a sync or async handler runs. This option applies to decoded Schema.validate(...) input and request bodies. Generated constructor keywords and explicit from_model(..., **extra) overrides keep their normal strict signatures. Each nested Schema uses its own configuration. An alias remains the only accepted wire name. If given_name has alias givenName , sending only given_name is ignored as an extra and the required givenName field remains missing; sending both names is still a duplicate-field error. OpenAPI marks an IGNORE schema with additionalProperties: true , while its response serialization still includes only declared fields. Schema(...) validates the final Python values immediately and raises ValidationError for invalid values. Pass Python objects such as UUID , timezone-aware datetime and nested Schema instances. Schema.validate(decoded_data) is the wire-input path: it accepts JSON-compatible values, resolves aliases and returns field errors using wire names. Request body binding uses that path before calling the handler. from_model() also validates the constructed Schema; naive datetimes returned by database drivers remain unchanged and are allowed on that model-conversion path. Return annotations describe OpenAPI and serialization; Hinoki does not validate handler return values at runtime.
docs.title: Class configuration

docs.text: Use a discriminated union when one field can contain one of several known Schema shapes. Declare the union on a Schema field with Annotated[Cat | Dog, Field(discriminator="kind")] . Every variant needs the same required string field, the same wire alias for that field, and exactly one Field(one_of=(...)) tag. Hinoki selects the variant by that tag in Rust; it does not try each schema in order. from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema , http class Cat ( Schema ): kind : Annotated [ str , Field ( alias = "type" , one_of = ( "cat" ,))] name : str class Dog ( Schema ): kind : Annotated [ str , Field ( alias = "type" , one_of = ( "dog" ,))] walks : int Pet = Annotated [ Cat | Dog , Field ( discriminator = "kind" )] class PetRequest ( Schema ): pet : Pet @http . post ( "/pets" ) async def create_pet ( data : PetRequest ) -> PetRequest : return data PetRequest.validate({"pet": {"type": "cat", "name": "Mugi"}}) returns a PetRequest whose pet is a Cat ; manual construction takes an already validated variant instance, such as PetRequest(pet=Dog(kind="dog", walks=2)) . A dict is not coerced into a variant. list[Pet] , nested Schema fields, nullable unions and Unset use the same discriminator rules. Unknown tags produce a field error at the tag's wire path without echoing the submitted value. The handler is not called for an invalid body, whether it is synchronous or asynchronous. Each variant's tag field is required and cannot have a default. Tags must be unique strings, variants must be distinct Schema classes, and variant classes cannot override dump() because the override could remove or change the tag on the wire. Plain unions without Field(discriminator=...) , Literal , non-Schema variants, and unions directly in handler body or return annotations are not supported; wrap the union in a Schema for route input and output. This does not add runtime response validation.
docs.title: Discriminated unions

docs.text: Use dump() when application code needs a JSON-compatible projection of a Schema. include and exclude accept Python field names and apply to the top-level fields only; exclusion wins if a field appears in both. There are no dotted paths or nested selection maps. Nested Schemas and supported lists are converted recursively, with by_alias applied at every Schema level. from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema class PersonOut ( Schema ): first_name : Annotated [ str , Field ( alias = "firstName" )] bio : str = "" person = PersonOut . validate ({ "firstName" : "Aki" }) assert person . dump () == { "firstName" : "Aki" , "bio" : "" } assert person . dump ( exclude_unset = True ) == { "firstName" : "Aki" } assert person . dump ( include = { "first_name" }, by_alias = False ) == { "first_name" : "Aki" } assert person . dump ( include = set ()) == {} exclude_unset=True omits values supplied by dataclass defaults or default factories when the caller did not provide that field. It does not compare values with defaults: explicitly passing bio="" , None , 0 , False or an empty collection keeps that value. UNSET is omitted regardless of this option. from_model() tracks attributes it actually reads and values passed via **extra ; missing optional attributes that use Schema defaults remain unset. A custom __post_init__ changing a field does not make it supplied. A custom __init__ has no reliable input-presence information, so exclude_unset=True raises TypeError for its instances. With no options, dump() preserves its current output and honors custom dump() overrides, including nested ones. Root-only include and exclude can select a custom-dumped nested value; recursive controls ( exclude_unset=True or by_alias=False ) refuse that value because Hinoki cannot safely inspect the override. A zero-argument override continues to work at runtime for automatic HTTP output, but widening the base signature means mypy flags that override; typed overrides that use the new options must accept the same keyword-only signature. Filtering a manually returned dictionary does not change the OpenAPI contract and is not an authorization mechanism; declare a response Schema containing only fields the caller may see. to_dict() remains the Python-value conversion and its existing exclude= behavior is unchanged. dump is reserved as a Schema method name. Declaring a field with that Python attribute name raises RegistrationError instead of treating the inherited method as a default value; rename the Python field to avoid the collision. A wire alias alone cannot resolve a Python attribute-name conflict.
