docs.text: Running an application ¶ cd examples uv run --project .. hinoki dev blog.main:create_app # development: reload on change uv run --project .. hinoki serve blog.main:create_app # production-style: no reload TARGET is module:name , where name is an application ( Hinoki ) or a function that returns one (a factory: the usual choice, because it builds the app inside each worker). The factory builds declarations only; databases and pools open in the worker's lifespan. With a declared app, settings load when the target module creates the Hinoki object. The database declared by the settings (or a configured DatabaseModule ) opens that worker's pool during lifespan startup and closes it during shutdown. The pool is per worker; no database connection is opened by importing model or route modules. See settings and database ownership . Both commands run the app under Granian unless you choose the Rust server with --server rust or server.server . In the Hinoki checkout, uv sync --locked installs the development environment, including Granian's reload support. A project created by hinoki new declares the server extra in its source dependency; run uv sync in that project. The extra includes Granian's reload support ( watchfiles ), which hinoki dev needs. If Granian was installed separately without watchfiles , dev reports the missing dependency and serve still works. For this checkout, use its locked source environment instead of installing hinoki[server] from the public package index; see installation for setup. Where host, port and workers come from ¶ From the application's server settings group ( settings guide ); flags override them: Setting Variable (prefix BLOG_ ) Default Flag server.host BLOG_SERVER__HOST 127.0.0.1 --host server.port BLOG_SERVER__PORT 8000 --port server.workers BLOG_SERVER__WORKERS 1 --workers (serve) server.runtime_threads BLOG_SERVER__RUNTIME_THREADS 1 server.backlog BLOG_SERVER__BACKLOG 1024 server.access_log BLOG_SERVER__ACCESS_LOG false server.server BLOG_SERVER__SERVER granian --server dev always runs one worker with reload. The settings command shows what is in effect: hinoki settings blog.settings:BlogSettings . The Rust server ¶ hinoki serve --server rust (or server.server = "rust" ) runs the application on a second server that is part of Hinoki's native extension. Granian stays the default and --server granian always selects it; nothing changes for an app that does not opt in. uv run --project .. hinoki serve blog.main:create_app --server rust uv run --project .. hinoki serve blog.main:create_app --server rust --workers 4 uv run --project .. hinoki dev blog.main:create_app --server rust from hinoki import settings class BlogSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "BLOG_" ): server : settings . ServerSettings = settings . ServerSettings ( server = "rust" , workers = 4 ) What is native and what still runs in Python ¶ The listener, HTTP/1.1 parsing, connection and header limits, body framing and its limits and timeouts, route matching, the request ID, and the answers that need no application code run on the native runtime without taking the Python interpreter lock. A request the native layer can answer by itself is answered there: unknown paths and methods ( 404 , 405 with Allow ), oversized request lines or headers, 503 while the worker is not ready or the in-flight limit is reached, and malformed requests. The response carries the same security headers, request ID, CORS and HSTS policy as one produced by the application. The lifespan, documentation and OpenAPI pages, and database calls still use Python. For matched routes that continue through the Python pipeline, the Rust server also percent-decodes the captured path values and passes them to Python; an invalid UTF-8 escape is carried as an error marker and reported at the same point where the pipeline previously decoded it. Host, CORS, HTTPS redirect and docs responses keep their earlier precedence. Python still applies str , int , UUID, bool and custom converters, and owns authentication, hooks, body/query binding, handlers, error translation and response assembly. For an eligible public GET function, the Rust server skips Python route matching and request binding. It accepts required str parameters from the path and query string, plus query parameters whose converter and default are both exactly the built-in str type. Rust decodes provided values, validates the full query, negotiates Accept , and prepares the handler arguments. An absent optional query uses its declared default, including when a wrapper observes the keyword arguments; an empty value is still an explicitly supplied empty string. Missing required or repeated query parameters use the same validation response as the Python pipeline. Error translation and Response creation remain in Python; JSON encoding uses Hinoki's Rust encoder, and Rust finalizes the response headers and suppresses the body for HEAD . An async handler runs in its ordinary asyncio task, while a sync handler uses the bounded executor. If a sync handler returns an awaitable, Hinoki awaits it on the same request task after the executor call completes. The automatic path does not accept body, file or Request parameters, non-string inputs, defaults on path parameters, access policies, transactions, custom response headers or renderers. Routes with host restrictions, CORS or HTTPS redirects also stay on the normal pipeline. Every other route uses the full Python request pipeline for binding, access policies, validation, error translation and response assembly. The request body is read natively only when that pipeline asks for it, after authentication, so an unauthenticated client cannot make the server buffer a body. Handlers themselves remain Python code; this is not an application written in Rust, and no performance figure is claimed here. Optional startup probe ¶ Hinoki(startup_url="/health") reserves one public, fixed GET / HEAD endpoint and returns {"status":"ok"} after that worker's lifespan startup has completed. The setting is off by default. Its path must be a literal ASCII path; query strings, fragments, parameters, percent escapes and dot segments are rejected. It must not match an application route or an enabled OpenAPI/docs path. The endpoint is not an application route and does not appear in OpenAPI or generated CRUD/MCP tools. This is a startup probe , not a general readiness or liveness check. A 200 says that startup completed (and, on the Rust server, its request wake reader was installed); it does not check database availability, downstream services, request capacity, or whether the Python event loop continues to make progress. It answers independently of the Python request queue when the Rust server can apply the response directly. Before readiness it returns 503 not_ready ; during shutdown readiness is cleared before graceful draining begins. ASGI/Granian and WSGI answer it in the Python pipeline after host, CORS and HTTPS-redirect checks. The Rust server can answer it on its Tokio thread without queuing work to Python when those policies do not require deferral. With host restrictions, CORS or HTTPS redirects configured, the Rust server sends it through the same Python checks. GET and HEAD negotiate application/json and validate query syntax; other methods return 405 with Allow: GET, HEAD , unless CORS answers a preflight first. WSGI reads request bodies before the pipeline, so its body-size behavior differs from the Rust server for a body sent to this GET / HEAD endpoint. WSGI also starts lazily on the first request and uses its adapter-level 503 if startup fails. Since WSGI exposes a decoded PATH_INFO rather than the raw request path, percent-encoded aliases may be indistinguishable from the literal probe path there. Limits ¶ HTTP/1.1, plus HTTP/2 over TLS when server.http2 is on (see below). No WebSocket or other protocol upgrades: an Upgrade header is ignored and the request is answered as plain HTTP, and the server never answers 101 . There is no cleartext HTTP/2 (neither prior knowledge nor Upgrade: h2c ). A request line plus headers larger than execution.max_header_bytes , or a query longer than execution.max_query_bytes , is refused ( 431 , 414 ). A body larger than execution.max_body_bytes is refused with 413 , by Content-Length before any byte is read or, for chunked bodies, as soon as the total passes the limit. A client that sends nothing for body_read_timeout seconds (10 by default, never more than half of execution.request_timeout ) gets 408 . A client that does not finish its request headers within header_read_timeout seconds (10 by default) is disconnected; the same timer closes idle keep-alive connections. TLS is optional: set server.tls_cert_file and server.tls_key_file (PEM; the key may be PKCS#8, PKCS#1 or SEC1) and the Rust server speaks HTTPS with rustls (TLS 1.2 and 1.3, the library's default cipher suites, no client certificates, ALPN http/1.1 , or h2 then http/1.1 with server.http2 ). The files are read once at start, so a renewed certificate needs a restart (a rolling restart of the workers is enough). A plaintext client on a TLS port gets a TLS alert, never an answer, and the handshake must finish within header_read_timeout . Requests over TLS have the scheme https , so the HSTS policy applies. Granian takes the same two settings (the framework asks it for TLS 1.2 and up and HTTP/1.1 only, as the Rust server does, unless server.http2 is on). A trusted proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto overrides the scheme, http included, on both servers. The handshake and the request head each have their own header_read_timeout , so a slow client can hold a connection slot for up to twice that time. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, leave them unset and list the proxy in trusted_proxies instead. HTTP/2 is opt-in: set server.http2 = true together with the TLS files (it is a settings error without them, on both servers). The server then offers ALPN h2 and http/1.1 and serves each connection with the protocol it negotiated; a client that offers only http/1.1 , or no ALPN, still gets HTTP/1.1. Requests reach the application unchanged, with http_version 2 in the ASGI scope; the :authority pseudo-header becomes the Host and wins over a host header that differs. Limits are fixed, not settings: 32 concurrent streams per connection (the 33rd is refused), a 64 KiB stream window, header lists bounded by execution.max_header_bytes and at most 100 header lines per request ( cookie fields count once; more is answered 431 ), and the h2 library's rapid-reset protections. A connection counts as one slot of max_connections , but every stream in flight uses backend capacity (the in-flight limit and the queue) like a request of its own, so size those limits for connections times 32. The server also drops a connection on which more than 100 streams end before their response completed (client resets) within a fixed 10-second window; it is closed without a GOAWAY . The count is per connection, not per client: a client can pass about twice the bound across a window boundary, and a new connection starts from zero. A connection with no open stream for header_read_timeout is closed gracefully ( GOAWAY ; a stream opened in the race with the GOAWAY is accepted and then cut when the shutdown timeout ends). A response that sends no data for write_timeout seconds (a client that keeps its flow-control window at zero, or stopped reading) also gets the connection a GOAWAY : hyper cannot reset one stream from outside, so the other streams have the shutdown timeout to finish and the stalled one is cut with the connection. Progress is tracked per response, so opening new streams does not hide a stalled one. Keep-alive pings every 30 seconds drop a peer that stopped answering. Set write_timeout above 32 x 16 KiB divided by the slowest client bandwidth you expect to serve: HTTP/2 shares the window between streams unevenly, so on a slow link each of 32 concurrent downloads can wait that long between two chunks and be taken for stalled while bytes still flow. A request with several host headers and no :authority is refused with 400 . A client that trickles the head of one stream while others are open is not bounded by header_read_timeout . On stop the server sends GOAWAY , lets streams in flight finish, and aborts what is left after the shutdown timeout. Not provided: cleartext HTTP/2 (h2c), server push, and WebSocket or CONNECT over HTTP/2. Granian with server.http2 negotiates HTTP/2 itself ( http mode auto ), under its own limits. A client that stops reading a response for write_timeout seconds (30 by default) is disconnected; any progress restarts the timer. max_connections (10000 by default) bounds open connections. Requests waiting for the application are bounded by an in-flight limit and a queue; beyond them the answer is 503 . Requests with ambiguous framing (for example Content-Length together with Transfer-Encoding , repeated lengths, or a bare line feed in the head) are refused with 400 and the connection is closed. There is no access log: server.access_log=true is refused with --server rust . A client that disconnects does not cancel its running handler; the handler finishes and its answer is discarded. Settings that apply to one server only ¶ hinoki serve refuses a setting the chosen server cannot honour, by name, and exits with status 2; it never ignores it or falls back to the other server. Setting Rust server Granian host , port , workers , runtime_threads , backlog , trusted_proxies , request_id_header , trust_request_id applied applied access_log refused when true applied max_connections , header_read_timeout , body_read_timeout , write_timeout applied when set refused when set If the native extension of a build has no Rust server, --server rust fails with an error that says so. Workers, signals and restarts ¶ With one worker hinoki serve runs the server in its own process. With several workers (and always under hinoki dev ) it starts a supervisor that opens the listening socket once (honouring backlog ), starts each worker as a fresh process that imports the target and builds the application, and passes the socket down. Workers share the one socket, so connections are spread by the operating system's accept; Hinoki does not balance them. Databases and pools open inside each worker's lifespan, never in the supervisor. SIGTERM , SIGINT (Ctrl-C) or SIGHUP stops accepting, lets running requests finish for up to lifecycle.shutdown_timeout , runs the lifespan shutdown and exits. A worker still running five seconds after that is killed. A second signal kills the workers immediately. Once the stop begins the supervisor closes its own copy of the socket, so a client that connects while the workers drain is refused. --workers must be 1 to 256 ( 0 uses server.workers ). A worker that exits on its own, whether it failed to start or crashed, is not restarted: the supervisor stops the other workers and exits with a non-zero status. Restart policy belongs to the process manager (systemd, a container runtime) that runs hinoki serve . The listening socket is opened before the lifespan startup of a supervised worker finishes, so connections wait in the backlog until a worker accepts them. With one worker the socket is opened after a successful startup. If the supervisor is killed without a chance to clean up, its workers notice within a second of finishing their startup and stop. The workers' copy of the listening socket is not inherited by processes a handler starts. A socket that cannot be opened (address in use, a bad port or host) is reported as error: cannot listen on HOST:PORT: ... with exit status 2, with one worker or several. hinoki dev --server rust ¶ The supervisor watches the project directory ( *.py , *.toml and .env files; .venv , .git and caches are ignored) and, on a change, stops the worker gracefully and starts a new one on the same socket, so a client connecting during the restart waits instead of being refused. If the new code fails to import or start, the error is printed (a short error: cannot load ... line for a missing module or name, a traceback for other failures), waiting for changes follows, and the next edit starts the worker again; connections wait in the meantime. The host, port, backlog and the choice of server are read once when hinoki dev starts: change them and restart the command. The other server settings (limits, trusted_proxies , runtime_threads ) are read again by every restarted worker. The watcher ignores .venv but not a virtual environment with another name, such as venv/ : keep it outside the project directory or it triggers reloads. The first import of the target happens in the command itself, so an error there stops it with a message instead of waiting. dev needs watchfiles (the hinoki[server] extra) and uses one worker. Behind a reverse proxy ¶ server.trusted_proxies works as described in settings : the native layer matches the TCP peer against it for the request ID and the HSTS and scheme policy of its own answers, and the request pipeline resolves the forwarded scheme and client address of the requests it handles from the same peer. Two points to know: Entries are IP addresses or CIDRs. An IPv6 address with a zone id such as fe80::1%lo0 is refused when settings load, for either server (earlier versions loaded it and the ASGI path matched it; the Rust server cannot take it). On a listener bound to :: that also accepts IPv4 (the default on many systems, for example Linux with bindv6only=0 and macOS), an IPv4 peer appears as ::ffff:a.b.c.d . A plain IPv4 entry such as 10.0.0.5 or 10.0.0.0/8 then never matches, and the proxy is treated as untrusted. That fails closed, and the ASGI path behaves the same. Either bind an IPv4 host ( --host 0.0.0.0 ) or list the mapped form, for example ::ffff:10.0.0.0/104 . A request ID that a trusted proxy sent and Hinoki refused is logged as ignored invalid request ID from trusted proxy ; for requests answered natively the warning is aggregated once a second with a count. Declaring where settings are read ¶ The settings class says its own prefix and .env file, so nothing is repeated at the call site: from hinoki import settings class BlogSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "BLOG_" , dotenv = ".env" ): database_url : settings . Secret app_settings = BlogSettings . load () # reads BLOG_* and .env Other runners ¶ dev and serve are conveniences. The application is a plain ASGI app, so granian --interface asgi --factory blog.main:create_app (or another ASGI server) works too; run that command from examples/ with the locked environment active. The server group is ignored, because only hinoki serve applies it. WSGI ¶ ASGI is the intended way to serve Hinoki. When a deployment can only run WSGI, wrap the application: # wsgi.py from hinoki.wsgi import WSGIAdapter from blog.main import create_app wsgi_app = WSGIAdapter ( create_app ()) $ granian --interface wsgi wsgi:wsgi_app The adapter drives the same ASGI callable on a background event loop that it owns, so routing, binding, access, errors, limits and the OpenAPI document behave as under ASGI. Specifics: Startup is lazy. Modules (including the database pool) start on the first request of each worker process, so a pre-forking server can import the file in its master process. If startup fails, every request answers 503 with not_ready and the error is logged. Shutdown runs on WSGIAdapter.close() or, otherwise, at interpreter exit. A server that kills workers without exiting normally skips it, as it would any atexit hook. Async handlers run on the adapter's loop and sync handlers on the bounded executor, as under ASGI. Each WSGI server thread blocks for the duration of its request, so concurrency is the server's thread count rather than the event loop. Bodies are buffered. Request bodies are read up to max_body_bytes plus one byte, so an oversized upload still answers 413 . Responses are complete before they are sent; streaming responses are not available, and a client disconnect is not reported to the handler. Paths. The server decodes the path once and the adapter passes it on without decoding again, so a client's %2520 reaches the handler as %20 , as under ASGI. A percent-encoded slash ( %2F ) cannot be told apart from a real one in WSGI and is not available inside a path parameter. A bad Content-Length answers 400 . One protocol per process. Do not serve the same application object over ASGI and WSGI in one process; the adapter owns its own loop and module lifespan. Run two processes if you need both. The path is checked against Granian's WSGI interface ( --interface wsgi , with one and two workers), not against every WSGI server.
docs.title: Serving

docs.text: cd examples uv run --project .. hinoki dev blog.main:create_app # development: reload on change uv run --project .. hinoki serve blog.main:create_app # production-style: no reload TARGET is module:name , where name is an application ( Hinoki ) or a function that returns one (a factory: the usual choice, because it builds the app inside each worker). The factory builds declarations only; databases and pools open in the worker's lifespan. With a declared app, settings load when the target module creates the Hinoki object. The database declared by the settings (or a configured DatabaseModule ) opens that worker's pool during lifespan startup and closes it during shutdown. The pool is per worker; no database connection is opened by importing model or route modules. See settings and database ownership . Both commands run the app under Granian unless you choose the Rust server with --server rust or server.server . In the Hinoki checkout, uv sync --locked installs the development environment, including Granian's reload support. A project created by hinoki new declares the server extra in its source dependency; run uv sync in that project. The extra includes Granian's reload support ( watchfiles ), which hinoki dev needs. If Granian was installed separately without watchfiles , dev reports the missing dependency and serve still works. For this checkout, use its locked source environment instead of installing hinoki[server] from the public package index; see installation for setup.
docs.title: Running an application

docs.text: From the application's server settings group ( settings guide ); flags override them: Setting Variable (prefix BLOG_ ) Default Flag server.host BLOG_SERVER__HOST 127.0.0.1 --host server.port BLOG_SERVER__PORT 8000 --port server.workers BLOG_SERVER__WORKERS 1 --workers (serve) server.runtime_threads BLOG_SERVER__RUNTIME_THREADS 1 server.backlog BLOG_SERVER__BACKLOG 1024 server.access_log BLOG_SERVER__ACCESS_LOG false server.server BLOG_SERVER__SERVER granian --server dev always runs one worker with reload. The settings command shows what is in effect: hinoki settings blog.settings:BlogSettings .
docs.title: Where host, port and workers come from

docs.text: hinoki serve --server rust (or server.server = "rust" ) runs the application on a second server that is part of Hinoki's native extension. Granian stays the default and --server granian always selects it; nothing changes for an app that does not opt in. uv run --project .. hinoki serve blog.main:create_app --server rust uv run --project .. hinoki serve blog.main:create_app --server rust --workers 4 uv run --project .. hinoki dev blog.main:create_app --server rust from hinoki import settings class BlogSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "BLOG_" ): server : settings . ServerSettings = settings . ServerSettings ( server = "rust" , workers = 4 )
docs.title: The Rust server

docs.text: The listener, HTTP/1.1 parsing, connection and header limits, body framing and its limits and timeouts, route matching, the request ID, and the answers that need no application code run on the native runtime without taking the Python interpreter lock. A request the native layer can answer by itself is answered there: unknown paths and methods ( 404 , 405 with Allow ), oversized request lines or headers, 503 while the worker is not ready or the in-flight limit is reached, and malformed requests. The response carries the same security headers, request ID, CORS and HSTS policy as one produced by the application. The lifespan, documentation and OpenAPI pages, and database calls still use Python. For matched routes that continue through the Python pipeline, the Rust server also percent-decodes the captured path values and passes them to Python; an invalid UTF-8 escape is carried as an error marker and reported at the same point where the pipeline previously decoded it. Host, CORS, HTTPS redirect and docs responses keep their earlier precedence. Python still applies str , int , UUID, bool and custom converters, and owns authentication, hooks, body/query binding, handlers, error translation and response assembly. For an eligible public GET function, the Rust server skips Python route matching and request binding. It accepts required str parameters from the path and query string, plus query parameters whose converter and default are both exactly the built-in str type. Rust decodes provided values, validates the full query, negotiates Accept , and prepares the handler arguments. An absent optional query uses its declared default, including when a wrapper observes the keyword arguments; an empty value is still an explicitly supplied empty string. Missing required or repeated query parameters use the same validation response as the Python pipeline. Error translation and Response creation remain in Python; JSON encoding uses Hinoki's Rust encoder, and Rust finalizes the response headers and suppresses the body for HEAD . An async handler runs in its ordinary asyncio task, while a sync handler uses the bounded executor. If a sync handler returns an awaitable, Hinoki awaits it on the same request task after the executor call completes. The automatic path does not accept body, file or Request parameters, non-string inputs, defaults on path parameters, access policies, transactions, custom response headers or renderers. Routes with host restrictions, CORS or HTTPS redirects also stay on the normal pipeline. Every other route uses the full Python request pipeline for binding, access policies, validation, error translation and response assembly. The request body is read natively only when that pipeline asks for it, after authentication, so an unauthenticated client cannot make the server buffer a body. Handlers themselves remain Python code; this is not an application written in Rust, and no performance figure is claimed here.
docs.title: What is native and what still runs in Python

docs.text: Hinoki(startup_url="/health") reserves one public, fixed GET / HEAD endpoint and returns {"status":"ok"} after that worker's lifespan startup has completed. The setting is off by default. Its path must be a literal ASCII path; query strings, fragments, parameters, percent escapes and dot segments are rejected. It must not match an application route or an enabled OpenAPI/docs path. The endpoint is not an application route and does not appear in OpenAPI or generated CRUD/MCP tools. This is a startup probe , not a general readiness or liveness check. A 200 says that startup completed (and, on the Rust server, its request wake reader was installed); it does not check database availability, downstream services, request capacity, or whether the Python event loop continues to make progress. It answers independently of the Python request queue when the Rust server can apply the response directly. Before readiness it returns 503 not_ready ; during shutdown readiness is cleared before graceful draining begins. ASGI/Granian and WSGI answer it in the Python pipeline after host, CORS and HTTPS-redirect checks. The Rust server can answer it on its Tokio thread without queuing work to Python when those policies do not require deferral. With host restrictions, CORS or HTTPS redirects configured, the Rust server sends it through the same Python checks. GET and HEAD negotiate application/json and validate query syntax; other methods return 405 with Allow: GET, HEAD , unless CORS answers a preflight first. WSGI reads request bodies before the pipeline, so its body-size behavior differs from the Rust server for a body sent to this GET / HEAD endpoint. WSGI also starts lazily on the first request and uses its adapter-level 503 if startup fails. Since WSGI exposes a decoded PATH_INFO rather than the raw request path, percent-encoded aliases may be indistinguishable from the literal probe path there.
docs.title: Optional startup probe

docs.text: HTTP/1.1, plus HTTP/2 over TLS when server.http2 is on (see below). No WebSocket or other protocol upgrades: an Upgrade header is ignored and the request is answered as plain HTTP, and the server never answers 101 . There is no cleartext HTTP/2 (neither prior knowledge nor Upgrade: h2c ). A request line plus headers larger than execution.max_header_bytes , or a query longer than execution.max_query_bytes , is refused ( 431 , 414 ). A body larger than execution.max_body_bytes is refused with 413 , by Content-Length before any byte is read or, for chunked bodies, as soon as the total passes the limit. A client that sends nothing for body_read_timeout seconds (10 by default, never more than half of execution.request_timeout ) gets 408 . A client that does not finish its request headers within header_read_timeout seconds (10 by default) is disconnected; the same timer closes idle keep-alive connections. TLS is optional: set server.tls_cert_file and server.tls_key_file (PEM; the key may be PKCS#8, PKCS#1 or SEC1) and the Rust server speaks HTTPS with rustls (TLS 1.2 and 1.3, the library's default cipher suites, no client certificates, ALPN http/1.1 , or h2 then http/1.1 with server.http2 ). The files are read once at start, so a renewed certificate needs a restart (a rolling restart of the workers is enough). A plaintext client on a TLS port gets a TLS alert, never an answer, and the handshake must finish within header_read_timeout . Requests over TLS have the scheme https , so the HSTS policy applies. Granian takes the same two settings (the framework asks it for TLS 1.2 and up and HTTP/1.1 only, as the Rust server does, unless server.http2 is on). A trusted proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto overrides the scheme, http included, on both servers. The handshake and the request head each have their own header_read_timeout , so a slow client can hold a connection slot for up to twice that time. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, leave them unset and list the proxy in trusted_proxies instead. HTTP/2 is opt-in: set server.http2 = true together with the TLS files (it is a settings error without them, on both servers). The server then offers ALPN h2 and http/1.1 and serves each connection with the protocol it negotiated; a client that offers only http/1.1 , or no ALPN, still gets HTTP/1.1. Requests reach the application unchanged, with http_version 2 in the ASGI scope; the :authority pseudo-header becomes the Host and wins over a host header that differs. Limits are fixed, not settings: 32 concurrent streams per connection (the 33rd is refused), a 64 KiB stream window, header lists bounded by execution.max_header_bytes and at most 100 header lines per request ( cookie fields count once; more is answered 431 ), and the h2 library's rapid-reset protections. A connection counts as one slot of max_connections , but every stream in flight uses backend capacity (the in-flight limit and the queue) like a request of its own, so size those limits for connections times 32. The server also drops a connection on which more than 100 streams end before their response completed (client resets) within a fixed 10-second window; it is closed without a GOAWAY . The count is per connection, not per client: a client can pass about twice the bound across a window boundary, and a new connection starts from zero. A connection with no open stream for header_read_timeout is closed gracefully ( GOAWAY ; a stream opened in the race with the GOAWAY is accepted and then cut when the shutdown timeout ends). A response that sends no data for write_timeout seconds (a client that keeps its flow-control window at zero, or stopped reading) also gets the connection a GOAWAY : hyper cannot reset one stream from outside, so the other streams have the shutdown timeout to finish and the stalled one is cut with the connection. Progress is tracked per response, so opening new streams does not hide a stalled one. Keep-alive pings every 30 seconds drop a peer that stopped answering. Set write_timeout above 32 x 16 KiB divided by the slowest client bandwidth you expect to serve: HTTP/2 shares the window between streams unevenly, so on a slow link each of 32 concurrent downloads can wait that long between two chunks and be taken for stalled while bytes still flow. A request with several host headers and no :authority is refused with 400 . A client that trickles the head of one stream while others are open is not bounded by header_read_timeout . On stop the server sends GOAWAY , lets streams in flight finish, and aborts what is left after the shutdown timeout. Not provided: cleartext HTTP/2 (h2c), server push, and WebSocket or CONNECT over HTTP/2. Granian with server.http2 negotiates HTTP/2 itself ( http mode auto ), under its own limits. A client that stops reading a response for write_timeout seconds (30 by default) is disconnected; any progress restarts the timer. max_connections (10000 by default) bounds open connections. Requests waiting for the application are bounded by an in-flight limit and a queue; beyond them the answer is 503 . Requests with ambiguous framing (for example Content-Length together with Transfer-Encoding , repeated lengths, or a bare line feed in the head) are refused with 400 and the connection is closed. There is no access log: server.access_log=true is refused with --server rust . A client that disconnects does not cancel its running handler; the handler finishes and its answer is discarded.
docs.title: Limits

docs.text: hinoki serve refuses a setting the chosen server cannot honour, by name, and exits with status 2; it never ignores it or falls back to the other server. Setting Rust server Granian host , port , workers , runtime_threads , backlog , trusted_proxies , request_id_header , trust_request_id applied applied access_log refused when true applied max_connections , header_read_timeout , body_read_timeout , write_timeout applied when set refused when set If the native extension of a build has no Rust server, --server rust fails with an error that says so.
docs.title: Settings that apply to one server only

docs.text: With one worker hinoki serve runs the server in its own process. With several workers (and always under hinoki dev ) it starts a supervisor that opens the listening socket once (honouring backlog ), starts each worker as a fresh process that imports the target and builds the application, and passes the socket down. Workers share the one socket, so connections are spread by the operating system's accept; Hinoki does not balance them. Databases and pools open inside each worker's lifespan, never in the supervisor. SIGTERM , SIGINT (Ctrl-C) or SIGHUP stops accepting, lets running requests finish for up to lifecycle.shutdown_timeout , runs the lifespan shutdown and exits. A worker still running five seconds after that is killed. A second signal kills the workers immediately. Once the stop begins the supervisor closes its own copy of the socket, so a client that connects while the workers drain is refused. --workers must be 1 to 256 ( 0 uses server.workers ). A worker that exits on its own, whether it failed to start or crashed, is not restarted: the supervisor stops the other workers and exits with a non-zero status. Restart policy belongs to the process manager (systemd, a container runtime) that runs hinoki serve . The listening socket is opened before the lifespan startup of a supervised worker finishes, so connections wait in the backlog until a worker accepts them. With one worker the socket is opened after a successful startup. If the supervisor is killed without a chance to clean up, its workers notice within a second of finishing their startup and stop. The workers' copy of the listening socket is not inherited by processes a handler starts. A socket that cannot be opened (address in use, a bad port or host) is reported as error: cannot listen on HOST:PORT: ... with exit status 2, with one worker or several.
docs.title: Workers, signals and restarts

docs.text: The supervisor watches the project directory ( *.py , *.toml and .env files; .venv , .git and caches are ignored) and, on a change, stops the worker gracefully and starts a new one on the same socket, so a client connecting during the restart waits instead of being refused. If the new code fails to import or start, the error is printed (a short error: cannot load ... line for a missing module or name, a traceback for other failures), waiting for changes follows, and the next edit starts the worker again; connections wait in the meantime. The host, port, backlog and the choice of server are read once when hinoki dev starts: change them and restart the command. The other server settings (limits, trusted_proxies , runtime_threads ) are read again by every restarted worker. The watcher ignores .venv but not a virtual environment with another name, such as venv/ : keep it outside the project directory or it triggers reloads. The first import of the target happens in the command itself, so an error there stops it with a message instead of waiting. dev needs watchfiles (the hinoki[server] extra) and uses one worker.
docs.title: hinoki dev --server rust

docs.text: server.trusted_proxies works as described in settings : the native layer matches the TCP peer against it for the request ID and the HSTS and scheme policy of its own answers, and the request pipeline resolves the forwarded scheme and client address of the requests it handles from the same peer. Two points to know: Entries are IP addresses or CIDRs. An IPv6 address with a zone id such as fe80::1%lo0 is refused when settings load, for either server (earlier versions loaded it and the ASGI path matched it; the Rust server cannot take it). On a listener bound to :: that also accepts IPv4 (the default on many systems, for example Linux with bindv6only=0 and macOS), an IPv4 peer appears as ::ffff:a.b.c.d . A plain IPv4 entry such as 10.0.0.5 or 10.0.0.0/8 then never matches, and the proxy is treated as untrusted. That fails closed, and the ASGI path behaves the same. Either bind an IPv4 host ( --host 0.0.0.0 ) or list the mapped form, for example ::ffff:10.0.0.0/104 . A request ID that a trusted proxy sent and Hinoki refused is logged as ignored invalid request ID from trusted proxy ; for requests answered natively the warning is aggregated once a second with a count.
docs.title: Behind a reverse proxy

docs.text: The settings class says its own prefix and .env file, so nothing is repeated at the call site: from hinoki import settings class BlogSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "BLOG_" , dotenv = ".env" ): database_url : settings . Secret app_settings = BlogSettings . load () # reads BLOG_* and .env
docs.title: Declaring where settings are read

docs.text: dev and serve are conveniences. The application is a plain ASGI app, so granian --interface asgi --factory blog.main:create_app (or another ASGI server) works too; run that command from examples/ with the locked environment active. The server group is ignored, because only hinoki serve applies it.
docs.title: Other runners

docs.text: ASGI is the intended way to serve Hinoki. When a deployment can only run WSGI, wrap the application: # wsgi.py from hinoki.wsgi import WSGIAdapter from blog.main import create_app wsgi_app = WSGIAdapter ( create_app ()) $ granian --interface wsgi wsgi:wsgi_app The adapter drives the same ASGI callable on a background event loop that it owns, so routing, binding, access, errors, limits and the OpenAPI document behave as under ASGI. Specifics: Startup is lazy. Modules (including the database pool) start on the first request of each worker process, so a pre-forking server can import the file in its master process. If startup fails, every request answers 503 with not_ready and the error is logged. Shutdown runs on WSGIAdapter.close() or, otherwise, at interpreter exit. A server that kills workers without exiting normally skips it, as it would any atexit hook. Async handlers run on the adapter's loop and sync handlers on the bounded executor, as under ASGI. Each WSGI server thread blocks for the duration of its request, so concurrency is the server's thread count rather than the event loop. Bodies are buffered. Request bodies are read up to max_body_bytes plus one byte, so an oversized upload still answers 413 . Responses are complete before they are sent; streaming responses are not available, and a client disconnect is not reported to the handler. Paths. The server decodes the path once and the adapter passes it on without decoding again, so a client's %2520 reaches the handler as %20 , as under ASGI. A percent-encoded slash ( %2F ) cannot be told apart from a real one in WSGI and is not available inside a path parameter. A bad Content-Length answers 400 . One protocol per process. Do not serve the same application object over ASGI and WSGI in one process; the adapter owns its own loop and module lifespan. Run two processes if you need both. The path is checked against Granian's WSGI interface ( --interface wsgi , with one and two workers), not against every WSGI server.
docs.title: WSGI

docs.text: Settings: how configuration, secrets and database pools work ¶ Hinoki uses typed, immutable settings classes . The declared app form loads its settings class while constructing the app; a factory can call Settings.load() itself. Secrets are redacted. Database connection pools have a separate worker lifecycle: settings describe how to connect, and a module opens and closes the pool. 1. Declare what your app needs ¶ from typing import Literal from hinoki import settings class BlogSettings ( settings . AppSettings ): # keeps the built-in groups database : settings . DatabaseSettings # url: settings.Secret, max_size: int jwt_secret : settings . Secret | None = None # optional secret admin_theme : Literal [ "studio" , "console" , "paper" , "bento" ] = "studio" Settings types live in the hinoki.settings namespace: from hinoki import settings , then settings.AppSettings , settings.DatabaseSettings , settings.Secret , settings.Settings and settings.SettingsError . Name your own subclass for your project ( BlogSettings above) and keep a loaded value in a variable such as app_settings , so the namespace is not shadowed. Earlier revisions exported these types from hinoki itself and called the base class FrameworkSettings ; from hinoki import FrameworkSettings now raises ImportError . settings.AppSettings brings eight groups every app has: execution (8 sync workers, queue limit 64, request timeout 30 seconds, 1 MiB body limit, 8 KiB query limit and 32 KiB header limit), lifecycle (30-second startup and 10-second shutdown limits), logging (level, text or JSON, optional request ID correlation), docs (title, version and optional OpenAPI/Swagger/ReDoc URLs), server (which server, host, port, workers and proxy trust), pagination (default page_size and max_page_size for PageNumberPagination , see pagination ), cors (which browser origins may read responses) and security (browser response headers and optional HTTPS redirect). Three values sit beside the groups: timezone , debug and allowed_hosts ; see Debug, allowed hosts and CORS . A field without a default is required . Request IDs and timeout responses are described in the request lifecycle . docs.openapi_url , docs.docs_url and docs.redoc_url default to None , so no API document or viewer route is served until configured. Swagger UI or ReDoc requires an openapi_url . The same values can be supplied as Hinoki(...) arguments; explicit arguments win over docs settings, and None disables a page. Built-in fields and defaults ¶ Group Field Default Constraint or effect execution sync_workers 8 1 to 1024 worker threads execution sync_queue 64 0 or greater queued calls execution request_timeout 30.0 seconds Must be positive; request expiry returns 504 execution max_body_bytes 1048576 (1 MiB) 1 to 1073741824 bytes; larger request bodies return 413 execution max_query_bytes 8192 (8 KiB) 1 to 1048576 raw query-string bytes; larger queries return 414 execution max_header_bytes 32768 (32 KiB) 1 to 1048576 combined header bytes; larger headers return 431 lifecycle startup_timeout 30.0 seconds Must be positive lifecycle shutdown_timeout 10.0 seconds Must be positive logging level info debug , info , warning , error or critical logging format text text or json logging include_request_id false Add the active request ID to Hinoki log records for request correlation docs title Hinoki API OpenAPI info title docs version 0.1.0 OpenAPI info version docs openapi_url None JSON document route; disabled when None docs docs_url None Swagger UI route; requires openapi_url docs redoc_url None ReDoc route; requires openapi_url server server granian granian or rust ; --server overrides it. See Running an application server host 127.0.0.1 Bind address used by hinoki dev/serve server port 8000 1 to 65535 server workers 1 1 to 256 ; dev uses one worker for reload server runtime_threads 1 Must be positive server backlog 1024 Must be positive server access_log false Enables Granian access logging; refused when true with the Rust server server max_connections unset (10000) Rust server only: open-connection limit, 1 to 1000000 ; refused under Granian server header_read_timeout unset (10 seconds) Rust server only: time to receive request headers, and the keep-alive idle limit; refused under Granian server body_read_timeout unset (10 seconds) Rust server only: silence allowed while a body is read (at most half of execution.request_timeout ); refused under Granian server write_timeout unset (30 seconds) Rust server only: how long a response write may make no progress before the connection is closed; above 0 and at most 3600; refused under Granian server tls_cert_file , tls_key_file unset PEM certificate chain and private key; both or neither, and both must exist. Serves HTTPS on either server; the Rust server reads them once at start server http2 false Serve HTTP/2 over TLS (ALPN h2 , with http/1.1 as fallback); needs tls_cert_file and tls_key_file , otherwise refused when settings load. No cleartext HTTP/2; on either server server trusted_proxies empty IP addresses or CIDRs allowed to supply forwarded client/protocol metadata; an IPv6 zone id ( fe80::1%lo0 ) is refused when settings load, whichever server runs server request_id_header x-request-id HTTP header used for generated request IDs; other framework-owned names are refused server trust_request_id false Accept a validated inbound ID only from a peer in trusted_proxies cors origins empty Allowed browser origins ( scheme://host[:port] ), or the single entry * ; empty disables CORS cors methods GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, QUERY Methods a preflight allows cors headers authorization, content-type Request headers a preflight allows cors expose_headers empty Response headers a browser script may read cors credentials false Allow cookies and HTTP authentication; refused together with * cors max_age 600 seconds 0 to 86400 ; how long a browser may cache a preflight security redirect_https false Send known HTTP requests to HTTPS with 308 ; requires explicit allowed_hosts security hsts_seconds 0 0 to 63072000 ; emit HSTS only when the effective scheme is HTTPS security hsts_include_subdomains false Add includeSubDomains ; requires nonzero hsts_seconds security hsts_preload false Add preload ; requires subdomains and at least one year of HSTS security frame_options sameorigin settings.FrameOptions.DENY or .SAMEORIGIN security referrer_policy same-origin A supported settings.ReferrerPolicy enum value (top level) timezone UTC IANA timezone name used by app.now() (top level) debug false Adds exception details to 500 answers; development only (top level) allowed_hosts * Host names, .domain or * ; other Host values receive 400 settings.DatabaseSettings is an optional field you declare in your own settings class, not a settings.AppSettings group. Its url defaults to sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 ; max_size defaults to 10 connections per worker and must be at least 1 . Reverse proxies and request IDs ¶ Forwarded metadata is ignored unless the immediate socket peer matches server.trusted_proxies . Configure only the addresses or CIDRs of proxies that remove client-supplied forwarding headers and write their own values. For example: class BlogSettings ( settings . AppSettings ): ... # The private address used by this deployment's ingress, not every private network. server : settings . ServerSettings = settings . ServerSettings ( trusted_proxies = ( "10.20.0.0/16" ,), request_id_header = "x-correlation-id" , trust_request_id = True , ) Set logging.include_request_id=true to add the resolved ID to Hinoki's own log records while a request is being handled. Text logs append request_id=<id> and JSON logs include a request_id field. The ID matches the response's configured request ID header. Startup and other records outside a request omit the field. This setting is off by default, and it does not change application or third-party logger handlers. From a trusted peer, Hinoki accepts a single X-Forwarded-Proto value of http or https and walks a bounded X-Forwarded-For chain from the peer side to the first untrusted address. Request.scheme and Request.client use those validated values. Invalid, repeated or ambiguous values fall back to the socket scope. X-Forwarded-Host is never used: Host , allowed_hosts and generated URLs continue to use the original Host header. On a listener bound to :: , an IPv4 peer can appear as ::ffff:a.b.c.d , which a plain IPv4 entry does not match (the proxy is then untrusted); see behind a reverse proxy . Request IDs are generated by default. With trust_request_id=True , one inbound configured header is accepted only from a trusted immediate peer and only when it is 1–128 visible ASCII characters without commas or controls. Otherwise Hinoki generates a new ID. The selected value appears in Request.request_id , built-in error JSON and the configured response header. The proxy must sanitize the incoming header before forwarding it; do not trust a broad network range merely because it is private. 2. Load them when the app is built ¶ from hinoki import Hinoki , settings class BlogSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "BLOG_" , dotenv = ".env" ): # where to read database : settings . DatabaseSettings # also opens the database for each worker def create_app () -> Hinoki : app_settings = BlogSettings . load () return Hinoki ( settings = app_settings ) load is the only place configuration files and environment variables are read. Where a value comes from, highest first: Source Example overrides= in code (used by tests) load(overrides={"admin_theme": "paper"}) the process environment BLOG_ADMIN_THEME=paper a *_FILE variable (container secrets) BLOG_JWT_SECRET_FILE=/run/secrets/jwt the .env file you named BLOG_ADMIN_THEME=paper in .env the TOML file you named admin_theme = "paper" in settings.toml the default in the class admin_theme: ... = "studio" TOML tables map to settings groups. For example, [database] with max_size = 12 sets database.max_size . Arrays remain typed arrays. Environment and dotenv values still use the strict text conversion described below. TOML cannot contain settings.Secret values; put secrets in environment variables, *_FILE files, or a secret manager that exports one of those sources. class BlogSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "BLOG_" , toml = "settings.toml" ): ... app_settings = BlogSettings . load () # reads the declared file by default Pass toml="path/to/settings.toml" to load or explain to override the class path. An explicitly selected TOML file must exist and parse correctly. 3. Names ¶ The variable is the prefix plus the field name in capitals; a group nests with a double underscore. Field Variable (prefix BLOG_ ) admin_theme BLOG_ADMIN_THEME jwt_secret BLOG_JWT_SECRET database.url BLOG_DATABASE__URL execution.sync_workers BLOG_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS logging.format BLOG_LOGGING__FORMAT timezone BLOG_TIMEZONE Values are converted strictly: integers are ASCII digits (no 1_000 , no 0x10 ), booleans are true/false/yes/no/on/off/1/0 , lists are comma separated (use tuple[str, ...] to keep them immutable), Literal[...] takes one of its choices, and an empty value for X | None means None . 4. Mistakes fail at startup, all at once ¶ A variable that starts with your prefix but names no field is an error (a typo guard; strict=False turns it off when another program shares the prefix). A missing required value, a bad number or a value that is not one of the choices is an error too, and every problem is listed together , with variable names and reasons but never values: invalid settings: BLOG_DATABASE__MAX_SIZE: must be an integer BLOG_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS: must be an integer BLOG_ADMN_THEME: unknown setting 5. Secrets ¶ Declare them as settings.Secret (or settings.Secret | None ). A settings.Secret prints as *** in repr , str , logs, error messages, describe() and the settings command; you get the real text only with secret.reveal() , at the one place that needs it ( JWTKey(..., settings.jwt_secret.reveal()) ). Put secrets in the environment, a secret manager that exports variables, or files : with Docker or Kubernetes secrets set BLOG_JWT_SECRET_FILE=/run/secrets/jwt ; the file's content (without the trailing newline) is the value. Only a regular file up to 64 KiB is read; setting both BLOG_JWT_SECRET and BLOG_JWT_SECRET_FILE is an error. A .env file is for development; never commit it. Pickling or serialising a settings object stores its secrets in plain text, so don't. A validate() method you add to a group shows its message in errors, so never put a field's value in it. 6. See what is in effect ¶ These commands inspect the checked-in Blog settings from the examples/ project directory; with the repository checkout, use its locked environment: cd examples uv run --project .. hinoki settings blog.settings:BlogSettings --prefix BLOG_ --dotenv .env --toml settings.toml BLOG_ADMIN_THEME .env paper BLOG_DATABASE__URL environment *** BLOG_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS default 8 BLOG_JWT_SECRET file *** The second column is where each value came from: override , environment , .env , toml , file or default . --format json prints the same for tools. --example prints a ready .env.example (every variable with its default and type; secrets and required values blank): uv run --project .. hinoki settings blog.settings:BlogSettings --prefix BLOG_ --example > .env.example 7. Use them ¶ Hinoki(settings=app_settings) derives the runtime limits, the docs URLs, logging setup and application timezone from the built-in settings (an explicit argument such as title= still wins). app.now() returns an aware datetime in the configured timezone; it defaults to UTC. The timezone is configured in settings, not as a Hinoki(...) argument. Your own fields are on app.settings , and modules reach them as ctx.settings in their lifespan. The server group (server, host, port, workers and the rest) is applied by hinoki serve / dev ( Running an application ). Hinoki does not connect to secret-manager services itself; use a provider that supplies environment values or secret files. Debug, allowed hosts and CORS ¶ These three are off or permissive by default, so an application behaves the same until you set them. Set them from the environment like any other field: BLOG_DEBUG = true BLOG_ALLOWED_HOSTS = api.example.com,.example.org BLOG_CORS__ORIGINS = https://app.example.com,http://localhost:5173 debug ¶ With debug on, the 500 internal_error answer for an unhandled exception also carries a debug object: { "error" : "internal_error" , "request_id" : "5f0c…" , "debug" : { "exception" : "builtins.RuntimeError" , "message" : "the cache is cold" , "traceback" : [ "Traceback (most recent call last):\n" , "…" ] } } Declared errors, validation errors and the other framework answers are unchanged, and the exception is logged either way. Exception messages can contain data you would not publish, so keep debug off in a deployment; each worker logs a warning at startup while it is on. debug changes nothing else: it does not enable documentation pages, relax authentication or skip the host check, and hinoki dev does not set it. allowed_hosts ¶ The Host header of every request must match one entry: Entry Matches * (the default) Any host; nothing is checked api.example.com That host, on any port .example.org example.org and every subdomain 127.0.0.1 , ::1 That address ( [::1]:8000 in the header) Matching ignores case, the port and a trailing dot. The header must be exactly one host with an optional port; a request for another host, with two Host headers or without a usable one, receives 400 disallowed_host before routing, authentication and body reading; documentation routes are covered too. Entries are names: a scheme, port, path or a partial wildcard such as *.example.com fails at load, and * cannot be mixed with other entries. A dot entry is as wide as it reads: .com allows every .com host. Set the list in a deployment that is reachable under more names than it should answer to. The in-process test clients send no Host header, so a test of an application with a restrictive list passes one: await client.get("/x", headers={"host": "api.example.com"}) . cors ¶ CORS is off while cors.origins is empty: no header is added and OPTIONS requests receive 405 . With origins configured: A request whose Origin is listed receives access-control-allow-origin with that origin and vary: origin , on every answer including errors, so a browser client can read a 401 or 422 body. credentials = true adds access-control-allow-credentials: true ; expose_headers is sent as access-control-expose-headers . A request from any other origin, or without an Origin , is served normally without the permission headers and still carries vary: origin , so a shared cache never hands one origin's answer to another; the browser refuses to hand the response to the page. CORS tells browsers what to allow. It is not authentication and does not stop a non-browser client. A preflight ( OPTIONS with Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method ) is answered with 204 , the configured methods , headers and max_age , without reaching a route or its access policy. A preflight from an origin that is not listed receives 403 cors_origin_denied . Origins are compared exactly, in lower case as browsers send them: https://app.example.com and https://app.example.com:8443 are different origins, and a trailing slash or path is refused at load. Browsers leave a default port out of Origin , so list https://app.example.com , not https://app.example.com:443 . The single entry * answers every origin with access-control-allow-origin: * ; it cannot be combined with credentials , and browsers will not send cookies or HTTP authentication to it. The policy applies to the whole application, including the ASGI and WSGI adapters; there is no per-route CORS option. An answer that already sets access-control-allow-origin itself (a Reply with that header) is sent as it is, without the policy's headers. Browser security headers and HTTPS ¶ Every HTTP response gets X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff , the configured X-Frame-Options and Referrer-Policy , including errors, OpenAPI/docs and admin responses. Defaults are SAMEORIGIN and same-origin , preserving the admin's existing referrer privacy default. These fields are owned by the app security policy: configured values replace same-named headers returned by a route. The choices are enums rather than arbitrary strings, and environment/TOML values must match the listed wire values exactly. FrameOptions provides deny and sameorigin . ReferrerPolicy provides no-referrer , no-referrer-when-downgrade , same-origin , origin , strict-origin , origin-when-cross-origin , strict-origin-when-cross-origin and unsafe-url . unsafe-url can disclose the full referring URL to another origin; use it only when that is intended. from hinoki import settings class BlogSettings ( settings . AppSettings ): security : settings . SecuritySettings = settings . SecuritySettings ( redirect_https = True , hsts_seconds = 31_536_000 , hsts_include_subdomains = True , frame_options = settings . FrameOptions . DENY , referrer_policy = settings . ReferrerPolicy . STRICT_ORIGIN , ) For configuration loaded from the environment, set BLOG_ALLOWED_HOSTS=api.example.com and BLOG_SECURITY__REDIRECT_HTTPS=true . A wildcard host policy cannot be combined with the redirect: Hinoki requires an explicit host allowlist before constructing an absolute Location , which avoids redirecting an attacker supplied Host value. The redirect is 308 , preserves the method and raw path/query, and runs before route lookup, authentication and body reading. A configured CORS preflight is answered before redirecting so browser preflight requests remain usable. HSTS defaults off. Hinoki emits it only when the request's effective scheme is HTTPS. Behind TLS termination, configure the exact proxy addresses in server.trusted_proxies ; an untrusted X-Forwarded-Proto does not enable HSTS or suppress the redirect. hsts_preload also requires hsts_include_subdomains and a max-age of at least one year. Use HSTS only after confirming that HTTPS is available for every covered host: browsers retain the policy after the response. 8. Database connection ownership ¶ For local development, DatabaseSettings.url defaults to sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 . Hinoki creates the hidden directory and database file when the module starts; it does not connect at module import or when models are imported. Configure a server database with one URL or with engine and its connection fields (see configure a database ). Environment, dotenv and constructor values can override the local default. The URL and the password are secrets and cannot be loaded from TOML; TOML can hold the other connection fields and the pool size. A database: DatabaseSettings field is enough: Hinoki installs DatabaseModule for it (a module declared in modules= or installed in a factory replaces it). The module opens a pool in each worker's startup lifespan, fails startup if the database is unreachable, and closes that worker's pool on shutdown. Each worker owns its own pool, so budget replicas × workers × max_size against the server database's connection limit. PostgreSQL URLs accept sslmode=disable , prefer , require , verify-ca or verify-full , and sslrootcert=/path/to/ca.pem . prefer tries TLS first and falls back to plaintext only if the server declines TLS; a certificate or handshake error fails closed. All TLS connections verify the server certificate chain and hostname. require , verify-ca and verify-full require TLS; Hinoki's verify-ca also verifies the hostname. Trust uses Mozilla WebPKI roots plus any PEM certificates in sslrootcert (maximum file size 1 MiB). sslmode=require therefore requires a trusted certificate too. sslmode=allow is unsupported. Keep the URL in a secret setting, and mount the CA file where each worker can read it. SQLite accepts a file URL such as sqlite:///srv/app/data.sqlite3 ; relative paths are relative to the process working directory. In-memory databases are not supported because each pooled connection has an independent database. SQLite uses bundled SQLite 3.35 or newer, a bounded connection pool and a single-writer model. UUID and timestamp columns use text storage; JSON uses JSON text. SQLite contains matching is ASCII case-insensitive. postgresql://app:password@db.example/app?sslmode=require&sslrootcert=/run/secrets/db-ca.pem class BlogSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "BLOG_" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = BlogSettings , include = [ health , Posts ]) The configuration is automatic in the useful sense: BLOG_DATABASE__URL (or the connection fields) is loaded from settings and the database module connects as the server starts. Resource creation and cleanup remain explicit in the module lifecycle; there is no process-global connection opened during import. Factories remain useful when the app's routes or modules depend on runtime choices. One-off scripts have a different lifecycle. examples/blog/seed.py opens a short-lived Database explicitly, applies migrations, inserts synthetic rows and closes the pool in finally . It runs outside the HTTP server, so there is no worker lifespan to own that resource. It is a one-time seed for a fresh disposable database, not a repeatable reset: cd examples BLOG_DATABASE__URL = postgres://... uv run --project .. python -m blog.seed Use a disposable database for the example. The seed command is not a production migration mechanism and is not run at app startup.

docs.text: Hinoki uses typed, immutable settings classes . The declared app form loads its settings class while constructing the app; a factory can call Settings.load() itself. Secrets are redacted. Database connection pools have a separate worker lifecycle: settings describe how to connect, and a module opens and closes the pool.
docs.title: Settings: how configuration, secrets and database pools work

docs.text: from typing import Literal from hinoki import settings class BlogSettings ( settings . AppSettings ): # keeps the built-in groups database : settings . DatabaseSettings # url: settings.Secret, max_size: int jwt_secret : settings . Secret | None = None # optional secret admin_theme : Literal [ "studio" , "console" , "paper" , "bento" ] = "studio" Settings types live in the hinoki.settings namespace: from hinoki import settings , then settings.AppSettings , settings.DatabaseSettings , settings.Secret , settings.Settings and settings.SettingsError . Name your own subclass for your project ( BlogSettings above) and keep a loaded value in a variable such as app_settings , so the namespace is not shadowed. Earlier revisions exported these types from hinoki itself and called the base class FrameworkSettings ; from hinoki import FrameworkSettings now raises ImportError . settings.AppSettings brings eight groups every app has: execution (8 sync workers, queue limit 64, request timeout 30 seconds, 1 MiB body limit, 8 KiB query limit and 32 KiB header limit), lifecycle (30-second startup and 10-second shutdown limits), logging (level, text or JSON, optional request ID correlation), docs (title, version and optional OpenAPI/Swagger/ReDoc URLs), server (which server, host, port, workers and proxy trust), pagination (default page_size and max_page_size for PageNumberPagination , see pagination ), cors (which browser origins may read responses) and security (browser response headers and optional HTTPS redirect). Three values sit beside the groups: timezone , debug and allowed_hosts ; see Debug, allowed hosts and CORS . A field without a default is required . Request IDs and timeout responses are described in the request lifecycle . docs.openapi_url , docs.docs_url and docs.redoc_url default to None , so no API document or viewer route is served until configured. Swagger UI or ReDoc requires an openapi_url . The same values can be supplied as Hinoki(...) arguments; explicit arguments win over docs settings, and None disables a page.

docs.text: Forwarded metadata is ignored unless the immediate socket peer matches server.trusted_proxies . Configure only the addresses or CIDRs of proxies that remove client-supplied forwarding headers and write their own values. For example: class BlogSettings ( settings . AppSettings ): ... # The private address used by this deployment's ingress, not every private network. server : settings . ServerSettings = settings . ServerSettings ( trusted_proxies = ( "10.20.0.0/16" ,), request_id_header = "x-correlation-id" , trust_request_id = True , ) Set logging.include_request_id=true to add the resolved ID to Hinoki's own log records while a request is being handled. Text logs append request_id=<id> and JSON logs include a request_id field. The ID matches the response's configured request ID header. Startup and other records outside a request omit the field. This setting is off by default, and it does not change application or third-party logger handlers. From a trusted peer, Hinoki accepts a single X-Forwarded-Proto value of http or https and walks a bounded X-Forwarded-For chain from the peer side to the first untrusted address. Request.scheme and Request.client use those validated values. Invalid, repeated or ambiguous values fall back to the socket scope. X-Forwarded-Host is never used: Host , allowed_hosts and generated URLs continue to use the original Host header. On a listener bound to :: , an IPv4 peer can appear as ::ffff:a.b.c.d , which a plain IPv4 entry does not match (the proxy is then untrusted); see behind a reverse proxy . Request IDs are generated by default. With trust_request_id=True , one inbound configured header is accepted only from a trusted immediate peer and only when it is 1–128 visible ASCII characters without commas or controls. Otherwise Hinoki generates a new ID. The selected value appears in Request.request_id , built-in error JSON and the configured response header. The proxy must sanitize the incoming header before forwarding it; do not trust a broad network range merely because it is private.

AppSettings , prefix = "BLOG_" , toml = "settings.toml" ): ... app_settings = BlogSettings . load () # reads the declared file by default Pass toml="path/to/settings.toml" to load or explain to override the class path. STRICT_ORIGIN , ) For configuration loaded from the environment, set BLOG_ALLOWED_HOSTS=api.example.com and BLOG_SECURITY__REDIRECT_HTTPS=true . A wildcard host policy cannot be combined with the redirect: Hinoki requires an explicit host allowlist before constructing an absolute Location , which avoids redirecting an attacker supplied Host value. The redirect is 308 , preserves the method and raw path/query, and runs before route lookup, authentication and body reading. A configured CORS preflight is answered before redirecting so browser preflight requests remain usable. HSTS defaults off. Hinoki emits it only when the request's effective scheme is HTTPS. Behind TLS termination, configure the exact proxy addresses in server.trusted_proxies ; an untrusted X-Forwarded-Proto does not enable HSTS or suppress the redirect. hsts_preload also requires hsts_include_subdomains and a max-age of at least one year. Use HSTS only after confirming that HTTPS is available for every covered host: browsers retain the policy after the response.

docs.text: For local development, DatabaseSettings.url defaults to sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 . Hinoki creates the hidden directory and database file when the module starts; it does not connect at module import or when models are imported. Configure a server database with one URL or with engine and its connection fields (see configure a database ). Environment, dotenv and constructor values can override the local default. The URL and the password are secrets and cannot be loaded from TOML; TOML can hold the other connection fields and the pool size. A database: DatabaseSettings field is enough: Hinoki installs DatabaseModule for it (a module declared in modules= or installed in a factory replaces it). The module opens a pool in each worker's startup lifespan, fails startup if the database is unreachable, and closes that worker's pool on shutdown. Each worker owns its own pool, so budget replicas × workers × max_size against the server database's connection limit. PostgreSQL URLs accept sslmode=disable , prefer , require , verify-ca or verify-full , and sslrootcert=/path/to/ca.pem . prefer tries TLS first and falls back to plaintext only if the server declines TLS; a certificate or handshake error fails closed. All TLS connections verify the server certificate chain and hostname. require , verify-ca and verify-full require TLS; Hinoki's verify-ca also verifies the hostname. Trust uses Mozilla WebPKI roots plus any PEM certificates in sslrootcert (maximum file size 1 MiB). sslmode=require therefore requires a trusted certificate too. sslmode=allow is unsupported. Keep the URL in a secret setting, and mount the CA file where each worker can read it. SQLite accepts a file URL such as sqlite:///srv/app/data.sqlite3 ; relative paths are relative to the process working directory. In-memory databases are not supported because each pooled connection has an independent database. SQLite uses bundled SQLite 3.35 or newer, a bounded connection pool and a single-writer model. UUID and timestamp columns use text storage; JSON uses JSON text. SQLite contains matching is ASCII case-insensitive. postgresql://app:password@db.example/app?sslmode=require&sslrootcert=/run/secrets/db-ca.pem class BlogSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "BLOG_" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = BlogSettings , include = [ health , Posts ]) The configuration is automatic in the useful sense: BLOG_DATABASE__URL (or the connection fields) is loaded from settings and the database module connects as the server starts. Resource creation and cleanup remain explicit in the module lifecycle; there is no process-global connection opened during import. Factories remain useful when the app's routes or modules depend on runtime choices. One-off scripts have a different lifecycle. examples/blog/seed.py opens a short-lived Database explicitly, applies migrations, inserts synthetic rows and closes the pool in finally . It runs outside the HTTP server, so there is no worker lifespan to own that resource. It is a one-time seed for a fresh disposable database, not a repeatable reset: cd examples BLOG_DATABASE__URL = postgres://... uv run --project .. python -m blog.seed Use a disposable database for the example. The seed command is not a production migration mechanism and is not run at app startup.

docs.text: Interactive shell ¶ Use hinoki shell to inspect application state and run ORM queries from an interactive Python prompt: cd examples uv run --project .. hinoki shell The project manifest supplies the application target and model modules. To open an app outside a project manifest, pass its module:attribute target and model modules explicitly: uv run --project .. hinoki shell blog.main:app --models blog.models The shell exposes app , its validated settings , and concrete model classes from registered modules. It supports multiline statements and top-level await on one persistent event loop: >>> notes = await Note . all () >>> len ( notes ) 3 >>> app . title 'Hinoki Blog' Use the async ORM methods with await in this shell. Synchronous ORM methods are intended for synchronous handlers and cannot block the shell's event loop. Each installed app module is started in dependency order and closed when the session ends. Application on_startup and on_shutdown hooks are not called. This avoids unrelated actions such as sending mail or seeding data. Hinoki does not apply migrations; run hinoki migrations apply explicitly when needed. The shell requires a terminal. Ctrl-D exits, Ctrl-C at the prompt exits, and Ctrl-C during a cell interrupts that cell. Unmanaged asyncio tasks are cancelled on exit; cleanup is bounded by the app's shutdown_timeout . A task that ignores cancellation is abandoned when that deadline expires. Startup is bounded too; if a module suppresses cancellation indefinitely while opening, the shell stops the loop and cannot guarantee that the partially started module released its own resources. Python entered at the prompt runs with the current user's privileges. Database operations use the configured database and may change its contents; use a development database while exploring. See the CLI reference for target selection and error behavior.
