docs.text: Project status ¶ Hinoki is pre-alpha. The public API and migration format may change; this repository is not published on PyPI. The hinoki project name currently belongs to an unrelated legacy package. Use this repository's source checkout for evaluation and test against disposable data. The documentation site separates current development docs from release-tagged versions. Until the first release, the site root points to the dev docs. Implemented and exercised ¶ The repository includes typed function and class APIs, optional model-backed CRUD route generation, request binding and strict schemas, built-in and custom Schema validation, bounded typed multipart uploads, opt-in Model write constraints and validators, access policies and declared errors, optional architecture rules, settings and worker modules, SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB ORM backends with relations, querysets and file-based migrations, sync and async handlers, OpenAPI, parsers, renderers, development and application MCP, and an optional admin with four styles. The examples are the best way to see the pieces together: Notes for a small declared app, Tracker for layers, ownership and rules, and Blog for relations, auth and admin. Current boundaries ¶ SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB are supported ORM databases; SQLite is the local-development default. MySQL and MariaDB have separate real-server integration coverage in CI. SQL Server and Oracle are not supported. See the database guide for backend-specific TLS, migration and feature limits, including MariaDB JSON behavior. Hinoki does not open database connections at import or apply migrations automatically. The ASGI adapter and application handler calls run in Python. The Rust extension currently provides path matching, selected query/header/cookie parsing, schema validation/serialization, cryptography and SQL ORM compilation/execution. Built-in security settings add browser response headers, HSTS on effective HTTPS requests, and an opt-in 308 HTTPS redirect that requires explicit allowed hosts. Generated typing for some keyword-based ORM calls is less precise than model construction; see typing . Many-to-many links use an explicit model with two foreign keys and a composite uniqueness constraint. Implicit join models, direct collection access such as post.tags , and advanced relation paths are not available. End-to-end performance claims are not made without comparable retained measurements; see the benchmark report and its limits. The default server is Granian. An opt-in Rust HTTP server ( hinoki serve --server rust ) is available for serve and dev : HTTP/1.1, optional TLS and, with server.http2 over TLS, HTTP/2 (no h2c, server push or WebSocket upgrades), no access log, handlers and most request-pipeline work still run in Python, and no performance figure is claimed. An optional startup_url can be answered on the Rust runtime when no host, CORS or HTTPS-redirect policy needs Python; it reports startup completion, not general application or database health. See serving . The server adapter is ASGI. hinoki.wsgi.WSGIAdapter wraps an application for WSGI servers (buffered bodies, no streaming); verified with Granian only, see serving . Responses are sent complete: streaming responses, server-sent events and WebSockets are not available on any server. CORS is one application-wide policy in the cors settings group; there is no per-route CORS option. Application MCP has its own allowed-origin check. Cursor pagination is not available; pagination currently uses page numbers. Pagination page-size defaults are 20 and 100 ; the pagination settings group changes them for the whole app and an action's own PageNumberPagination values win. See pagination . OpenAPI generation creates operation IDs and reads summary/description from handler docstrings. Per-action tags , deprecated , custom operation_id and include_in_schema controls are not available. There is no maintained Docker image or deployment recipe. hinoki serve runs the app with Granian (or the opt-in Rust server); container packaging and process orchestration are application deployment choices. See the roadmap for project direction and contributing for local checks.

docs.text: Sync and async execution ¶ Hinoki runs on one event loop per worker. Async is the native way; sync is a supported way , not a second-class one: a plain def handler or hook runs on a bounded thread pool ( settings.ExecutionSettings.sync_workers , sync_queue ; a full queue answers 503 overloaded , in handlers and in sync hooks), the request's context follows it, and the sync ORM methods hand their work back to the worker's loop and block that thread, never the loop. Naming convention ¶ A name with the a prefix awaits the database ( aget , acreate , acount ); the same name without it is the blocking twin for sync handlers. A query builder is lazy until you evaluate it, and awaiting the queryset itself is the async twin of .list() : posts = await Post . filter ( published = True ) . order_by ( "-created" ) # async posts = Post . filter ( published = True ) . order_by ( "-created" ) . list () # sync handler first = await Post . all () . afirst () aall() was removed: await Post.all() replaces await Post.all().aall() . Parity table ¶ Surface Async Sync Notes Action handlers async def def Sync runs on the executor Generated CRUD hooks ( get_queryset , written_queryset , to_schema , perform_* ) async def def Sync overrides run on the same bounded executor; use the matching sync or async ORM methods Auth providers ( authenticate , resolve , resolve_token , JWT resolve_claims ) async def def Sync hooks run on the executor, so sync model calls are safe inside them Model: create / get / update / delete acreate , aget , aget_or_none , aupdate , aupdate_where , adelete , asave , aupdate_from create , get , get_or_none , update , update_where , delete , save , update_from Sync calls only work inside a sync handler or hook served by Hinoki. The sync writes take the same returning=False option as their async twins ( models ) QuerySet: read await queryset , afirst , aget , acount , aexists , apaginate list , first , get , count , exists , paginate QuerySet: write aupdate , adelete update , delete Relations explicit loading ( select_related , prefetch_related ) same never lazy, so no hidden I/O in either style Raw SQL ( Database.fetch , fetch_one , execute ) async none Use the model/queryset methods from sync code; raw SQL is an async-only escape hatch Transactions transaction=True on the action same The runtime owns it for both styles Schema , Request , Reply , parsers, renderers plain code same No I/O Password hashing await hasher.hash/verify hash_sync , verify_sync The async calls use a bounded thread pool Error handlers ( app.errors.handle ) async def def Run on the loop: no blocking calls inside Module lifespans async context manager none Resources belong to the worker's loop App startup/shutdown hooks async def hook(ctx) def hook(ctx) on the sync executor Listed in Hinoki(on_startup=..., on_shutdown=...) Admin hooks ( stats , check , save , remove ) async def none The admin runs on the loop; override with async def Tests ASGIClient SyncClient Same behaviour through both Dev MCP run_scenario n/a n/a Runs the app in-process Limits to know ¶ Sync hooks use the same pool as sync handlers. Sync auth and CRUD hooks take an executor slot; a flood of bad credentials or long-running hooks can fill the queue and make legitimate sync work answer 503 ( overloaded , with Retry-After ). Keep sync hooks short, reject malformed credentials before touching the database, and prefer async hooks when they can use async APIs. A sync auth hook runs before the action's transaction opens , so it is never part of it. Sync model calls only work inside the application's sync handlers and hooks. In a test body use the async API (an async fixture) or your own connection, also with SyncClient . No sync lifespan, sync admin hooks, sync background tasks ( ctx.tasks.start_soon takes coroutines) or sync Database SQL. A sync error handler runs on the loop and must not call the ORM (its failure is treated as "unhandled"). SyncClient is available only inside its with block and raises a timeout error after timeout seconds. Rules of thumb ¶ Prefer async handlers; use def for code that is naturally blocking (a library without async support, CPU work measured to be short). Never call blocking code from an async def ; never call an a... coroutine from a def without run_sync -style helpers (the sync model methods already do that for you). CPU-heavy work belongs in a separate process or worker, not in either pool. A sync call made on the event loop itself raises, with a message naming the a... variant. Verified ¶ The test suite exercises sync and async handlers, synchronous authentication hooks, ORM calls through both clients, mixed traffic and cancellation against a disposable database. There are no synchronous module lifespans, admin hooks or background task APIs; those surfaces are async-only by design.

docs.text: Testing ¶ Hinoki has two useful levels of application tests: call the operation functions directly, then exercise the app through its ASGI interface. Test the application over ASGI ¶ ASGIClient drives startup, HTTP requests and shutdown without opening a network socket: from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient # create_app and TEST_DATABASE_URL come from the application under test. async with ASGIClient ( create_app ( TEST_DATABASE_URL ), strict_errors = True ) as client : response = await client . post ( "/tasks" , json = { "title" : "Write docs" }, token = "member" ) assert response . status == 201 Its context manager runs module lifespans and the application's startup and shutdown hooks. If the application declares a database, point it to a disposable PostgreSQL database. strict_errors=True catches an HTTP error returned by an action but missing from its errors= declaration. Both clients have get , post , put , patch , delete , head , options and query (the HTTP QUERY method; its body goes in json= or body= , while the query= option of every call is the query string), plus request(method, path, ...) for any other method. Test file uploads ¶ ASGIClient and SyncClient accept data= and files= and build the multipart boundary and Content-Type header for you. Use a sequence of file tuples to send repeated field names in order: async with ASGIClient ( create_app ()) as client : response = await client . post ( "/documents" , data = { "title" : "Report" }, files = [( "document" , "report.txt" , b "contents" , "text/plain" )], ) assert response . status == 201 Each file tuple is (field_name, filename, content_bytes, content_type) . Form data may be a mapping or an ordered sequence of (name, text) pairs; sequences retain repeated names. Do not pass json= or raw body= together with data= / files= ; the helper owns the multipart content type and boundary. The application enforces its configured complete-body and per-part limits. This helper sends complete in-memory bodies and does not model streaming uploads. headers= accepts a mapping or a sequence of (name, value) pairs. Use pairs to send a repeated header; Hinoki's request header mapping joins repeated values with ", " . A client can add a default Host header to each request: async with ASGIClient ( create_app (), host = "api.example.com" ) as client : response = await client . get ( "/health" , headers = [( "X-Trace" , "first" ), ( "X-Trace" , "second" )] ) The default remains no Host header. Set headers={"host": "other.example.com"} on a call to override the client's host. SyncClient is available for synchronous test functions. It runs the app's lifespan and refuses unsafe nested use from a running event loop. For deterministic time, ManualClock is a thread-safe callable clock. It accepts and returns timezone-aware instants normalized to UTC; advance(seconds=...) and set(datetime) control its value. A naive datetime raises ValueError . Pass it to app.now(clock) or other code that accepts a Clock . Test the layers separately ¶ Keep business operations independent of Request and HTTP response types when practical. Test ownership and state transitions against a disposable database, then test route binding, access, status codes and error declarations through ASGIClient . Use synthetic rows and credentials. Never point test settings at production data. Repository checks ¶ From the checkout, the documented gates are: uv run --locked ruff check . uv run --locked ruff format --check . uv run --locked mypy uv run --locked pytest --cov cargo fmt --all --check cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings cargo test --workspace PostgreSQL-dependent Python and Rust tests require HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL ; without it those tests are skipped. Migration conformance tests for MySQL and MariaDB also require HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL and HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL , respectively. CI provides disposable real-server services. See toolchain and CI for packaging and docs checks too.

Cognitive complexity is capped at 15 for every Python function and Rust function/closure. CI runs pinned complexipy and rust-code-analysis-cli ; test and development code are included. Refactor over-budget functions instead of suppressing analyzer findings. Dependency groups: lint , typecheck , test , aggregated by dev . Two environments, two responsibilities ¶ uv owns the project: .venv , uv.lock , the dependency groups and every tool declared in them ( ruff , mypy , pytest , pre-commit itself). Run them with uv run --locked ... . pre-commit builds its own isolated environments for the hooks it fetches (e.g. ruff-pre-commit ); these are not the project .venv and are not managed by uv. That is why the Ruff revision in .pre-commit-config.yaml must equal the ruff== pin in pyproject.toml ( uv.lock ). Hooks never rewrite sources/ -style historical snapshots (excluded globally). CI never applies fixes: it fails if a hook would change a file. pre-commit install is a manual step in a Git checkout, never triggered by importing the framework. To update one, resolve the new tag to its commit ( gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/git/ref/tags/TAG ), replace the SHA and the comment together, and let the PR's CI run prove it. Each Python X job sets UV_PYTHON to its matrix version and asserts the interpreter before testing. Without it uv run follows .python-version and every job would test 3.13. Locally, run another version with uv run --locked --python 3.14 pytest (use UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT to keep its environment apart). ci.yml checks out with persist-credentials: false : no CI job pushes. deploy-docs.yml keeps the token because it pushes to gh-pages . The audit job checks Cargo.lock ( cargo audit , cargo deny check ) and uv.lock ( uv export of every group and extra, then pip-audit --require-hashes --disable-pip ). Locally: uv export --locked --all-groups --all-extras --no-emit-project --format requirements-txt -o /tmp/requirements.txt && uvx pip-audit==2.10.1 --require-hashes --disable-pip -r /tmp/requirements.txt . docs.text: Transactions ¶ An action opts into a database transaction with transaction=True . The transaction is opened for the request and commits only after the handler returns and the response body is encoded and rendered successfully. Hinoki does not validate the returned Python value against the handler's response annotation at runtime; see OpenAPI limits . @http . post ( "/tasks" , transaction = True , status = 201 ) async def create_task ( data : TaskInput ) -> TaskOutput : task = await Task . acreate ( data ) await AuditEvent . acreate ( task_id = task . id , action = "created" ) return TaskOutput . from_model ( task ) If the handler raises, response encoding/rendering fails, the request times out, or the task is cancelled, the transaction rolls back before the error response is translated. A value that does not match the response annotation is not necessarily rejected. Do not send email or perform another irreversible side effect inside the transaction; arrange it after the transaction commits, or use an outbox owned by the application. Nested db.transaction() scopes in the same owning task use savepoints. A child task cannot share its parent's active transaction. Raw database operations are async-only; see sync and async . For a function route group, RouteGroup(..., atomic=True) makes write methods transactional by default. An individual action can opt out explicitly with transaction=False .

docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ cannot load module:attribute ¶ Run the command from the application checkout and check both the module path and attribute spelling. hinoki adds the current directory when importing targets, but the package still needs to be importable Python code. Settings report a missing or unknown variable ¶ Check the settings class's prefix= and nested field names. Nested groups use __ , for example APP_DATABASE__URL . Run hinoki settings module:SettingsClass --example to inspect expected names. settings.Secret values are redacted by design. Database connection fails at startup ¶ The database module opens a pool in each worker's startup. Confirm the selected backend URL, network reachability and database availability from the same environment as the worker. Check the backend-specific URL, TLS and migration limits in Configure a database . Use one worker and a small pool while debugging; total maximum connections are replicas × workers × pool size. A related field is not loaded ¶ Foreign-key attributes do not trigger queries. Add select_related("author") or prefetch_related("posts") to the query that needs the relation. hinoki check reports unverifiable ¶ The rule could not establish its promise. Read the diagnostic explanation and any fix: line. Some rules inspect only declarations; effectful checks require the explicit --allow-effects flag. A sync handler or auth provider stalls ¶ Sync code runs on a bounded executor and can saturate. Prefer async database and network calls in async handlers. See sync and async for limits and server settings for worker configuration. A migration is marked destructive ¶ Review the generated SQL and the data it may remove. Test the change against a disposable database backup before using --allow-destructive . See migrations . If the issue persists, include the Hinoki version, the command or route, the complete diagnostic, and a minimal example. Remove credentials and user data first. For a version report, run hinoki version --verbose --format json . The output includes installed runtime details without reading application settings or opening a database. For a consolidated local report, run hinoki doctor . It imports the selected app target, but does not start its lifecycle, run rules, connect to a database or write files. Use the focused commands above for database and migration state.

docs.text: Type checking Hinoki applications ¶ Hinoki's public APIs use Python annotations so a type checker can catch mistakes in handlers, decorators and schema construction. The repository is checked with mypy in strict mode; other checkers and IDEs have not been evaluated systematically. Run the project's check from its checkout: uv run --locked mypy Typed surfaces ¶ Contract Result HTTP decorators Preserve a handler's parameter and return types. Invalid decorator options such as transaction="yes" are type errors. Schema classes Generated constructors check required, unknown and mistyped fields; Field(default_factory=...) preserves the value type. Application and route groups Hinoki.include , API classes and RouteGroup provide typed declarations. Unknown include items fail at app construction. Authentication context Annotate a parameter as Caller[User] to receive the typed caller and application user. Decorator composition User decorators should preserve signatures with functools.wraps , ParamSpec and TypeVar . For standalone handlers the final decorated function is dispatched. With RouteGroup , put the HTTP decorator outermost so it captures the final handler. ORM method signatures ¶ Model construction and common instance operations are typed. Some ORM methods that accept arbitrary model field names still have broad keyword signatures, so a checker may not catch a misspelled field passed to these methods: task = Task ( title = "Write docs" ) # constructor fields and values are checked await task . asave () Fields inherited from an abstract model are part of the checked constructor. Fields that come from a plain (non-model) mixin exist at run time but are not constructor arguments for a type checker; use an abstract model when you need them checked. Model.acreate(**values) and some filter/update keyword calls cannot currently verify each field name against the model class. Use the constructor plus asave() when you want field-level checking on insertion. This limitation does not affect runtime validation of model fields or database constraints. The return types of the write methods are checked: aupdate returns the model, aupdate_where and QuerySet.aupdate a list of it, and with a literal returning=False each returns int ( writes that do not read the row back ). A returning value that is a plain bool gives the union of both. acreate and insert return the model either way. Unpacking a dictionary into aupdate(**values) or update(**values) gives Any , because the dictionary could hold returning ; pass returning=True explicitly to keep the model type. The Python package includes typing metadata, and the compiled hinoki.core module has a matching stub. See the API reference for the public signatures.

docs.text: Utilities ¶ Hinoki includes a small set of helpers where the framework can define clear behavior. Use the Python standard library for ordinary IDs, paths, and application-specific formatting. UTC time ¶ utc_now() returns a timezone-aware datetime in UTC. It is suitable for field factories and application code: from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Event ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) The clock is a callable, so code that depends on time can accept a Clock and tests can supply a fixed function. No process-wide clock patch is needed. For tests that need to move time more than once, use ManualClock from hinoki.testing : from datetime import UTC , datetime from hinoki.testing import ManualClock clock = ManualClock ( datetime ( 2026 , 1 , 1 , tzinfo = UTC )) first = clock () clock . advance ( seconds = 60 ) second = clock () It stores instants in UTC, accepts only timezone-aware values, and can be passed to app.now(clock) or utc_today(clock) . Application timezone ¶ Set an IANA timezone name in the app's global settings. It defaults to UTC ; invalid names fail while settings are constructed: from hinoki import Hinoki , settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings ): timezone : str = "Europe/Rome" app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings ) current_time = app . now () # aware datetime in Europe/Rome app.now() reads the timezone from that app's settings and returns an aware datetime . Apps in one process can use different settings. There is no Hinoki(timezone=...) argument. To make time-dependent code deterministic, pass a Clock to app.now(clock) . utc_today(clock=utc_now) returns the calendar date in UTC. The framework uses it for waiver expiry so the result does not depend on the machine's local timezone. For example, 2026-01-02 00:30+02:00 is 2026-01-01 in UTC. Model update timestamps ¶ Declare the columns explicitly and decorate the model with @timestamps() to refresh updated_at on each ORM update: from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field , timestamps from hinoki.utils import utc_now @timestamps () class Note ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) title : str created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) updated_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) The decorator requires a non-nullable datetime field named updated_at . Use @timestamps("modified_at", clock=my_clock) for another field or an injected clock. Clock values must be timezone-aware; Hinoki converts them to UTC. A value supplied for the managed field in an update is replaced by the clock value. The behavior applies to Model.aupdate / update_where , instance asave / aupdate_from , and QuerySet.aupdate , including sync counterparts. All rows changed by one statement receive the same time. Creation uses the declared field factories. Raw SQL bypasses this ORM behavior; use an explicit database trigger if independent writers need database-authoritative timestamps. These fields are ordinary model columns. They remain visible to type checkers and the migration planner; Hinoki does not add hidden fields or apply migrations automatically. Other common needs ¶ Use uuid.uuid4() for ordinary UUID identifiers. Use secrets or hinoki.crypto.random_token for secret tokens, depending on whether the token is part of Hinoki authentication. docs.text: utc_now() returns a timezone-aware datetime in UTC. It is suitable for field factories and application code: from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Event ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) The clock is a callable, so code that depends on time can accept a Clock and tests can supply a fixed function. No process-wide clock patch is needed. For tests that need to move time more than once, use ManualClock from hinoki.testing : from datetime import UTC , datetime from hinoki.testing import ManualClock clock = ManualClock ( datetime ( 2026 , 1 , 1 , tzinfo = UTC )) first = clock () clock . advance ( seconds = 60 ) second = clock () It stores instants in UTC, accepts only timezone-aware values, and can be passed to app.now(clock) or utc_today(clock) .
docs.title: UTC time

docs.text: Set an IANA timezone name in the app's global settings. It defaults to UTC ; invalid names fail while settings are constructed: from hinoki import Hinoki , settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings ): timezone : str = "Europe/Rome" app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings ) current_time = app . now () # aware datetime in Europe/Rome app.now() reads the timezone from that app's settings and returns an aware datetime . Apps in one process can use different settings. There is no Hinoki(timezone=...) argument. To make time-dependent code deterministic, pass a Clock to app.now(clock) . utc_today(clock=utc_now) returns the calendar date in UTC. The framework uses it for waiver expiry so the result does not depend on the machine's local timezone. For example, 2026-01-02 00:30+02:00 is 2026-01-01 in UTC.
docs.title: Application timezone

docs.text: Declare the columns explicitly and decorate the model with @timestamps() to refresh updated_at on each ORM update: from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field , timestamps from hinoki.utils import utc_now @timestamps () class Note ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) title : str created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) updated_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) The decorator requires a non-nullable datetime field named updated_at . Use @timestamps("modified_at", clock=my_clock) for another field or an injected clock. Clock values must be timezone-aware; Hinoki converts them to UTC. A value supplied for the managed field in an update is replaced by the clock value. The behavior applies to Model.aupdate / update_where , instance asave / aupdate_from , and QuerySet.aupdate , including sync counterparts. All rows changed by one statement receive the same time. Creation uses the declared field factories. Raw SQL bypasses this ORM behavior; use an explicit database trigger if independent writers need database-authoritative timestamps. These fields are ordinary model columns. They remain visible to type checkers and the migration planner; Hinoki does not add hidden fields or apply migrations automatically.

docs.text: Auth and crypto ¶ JWTAuth delegates signature and registered-claim verification to the Rust core. Its current key and policy values are captured for each token verification, while the application-defined resolve_claims hook remains Python and runs for every verified token. hinoki.auth.Caller dataclass ¶ Who is making the request, as decided by authentication. id is a stable string, user is your own object (the user row, a service account) and permissions is what the caller may do:: Caller(id="u1", user=user, permissions=frozenset({"posts:write"})) hinoki.auth.Credentials dataclass ¶ The parts of a request a provider may inspect. hinoki.auth.BaseAuth ¶ Bases: ABC Base class of providers. authenticate returns a principal, None when the request carries no credentials, and raises Unauthorized when credentials are present but invalid. Providers hold no per-request state. openapi_scheme ¶ openapi_scheme () -> dict [ str , object ] | None OpenAPI security scheme describing this provider, if it has one. authenticate abstractmethod ¶ authenticate ( credentials : Credentials , ) -> Caller [ T ] | None | Awaitable [ Caller [ T ] | None ] async def or plain def (a plain one runs on the sync executor). hinoki.auth.HeaderAuth ¶ Bases: BaseAuth [ T ] Credential carried in a named header; subclasses implement resolve . resolve abstractmethod ¶ resolve ( value : str , ) -> Caller [ T ] | None | Awaitable [ Caller [ T ] | None ] The principal for a header value or None if invalid; async def or plain def . hinoki.auth.BearerAuth ¶ Bases: HeaderAuth [ T ] Authorization: Bearer <token> ; subclasses implement resolve_token . resolve_token abstractmethod ¶ resolve_token ( token : str , ) -> Caller [ T ] | None | Awaitable [ Caller [ T ] | None ] async def or plain def , as resolve . hinoki.auth.APIKeyAuth ¶ Bases: HeaderAuth [ T ] API key in x-api-key (override header to change it). hinoki.crypto.JWTKey dataclass ¶ One verification (and optionally signing) key. HMAC secrets must be at least as long as the hash (32/48/64 bytes). For EdDSA the key is the 32-byte private seed, or with public=True the 32-byte public key of a verify-only deployment. kid is required when several keys are configured. The key is excluded from repr . verify_only classmethod ¶ verify_only ( kid : str | None , public_key : bytes ) -> JWTKey An Ed25519 public key (32 bytes) that can verify but never sign. Use this, not the plain constructor, wherever you hold only the public key: a public key passed as a seed would let anyone who knows it forge tokens. hinoki.crypto.JWTAuth ¶ Bases: BearerAuth [ T ] Bearer-token provider for JWTs. Subclass, set keys (and usually issuer and audience ) and implement resolve_claims :: class Tokens(JWTAuth[User]): keys = [JWTKey("2026-11", "HS256", settings.jwt_secret)] issuer = "https://api.example.com" audience = "blog" async def resolve_claims(self, claims): subject, raw = claims.get("sub"), claims.get("scopes", []) if not isinstance(subject, str) or not isinstance(raw, list): return None # claims are signed, but still untyped JSON try: user = await User.aget_or_none(id=UUID(subject)) except ValueError: # a signed token can still carry any text return None if user is None: return None scopes = frozenset(s for s in raw if isinstance(s, str)) return Caller(subject, user, scopes) now ¶ now () -> int The clock (override in tests). resolve_claims abstractmethod ¶ resolve_claims ( claims : dict [ str , Any ], ) -> Caller [ T ] | None | Awaitable [ Caller [ T ] | None ] The principal for verified claims, or None to refuse; async def or plain def . issue ¶ issue ( claims : dict [ str , Any ], ttl : int = 900 ) -> str A signed token for claims valid for ttl seconds, signed with the first non-public key. iat and exp are always set by the server (a value in claims is replaced); iss and aud are added when configured, unless claims already has them. hinoki.crypto.PasswordHasher ¶ Argon2id hashes in PHC format, computed off the event loop. Parameters below the OWASP floor are refused unless allow_weak=True (tests only). workers bounds concurrent hashing, max_pending the queue; beyond that hash / verify raise HashingBusy (503). A task cancelled while its hash runs frees its slot but the thread finishes, so at most workers extra hashes can be in flight; hash_sync / verify_sync are not bounded. Only argon2id hashes are verified. For unknown users, verify against a fixed dummy hash so timing does not reveal who exists. hash_sync ¶ hash_sync ( password : str ) -> str Blocking hash (for scripts and sync handlers). verify_sync ¶ verify_sync ( password : str , stored : str ) -> bool False for a wrong password; ValueError for a malformed hash. needs_rehash ¶ needs_rehash ( stored : str ) -> bool True when stored was made with other parameters than these. hinoki.crypto.random_token ¶ random_token ( size : int = 32 ) -> str size random bytes (1 to 1024) as URL-safe text, from the OS CSPRNG.

docs.text: Argon2id hashes in PHC format, computed off the event loop. Parameters below the OWASP floor are refused unless allow_weak=True (tests only). workers bounds concurrent hashing, max_pending the queue; beyond that hash / verify raise HashingBusy (503). A task cancelled while its hash runs frees its slot but the thread finishes, so at most workers extra hashes can be in flight; hash_sync / verify_sync are not bounded. Only argon2id hashes are verified. For unknown users, verify against a fixed dummy hash so timing does not reveal who exists.

docs.text: Database API ¶ For setup, application settings, URL examples and migration workflow, see configure a database . The ORM supports PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB. SQLite is the local-development default; configure an explicit URL to select a server backend. Raw SQL uses the selected driver's placeholders: PostgreSQL uses $1 , while SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB use ? . ORM-generated queries select the dialect automatically. Configure a backend ¶ Database URLs are secrets, so configure them through the environment rather than TOML. For local development, leave the URL unset to use the default SQLite file. To select another database for migration commands, set HINOKI_DATABASE_URL ; an app can use its own secret environment setting. TOML may configure non-secret pool options, for example: [database] max_size = 8 For PostgreSQL, use a driver URL such as postgresql://user:password@host/db . For MySQL, use mysql://user:password@host/db . MySQL connections require TLS by default; the driver verifies the server certificate and hostname. Configure the system trust store to trust your server certificate. require_ssl=false is only suitable for isolated local testing and disables transport encryption. Do not put production credentials in source-controlled settings files. For MariaDB, use mariadb://user:password@host/db ; it is selected and tested as a distinct backend even though it uses the MySQL wire driver and SQL dialect. Backend behavior and limits ¶ Backend Status Notes SQLite Supported Default for local development. SQLite permits one writer at a time. Schema changes that SQLite cannot express directly use a table rebuild. PostgreSQL Supported Uses PostgreSQL-native UUID, timestamp, JSON and byte types. MySQL Supported Uses InnoDB tables, binary UUIDs and MySQL-native JSON. MySQL DDL implicitly commits, so a failed migration can leave earlier DDL applied; inspect migration status and database schema before retrying. RETURNING is not supported by the compiler; ORM create/update operations use follow-up reads. TLS is required by default. MariaDB Supported Tested independently on MariaDB 11.4. Its JSON alias is text, so typed ORM dict / list fields are decoded from the model declaration. Low-level Database.fetch() returns JSON values as bytes because arbitrary text columns cannot be safely inferred as JSON. DDL can implicitly commit; TLS is required by default. SQL Server and Oracle are not currently supported. Do not assume that MySQL compatibility implies MariaDB compatibility. Hinoki does not silently roll back MySQL-family DDL: review generated migrations and keep a recoverable backup before applying schema changes. Datetime values stored in MySQL DATETIME columns use Hinoki's UTC-naive storage convention; values returned by the ORM are interpreted as UTC. MySQL pool capacity and acquisition wait are bounded by the database pool settings. Raw SQL must use the placeholders for the configured backend. Prefer ORM query methods when the same code should work across backends; raw SQL and migration operations may need backend-specific SQL. hinoki.db.Database ¶ A connection pool for one configured database backend. engine instance-attribute ¶ engine = engine dialect property ¶ dialect : str The selected dialect: postgres , sqlite , mysql or mariadb . __init__ ¶ __init__ ( engine : Database ) -> None connect async classmethod ¶ connect ( url : str , * , max_size : int = 8 , wait : float = 5.0 ) -> Database Open the pool and check the server; PostgreSQL URLs may configure TLS. active ¶ active () -> ActiveTransaction | None fetch async ¶ fetch ( sql : str , * params : Param ) -> list [ Row ] Rows as dicts, with placeholders selected by the active backend. _fetch_page_wire async ¶ _fetch_page_wire ( sql : str , params : list [ Param ], plan : _RowPlan , page : int , page_size : int , total : int , ) -> bytes | list [ Row ] Private generated-list fetch; fallback rows are already fetched. fetch_one async ¶ fetch_one ( sql : str , * params : Param ) -> Row | None execute async ¶ execute ( sql : str , * params : Param ) -> int Number of affected rows; raw SQL placeholders follow the backend. transaction ¶ transaction () -> TransactionScope migration ¶ migration () -> TransactionScope An exclusive migration transaction with backend locking semantics. close ¶ close () -> None status ¶ status () -> tuple [ int , int ] (connections, idle) in the pool. hinoki.db.DatabaseModule ¶ Bases: Module Opens a Database for the worker and provides it to other modules. app.install(DatabaseModule(url)) ; actions with transaction=True and other modules obtain it with ctx.get(Database) . The pool is created in the worker's lifespan and closed when it ends. name class-attribute instance-attribute ¶ name = 'database' url instance-attribute ¶ url = url max_size instance-attribute ¶ max_size = max_size wait instance-attribute ¶ wait = wait __init__ ¶ __init__ ( url : str , * , max_size : int = 8 , wait : float = 5.0 ) -> None from_settings classmethod ¶ from_settings ( settings : object ) -> DatabaseModule The module for settings.database (a DatabaseSettings : url and max_size), so Hinoki(settings=..., modules=[DatabaseModule]) works. lifespan async ¶ lifespan ( ctx : ModuleContext ) -> AsyncIterator [ None ] hinoki.db.DatabaseError ¶ Bases: builtins.Exception hinoki.db.UniqueViolation ¶ Bases: hinoki.core.DatabaseError hinoki.db.ForeignKeyViolation ¶ Bases: hinoki.core.DatabaseError hinoki.db.NotNullViolation ¶ Bases: hinoki.core.DatabaseError hinoki.db.CheckViolation ¶ Bases: hinoki.core.DatabaseError

-> None Two bases may not give one field name different types: which one the model would get depends on base order, and the other would be lost. CompiledSchema The Rust validator for this schema and everything it refers to, compiled on first use and cached on the class. validate classmethod ¶ validate ( data : object ) -> Self Build an instance from decoded JSON or raise ValidationError (validated in Rust). _validate_instance classmethod ¶ _validate_instance ( instance : Schema , * , allow_naive_datetime : bool = False , skip_fields : set [ str ] | None = None , use_aliases : bool = False , path_prefix : str = "" , ) -> None Validate final Python values on a manually constructed instance. fields classmethod ¶ fields () -> dict [ str , FieldSpec ] Immutable description shared by binding, docs and rules. to_dict ¶ to_dict ( * , exclude : Iterable [ str ] = ()) -> dict [ str , Any ] The field values as Python objects (UUID, datetime stay what they are), nested schemas converted too. Fields left UNSET are omitted, so the result is exactly "what the client sent" for a partial update. from_models classmethod ¶ from_models ( rows : Iterable [ object ], ** extra : Any ) -> list [ Self ] Build a list from a synchronous iterable of model rows. Each row follows from_model exactly. The iterable is consumed once, eagerly; this reads already-loaded attributes and never performs I/O. from_model classmethod ¶ from_model ( row : object , ** extra : Any ) -> Self Build this schema from a model instance: every field is read from the attribute of the same name, extra supplies or overrides values (for computed fields). Nested models become nested schemas. A field the row lacks is an error, and an unloaded relation still raises RelationNotLoaded : nothing here does I/O. dump ¶ dump ( * , include : Iterable [ str ] | None = None , exclude : Iterable [ str ] = (), exclude_unset : bool = False , by_alias : bool = True , ) -> dict [ str , Any ] Return JSON-compatible data with optional projection controls. Selectors use Python field names. exclude_unset omits defaulted fields not supplied at construction. HTTP responses use default options. hinoki.schemaconfig.SchemaConfig dataclass ¶ Immutable class-level Schema behavior configuration. hinoki.schemaconfig.SchemaExtra ¶ Bases: StrEnum Policy for unknown string keys in decoded Schema input. hinoki.fields.Field ¶ Field ( * , default_factory : Callable [[], T ], alias : str | None = None , ) -> T Field ( * , alias : str , min_length : int | None = None , max_length : int | None = None , pattern : str | None = None , ge : float | None = None , le : float | None = None , gt : float | None = None , lt : float | None = None , one_of : Sequence [ Any ] | None = None , format : str | None = None , discriminator : str | None = None , ) -> Any Field ( * , min_length : int | None = None , max_length : int | None = None , pattern : str | None = None , ge : float | None = None , le : float | None = None , gt : float | None = None , lt : float | None = None , one_of : Sequence [ Any ] | None = None , format : str | None = None , alias : str | None = None , discriminator : str | None = None , ) -> FieldInfo Field ( ** options : Any ) -> Any Declare constraints (inside Annotated ) or a default factory. tags: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list) gives a per-instance default; title: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1)] adds constraints. hinoki.schema.Invalid ¶ Bases: Exception Raised by a check to refuse a value: a stable code , a readable message and optionally the path it concerns (default: the field the check is attached to, or the object itself). hinoki.schema.Unset ¶ Type of UNSET : a field that was absent from the input (PATCH). hinoki.schema.field_check ¶ field_check ( * names : str ) -> Callable [[ F ], F ] Mark a method as a check on one or more fields: def ok(self, value) . It runs after the structural validation succeeded, so value already has the declared type, and may read the other fields through self . Raise Invalid(code, message) to refuse; it never changes the value. Checks are synchronous and must not do I/O: a rule that needs the database belongs in an operation, not in a schema. hinoki.schema.field_normalize ¶ field_normalize ( name : str ) -> Callable [[ F ], F ] Mark a typed field canonicalizer: def trim(self, value: str) -> str . docs.text: Application MCP and scaffold API ¶ hinoki.mcpapp.expose_as_mcp ¶ expose_as_mcp ( app : Hinoki , * , tools : Iterable [ str ], access : Access | None , path : str = "/mcp" , allow_writes : bool = False , public : bool = False , allowed_origins : Iterable [ str ] = (), ) -> list [ Callable [ ... , Any ]] The MCP action to app.include(...) , publishing the matching actions. tools are fnmatch patterns over qualified action names; call this after the exposed actions are included. access protects the endpoint ( None only with public=True ). The endpoint answers only application/json POSTs and refuses a request that carries an Origin outside allowed_origins (browsers send one; agents and CLI clients do not) or Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site : this keeps a web page from driving the tools with the user's cookie and covers the MCP DNS-rebinding rule. Cookie authentication together with allow_writes is still a risky combination; prefer bearer credentials. hinoki.mcpapp.ExposureError ¶ Bases: ValueError The MCP exposure is configured wrongly (raised when it is built). Project scaffolding is a command-line interface; see command line . For the stdio development server and its tools, see the development MCP guide . Application MCP is mounted separately on selected routes.

docs.text: expose_as_mcp ( app : Hinoki , * , tools : Iterable [ str ], access : Access | None , path : str = "/mcp" , allow_writes : bool = False , public : bool = False , allowed_origins : Iterable [ str ] = (), ) -> list [ Callable [ ... , Any ]] The MCP action to app.include(...) , publishing the matching actions. tools are fnmatch patterns over qualified action names; call this after the exposed actions are included. access protects the endpoint ( None only with public=True ). The endpoint answers only application/json POSTs and refuses a request that carries an Origin outside allowed_origins (browsers send one; agents and CLI clients do not) or Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site : this keeps a web page from driving the tools with the user's cookie and covers the MCP DNS-rebinding rule. Cookie authentication together with allow_writes is still a risky combination; prefer bearer credentials.

docs.text: Core API: application, routing and HTTP ¶ hinoki.app.Hinoki ¶ A Hinoki application. Registering routes builds the native router; nothing connects to anything, so factories returning Hinoki are safe to import and call. The instance is itself an ASGI callable ( granian --interface asgi module:app ); the first call freezes the declarations. on_startup and on_shutdown list functions taking the worker's ModuleContext ( async def or def ). Startup hooks run once per worker after the modules have started; shutdown hooks run before they are closed, and only after a startup that completed. startup_url optionally reserves a public GET/HEAD endpoint that returns {"status": "ok"} after worker startup. It reports startup completion, not application, database, or event-loop health. _startup_url instance-attribute ¶ _startup_url = check_startup_url ( startup_url ) _timezone instance-attribute ¶ Binding , ... ] modules property ¶ modules : tuple [ Module , ... ] commands property ¶ commands : tuple [ Command , ... ] The app's explicitly registered management commands. on_startup property ¶ module_of ¶ module_of ( module : Module | type [ Module ]) -> Module An instance as given, or a class built from this app's settings. include ¶ include ( * items : object ) -> None Register decorated functions, API subclasses and objects that expose an api() (the admin). Lists and tuples of those are flattened, so a feature package can export one routes list, and Mount(prefix, ...) places a feature under a path chosen here. All-or-nothing per call: on conflict the application is unchanged. _collect_routes ¶ _collect_routes ( items : tuple [ object , ... ], ) -> tuple [ list [ Route ], list [ RouteGroup ]] _stage_router ¶ _stage_router ( pending : list [ Route ]) -> Router routes_of staticmethod ¶ routes_of ( item : object ) -> list [ Route ] The routes an item declares: an API class, a decorated function, or an object exposing api() (the admin). inherited_parsers ¶ inherited_parsers ( route : Route ) -> tuple [ Parser , ... ] Parsers for an action without its own: the application's, unless an upload action needs multipart and they do not include it. with_defaults ¶ with_defaults ( route : Route ) -> Route The route with this application's default parsers/renderers filled in where the action did not choose its own. install ¶ install ( * modules : Module ) -> None Install modules and include their APIs. Hinoki(include=[ health, Mount("/tasks", tasks.routes), Mount("/billing", billing.routes), ]) The feature keeps paths relative to itself ( / and /{id} ) and the root declaration shows where each feature lives. Items are anything include accepts, including lists and other mounts; prefixes join outside in. prefix instance-attribute ¶ prefix = prefix items instance-attribute ¶ items = items __init__ ¶ __init__ ( prefix : str , * items : object ) -> None hinoki.routing.Route dataclass ¶ Declared contract of one action, before it is bound to an application. method instance-attribute ¶ method : str path instance-attribute ¶ path : str handler instance-attribute ¶ handler : Callable [ ... , object ] status instance-attribute ¶ status : int access instance-attribute ¶ access : Access | None transaction instance-attribute ¶ transaction : bool owner class-attribute instance-attribute ¶ owner : type | None = None pagination class-attribute instance-attribute ¶ pagination : PageNumberPagination | None = None replaces class-attribute instance-attribute ¶ replaces : str = '' parsers class-attribute instance-attribute ¶ parsers : tuple [ Parser , ... ] = DEFAULT_PARSERS renderers class-attribute instance-attribute ¶ renderers : tuple [ Renderer , ... ] = DEFAULT_RENDERERS errors class-attribute instance-attribute ¶ errors : tuple [ type [ APIError ], ... ] = () is_async property ¶ is_async : bool name property ¶ name : str __init__ ¶ __init__ ( method : str , path : str , handler : Callable [ ... , object ], status : int , access : Access | None , transaction : bool , owner : type | None = None , pagination : PageNumberPagination | None = None , replaces : str = "" , parsers : tuple [ Parser , ... ] = DEFAULT_PARSERS , renderers : tuple [ Renderer , ... ] = DEFAULT_RENDERERS , errors : tuple [ type [ APIError ], ... ] = (), ) -> None For model-backed route generation, see Generate CRUD routes and the CRUD API reference . docs.text: Tutorial: a task tracker, layer by layer ¶ Chapters 1–6 follow the Tracker in examples/tracker : members keep their own tasks, complete them, and a few rules stop it from rotting. Chapter 7 uses standalone validation examples. Chapter 8 starts a fresh project with the scaffold and app commands. Step You add You learn 1. Models tables, an index, a default order how a model and a migration relate 2. Schemas what clients send and see strict validation, schemas derived from models 3. Operations the business rules row permission inside the statement 4. Endpoints the HTTP layer access, transactions, declared errors 5. Rules checks that keep the layers apart hinoki check , import boundaries 6. Run and test it settings, serving, tests dev , serve , the test client 7. Validate input Schema config, normalization/checks and Model write validators ignored external metadata, canonical fields, field-level and cross-field errors 8. Projects and apps hinoki new , modular apps and migration commands generated project manifest, automatic migration names and local SQLite setup The Tracker chapters build and run an existing, versioned example. The validation chapter uses focused examples; the final chapter separately walks through creating a project and app, where Hinoki writes the manifest and discovers migrations automatically. The shape you end with: api.py HTTP: shapes, status codes, access, transactions ↓ operations.py business rules, plain async functions, no HTTP types ↓ models.py tables and relations Prerequisites: install from a checkout. A disposable PostgreSQL configured as HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL is needed to run the database-backed Tracker tests in chapters 1–6. The standalone validation examples in chapter 7 need no database; chapter 8 uses local SQLite by default.

docs.text: 1. Models ¶ A model is a table. Hinoki's models are active records over a Rust query compiler: no lazy loading, no surprises. from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , OnDelete , field , foreign_key , indexed , ordered_by from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Member ( Model , table = "tracker_members" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) name : str = field ( max_length = 80 ) token : str = field ( unique = True ) @indexed ( "owner_id" , "created_at" ) @ordered_by ( "-created_at" , "-id" ) class Task ( Model , table = "tracker_tasks" , label = "Task" , plural = "Tasks" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) owner_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Member , on_delete = OnDelete . RESTRICT , related_name = "tasks" ) title : str = field ( max_length = 120 ) done : bool = False created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) completed_at : datetime | None = None The explicit tracker_members and tracker_tasks names above are pinned to the example's checked-in migration history. New models can omit table= : from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field class Invoice ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) reference : str That declaration derives the table invoices , the singular display name Invoice and the plural Invoices . label= and plural= override the display names; set table= explicitly for irregular/localized names and to keep a physical table stable when a Python class is renamed. The fallback pluralizer is deterministic and English-oriented, so use explicit names for irregular nouns. @indexed and @ordered_by are decorators that state facts about the model below them ( model options ). The default order applies to every query that does not call order_by . foreign_key(Member, ...) is a column holding the owner's id; the relation ( task.owner ) is never fetched by accident. The migration ¶ The Tracker example already includes the migrations for this model and its index. Inspect the checked-in SQL and apply it to a disposable database: cd examples uv run --project .. hinoki migrations status uv run --project .. hinoki migrations sql --app tracker 0001 -initial uv run --project .. hinoki migrations sql --app tracker 0002 -indexes uv run --project .. hinoki migrations apply --app tracker CREATE TABLE "tracker_tasks" ( ... ); CREATE INDEX "ix_tracker_tasks_owner_id_created_at" ON "tracker_tasks" ( "owner_id" , "created_at" ); The repository's examples/hinoki.toml registers Tracker alongside Notes and Blog, each with a separate model module and migration package. When you change a model, hinoki migrations plan --app tracker compares declarations with the recorded state and writes the next migration; the number and slug are derived automatically, and --name can override the slug. Review the SQL before applying it; migrations never run at app startup. Destructive changes are flagged and need --allow-destructive . Chapter 8 creates a new manifest-based project with hinoki new and adds apps with hinoki app create . Next: 2. Schemas .

docs.text: 2. Schemas ¶ A model describes a table; a Schema describes what crosses the API. A column reaches a client only when a schema names it. from typing import Annotated from tracker.models import Task from hinoki import Field , Schema , derive class TaskIn ( Schema ): """What a client may set. The owner is the caller, never a field.""" title : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 120 )] @derive ( exclude = ( "owner_id" ,)) class TaskOut ( Schema , model = Task ): """Every column of a task except its owner (derived from the model).""" TaskIn is strict: no coercion, no unknown keys, every problem reported with its path. Validation runs in Rust before your code does. TaskOut takes the columns of Task : types and limits come from the model, and exclude=("owner_id",) keeps owner_id out. Relations are never derived; you name them on purpose. Because the owner is not a field of TaskIn , a client cannot choose it. If it were, Task.acreate(data, owner_id=me) would still win (server values beat the client's), and a schema can never carry the primary key. When one property can contain more than one shape, put an explicit tagged union inside a wrapper Schema. Every variant has a required tag with a distinct one_of value and the same wire alias: from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema class Cat ( Schema ): kind : Annotated [ str , Field ( alias = "type" , one_of = ( "cat" ,))] name : str class Dog ( Schema ): kind : Annotated [ str , Field ( alias = "type" , one_of = ( "dog" ,))] walks : int Pet = Annotated [ Cat | Dog , Field ( discriminator = "kind" )] class PetRequest ( Schema ): pet : Pet PetRequest.validate({"pet": {"type": "cat", "name": "Mugi"}}) builds a Cat ; the same tag also produces an OpenAPI oneOf with a discriminator mapping. See discriminated unions for request errors, lists, nullable fields and limits. More: Schemas , model-derived schemas . Next: 3. Operations . Validation patterns continue in 7. Validate input .

docs.text: 3. Operations ¶ The rules of the application live in plain async functions that take the acting member's id and plain values. No Request , no HTTP types: an action, a CLI, a test or an admin hook can all call them. This excerpt follows examples/tracker/operations.py . from uuid import UUID from tracker.errors import TaskAlreadyDone from tracker.models import Task from tracker.schemas import TaskIn from hinoki.orm import QuerySet from hinoki.pagination import Page , PageParams from hinoki.utils import utc_now def mine ( owner_id : UUID ) -> QuerySet [ Task ]: return Task . filter ( owner_id = owner_id ) async def list_tasks ( owner_id : UUID , page : PageParams ) -> Page [ Task ]: return await mine ( owner_id ) . apaginate ( page ) # Task is @ordered_by newest first async def create_task ( owner_id : UUID , data : TaskIn ) -> Task : return await Task . acreate ( data , owner_id = owner_id ) # the server's value wins async def complete_task ( owner_id : UUID , task_id : UUID ) -> Task : """Mark an own open task done in one statement.""" changed = await Task . aupdate_where ( { "id" : task_id , "owner_id" : owner_id , "done" : False }, { "done" : True , "completed_at" : utc_now ()}, ) if changed : return changed [ 0 ] await mine ( owner_id ) . filter ( id = task_id ) . aget () # missing or not yours: 404 raise TaskAlreadyDone () The important line is the WHERE : the owner is part of the statement. There is no "read the row, check the owner, then update" gap, and another member's task looks exactly like a missing one (404), so nothing leaks. The business failures are named after the rule they report: from hinoki import errors class TaskAlreadyDone ( errors . Conflict ): code = "task_already_done" message = "The task is already done." Each error carries its HTTP status (409 here) and a stable code. Next: 4. Endpoints .

docs.text: 4. Endpoints ¶ The HTTP layer maps requests to operations and operations to responses. It contains no business rule and no SQL. from uuid import UUID from tracker import operations from tracker.errors import DoneTasksAreKept , TaskAlreadyDone from tracker.models import Member , Task from tracker.schemas import TaskIn , TaskOut from tracker.security import member_only from hinoki import Caller , Hinoki , RouteGroup , errors , http from hinoki.pagination import Page , PageNumberPagination , PageParams def out ( task : Task ) -> TaskOut : return TaskOut . from_model ( task ) tasks = RouteGroup ( "/tasks" , access = member_only , atomic = True ) # stated once @tasks . get ( "/" , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_tasks ( page : PageParams , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> Page [ TaskOut ]: """Your tasks, newest first.""" return ( await operations . list_tasks ( caller . user . id , page )) . map ( out ) @tasks . post ( "/" , status = 201 ) async def create_task ( data : TaskIn , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> TaskOut : return out ( await operations . create_task ( caller . user . id , data )) @tasks . post ( "/ {task_id} /complete" , errors = ( errors . NotFound , TaskAlreadyDone )) async def complete_task ( task_id : UUID , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> TaskOut : return out ( await operations . complete_task ( caller . user . id , task_id )) @tasks . delete ( "/ {task_id} " , status = 204 , errors = ( errors . NotFound , DoneTasksAreKept )) async def delete_task ( task_id : UUID , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> None : await operations . delete_task ( caller . user . id , task_id ) app = Hinoki ( include = [ tasks ]) Access is a reusable policy ( member_only ) naming the provider that authenticates (a bearer token here) and the permissions required. Public is the default, so protect on purpose; a rule below enforces it. atomic=True wraps writes in a transaction that commits after the response is encoded and rolls back before an error becomes HTTP. errors=(...) declares what an action may raise. The status and code come from each error class; OpenAPI, the MCP tool description and the strict test client all use it. caller: Caller[Member] is who is asking, typed: caller.user is your Member . The request object is optional: declare request: Request first only when you need headers, cookies or the raw body. For bounded file uploads, declare UploadedFile or list[UploadedFile] parameters and Hinoki selects MultiPartParser for that action. The endpoint guide covers optional files, limits and OpenAPI output. Next: 5. Rules .
docs.title: 4. Endpoints

docs.text: The HTTP layer maps requests to operations and operations to responses. It contains no business rule and no SQL. from uuid import UUID from tracker import operations from tracker.errors import DoneTasksAreKept , TaskAlreadyDone from tracker.models import Member , Task from tracker.schemas import TaskIn , TaskOut from tracker.security import member_only from hinoki import Caller , Hinoki , RouteGroup , errors , http from hinoki.pagination import Page , PageNumberPagination , PageParams def out ( task : Task ) -> TaskOut : return TaskOut . from_model ( task ) tasks = RouteGroup ( "/tasks" , access = member_only , atomic = True ) # stated once @tasks . get ( "/" , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_tasks ( page : PageParams , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> Page [ TaskOut ]: """Your tasks, newest first.""" return ( await operations . list_tasks ( caller . user . id , page )) . map ( out ) @tasks . post ( "/" , status = 201 ) async def create_task ( data : TaskIn , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> TaskOut : return out ( await operations . create_task ( caller . user . id , data )) @tasks . post ( "/ {task_id} /complete" , errors = ( errors . NotFound , TaskAlreadyDone )) async def complete_task ( task_id : UUID , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> TaskOut : return out ( await operations . complete_task ( caller . user . id , task_id )) @tasks . delete ( "/ {task_id} " , status = 204 , errors = ( errors . NotFound , DoneTasksAreKept )) async def delete_task ( task_id : UUID , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> None : await operations . delete_task ( caller . user . id , task_id ) app = Hinoki ( include = [ tasks ]) Access is a reusable policy ( member_only ) naming the provider that authenticates (a bearer token here) and the permissions required. Public is the default, so protect on purpose; a rule below enforces it. atomic=True wraps writes in a transaction that commits after the response is encoded and rolls back before an error becomes HTTP. errors=(...) declares what an action may raise. The status and code come from each error class; OpenAPI, the MCP tool description and the strict test client all use it. caller: Caller[Member] is who is asking, typed: caller.user is your Member . The request object is optional: declare request: Request first only when you need headers, cookies or the raw body. For bounded file uploads, declare UploadedFile or list[UploadedFile] parameters and Hinoki selects MultiPartParser for that action. The endpoint guide covers optional files, limits and OpenAPI output. Next: 5. Rules .

docs.text: 5. Rules ¶ Rules turn promises into failures with a stable id and a location. from hinoki import Actions , Imports , Schemas , Transactions from hinoki.rules import RuleSet tracker_rules = RuleSet ( Actions . require_access ( match = "tracker.*" , except_ = [ "tracker.api.health" ]), Actions . forbid_model_responses ( match = "tracker.*" ), Transactions . require_atomic ( except_ = [ "hinoki.mcpapp.*" ]), Schemas . forbid_exposure ( "token" ), # api -> operations -> models, never the other way Imports . forbid ( source = "tracker.models" , target = "tracker.operations" ), Imports . forbid ( source = "tracker.models" , target = "tracker.api" ), Imports . forbid ( source = "tracker.operations" , target = "tracker.api" ), ) Run them from the command line or let the app enforce them when it starts ( Hinoki(rules=tracker_rules) ): cd examples uv run --project .. hinoki check tracker.app:create_app \ --rules tracker.rules:tracker_rules --package tracker 7 rule(s): 0 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived Break one on purpose (remove access= from an action) and the failure names the rule and the line: tests/projects/rulesapp.py:7: HNK-ACC-001 [violated] GET /health (health) declares no access policy tests/projects/rulesapp.py:12: HNK-TXN-001 [violated] POST /items (create) does not declare transaction=True An exception is a waiver in hinoki-rules.toml with a reason, an owner and a bounded target. The owner writes waivers; tools and agents read them but never edit them to pass a check. See Rules . Next: 6. Run and test it .

docs.text: 6. Run and test it ¶ Settings and serving ¶ The Tracker example's factory assembles the HTTP routes, rules and MCP tool; the database field of its settings opens the database. It uses typed TrackerSettings ; local SQLite is the default and TRACKER_DATABASE__URL selects another database. from tracker import api from tracker.rules import tracker_rules from tracker.security import member_only from tracker.settings import TrackerSettings from hinoki import Hinoki from hinoki.mcpapp import expose_as_mcp def create_app ( database_url : str | None = None ) -> Hinoki : overrides = ( { "database" : { "url" : database_url }} if database_url is not None else {} ) app_settings = TrackerSettings . load ( overrides = overrides ) app = Hinoki ( settings = app_settings , title = "Tracker" , openapi_url = "/openapi.json" , docs_url = "/docs" , redoc_url = "/redoc" , rules = tracker_rules , ) app . include ( api . health , api . tasks ) app . include ( * expose_as_mcp ( app , tools = [ f " { api . __name__ } .list_tasks" ], access = member_only ) ) return app # Omit these variables to use .hinoki/local.sqlite3. export TRACKER_DATABASE__URL = 'postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/tracker' export HINOKI_DATABASE_URL = " $TRACKER_DATABASE__URL " uv run --project .. hinoki migrations status uv run --project .. hinoki migrations sql --app tracker 0001 -initial uv run --project .. hinoki migrations sql --app tracker 0002 -indexes uv run --project .. hinoki migrations apply --app tracker uv run --project .. hinoki dev tracker.app:create_app The Tracker example already includes its initial and index migrations, so this command sequence inspects and applies those checked-in files. After changing a model, generate a new migration with hinoki migrations plan --app tracker and review its SQL before applying it to a disposable database; do not expect the planner to recreate the existing initial migration. dev reloads on change; serve runs without reload and takes host, port and workers from the server settings ( serving ). Open /docs or /redoc . Test it ¶ Operations need no HTTP at all, so test them directly; then drive the whole stack with the in-process client. The repository test fixture applies the migrations and creates the Ann and Ben members used by the bearer tokens below: tests/trackertest.py . import os import pytest from tracker.app import create_app from tracker.models import Member from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient URL = os . environ . get ( "HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL" ) needs_database = pytest . mark . skipif ( URL is None , reason = "no database" ) @needs_database async def test_tracker_api ( members : tuple [ Member , Member ]) -> None : assert URL is not None async with ASGIClient ( create_app ( URL ), strict_errors = True ) as client : made = await client . post ( "/tasks" , json = { "title" : "x" }, token = "ann-token" ) path = f "/tasks/ { made . body [ 'id' ] } " assert ( await client . post ( f " { path } /complete" , token = "ben-token" )) . status == 404 assert ( await client . post ( f " { path } /complete" , token = "ann-token" )) . status == 200 assert ( await client . post ( f " { path } /complete" , token = "ann-token" )) . status == 409 This is an excerpt of test_every_business_error_of_the_tracker_is_declared ; its members fixture creates the two users and provides a fresh migrated database. Run the repository test with a disposable PostgreSQL URL: HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL = " $TRACKER_DATABASE__URL " uv run pytest tests/trackertest.py strict_errors=True fails the test if an action answers an error it did not declare. For tests without async , use SyncClient . Where next ¶ Patterns and best practices , the application MCP (the tracker already exposes list_tasks to MCP clients), and development tools .

docs.text: 7. Validate input ¶ Schema validation combines built-in type and value constraints with optional synchronous normalization and rejection checks. Constraints reject invalid input first; normalizers canonicalize valid strings; checks can then reject values based on one field or compare several fields. All of this happens before a validated schema reaches an operation. from typing import Annotated from hinoki import ( Field , Invalid , Schema , errors , field_check , field_normalize , object_check , ) class Registration ( Schema ): username : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 3 , max_length = 32 , pattern = r "[a-z0-9_]+" ), ] email : Annotated [ str , Field ( format = "email" )] password : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 12 )] confirmation : str @field_normalize ( "email" ) def lowercase_email ( self , value : str ) -> str : return value . lower () @field_check ( "password" ) def reject_common_password ( self , value : str ) -> None : if value . lower () in { "password12345" , "qwerty123456" }: raise Invalid ( "common_password" , "choose a less common password" ) @object_check def passwords_match ( self ) -> None : if self . password != self . confirmation : raise Invalid ( "password_mismatch" , "passwords do not match" , path = "confirmation" , ) valid = Registration . validate ( { "username" : "mari_23" , "email" : "mari@example.test" , "password" : "correct-horse-battery" , "confirmation" : "correct-horse-battery" , } ) assert valid . username == "mari_23" assert valid . email == "mari@example.test" try : Registration . validate ( { "username" : "mari_23" , "email" : "mari@example.test" , "password" : "password12345" , "confirmation" : "different-password" , } ) except errors . ValidationError as error : for detail in error . details : print ( detail . path , detail . code , detail . message ) The invalid call reports a common_password error on password and a password_mismatch error on confirmation . min_length , max_length and pattern are built-in field constraints. format="email" is a ready-made pattern; url , slug and hex_color are also available. Numeric fields can use gt , ge , lt and le , and one_of restricts a value to a fixed set. An invalid built-in constraint prevents normalizers and custom checks from running. @field_normalize("email") receives a structurally valid string and must return a str . Its result is checked against the same constraints before it is applied. Normalization also runs when you manually construct a Schema(...) or call from_model(...) ; it does not run twice when an existing nested Schema is passed to a new parent. Inputs that fail the original constraints cannot be rescued by normalization. @field_check("password") receives the final value. @object_check receives the complete schema and can compare final fields. Raise Invalid(code, message) to report a failure; checks must return None and do not transform the value. Normalizers and checks are synchronous, have no I/O, and run the same way before both sync and async handlers. A check that needs current database state, such as whether an email is already registered, belongs in an operation where it can be made race-safe. Ignore unknown fields from external payloads ¶ Unknown fields are rejected by default. For an external payload that adds unrelated metadata, opt in to discarding unknown string keys on that Schema: from hinoki import Schema , SchemaConfig , SchemaExtra class Webhook ( Schema , config = SchemaConfig ( extra = SchemaExtra . IGNORE )): event_id : str revision : int event = Webhook . validate ( { "event_id" : "evt-1" , "revision" : 2 , "provider_data" : { "trace" : "abc" }} ) assert event . dump () == { "event_id" : "evt-1" , "revision" : 2 } Known fields still require the declared types and constraints, and required fields remain required. Ignored keys are discarded; they are never attached to the object or returned by dump() . The policy affects Schema.validate(...) and request bodies before sync or async handlers. Constructor keywords and explicit from_model(..., **extra) overrides remain strict. Nested Schemas each use their own policy. Aliases also remain canonical: a Python field name does not substitute for its alias, and supplying both spellings is still an error. Validate values at Model write boundaries ¶ Use the same built-in constraints on Model fields when data can be written outside an HTTP Schema, such as from a management command or the admin. Custom callbacks are synchronous and raise ValueError to refuse a value: from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import Field from hinoki.orm import Model , field def normalized ( value : str ) -> None : if value != value . strip (): raise ValueError ( "surrounding whitespace is not allowed" ) class Product ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) sku : str = field ( max_length = 32 , constraints = Field ( min_length = 3 , pattern = r "[A-Z0-9-]+" ), ) name : str = field ( max_length = 120 , validators = ( normalized ,)) price : float = field ( constraints = Field ( gt = 0 )) The checks run before await Product.acreate(...) , await product.asave() and await Product.filter(...).aupdate(...) , as well as their synchronous counterparts. Construction and assignment stay ordinary dataclass operations; existing rows are not revalidated when read. Invalid writes raise ModelValidationError with structured details , and no SQL is issued for that write. Validators must not perform I/O or change values. Keep request parsing in a Schema, and put rules that depend on other rows or permissions in an operation. See Model field constraints and validators . More: Schema constraints and checks , schemas derived from models .

docs.text: 8. Create a project and modular app ¶ The Tracker steps above use an existing example with checked-in migrations. For a new project, hinoki new creates the hinoki.toml manifest and registers its first app. Each additional app owns its model and migration modules. uv run --locked hinoki new notes cd notes uv sync The generated manifest registers notes.models and notes.migrations . The scaffold also includes a health endpoint, typed settings, rules, a test, and agent instructions. Hinoki does not scan installed packages for apps. Add an independently organized app: uv run hinoki app create billing This creates notes/apps/billing/models.py and notes/apps/billing/migrations/ , then adds the module paths to hinoki.toml . If billing references a model from another app, add that app to billing's requires list so Hinoki can validate and order migrations. Add a model to the generated notes/apps/billing/models.py (or the app's declared models module): from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field class Invoice ( Model ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) reference : str = field ( max_length = 40 , unique = True ) Plan its migration from the project root. The app name is required when more than one app is registered: uv run hinoki migrations plan --app billing --dry-run uv run hinoki migrations plan --app billing uv run hinoki migrations status uv run hinoki migrations sql --app billing 0001 -create-table-invoices uv run hinoki migrations apply Hinoki assigns the next migration number and derives a stable slug from the first schema change, such as create-table-invoices . You can optionally override just the slug with --name add-invoice-table . Review the generated SQL and state file before applying it. With no database URL configured, status and apply initialize the local SQLite database at .hinoki/local.sqlite3 . Set HINOKI_DATABASE_URL to target another supported backend. Migrations are explicit commands and never run automatically when the app starts. See project migrations for dependency ordering, destructive changes and existing projects that still use explicit --models and --dir targets.
